Contributed to provide a translation for a work that previously had no English translation in the corpus.

div.p: As I ponder this often, brother Quintus, and recall in memory the men of old, those seem to me to have been singularly blessed who, in the best days of the commonwealth, while they flourished in public honours and in the glory of their achievements, were able to hold to such a course of life that they could either engage in public business without danger or enjoy their leisure with dignity. And there was a time when I too thought it would be reasonable, and almost universally conceded, that I should at last begin to rest and to recall my mind to those noble studies dear to us both, once the endless toil of public affairs and the demands of ambition had come to a halt with the completion of my career of office and with the decline of my years as well.

When we were boys, brother Quintus—if you remember—there was a strong belief that Lucius Crassus had attained no more learning than that first boyish instruction could give him, and that Marcus Antonius was altogether without and ignorant of all culture; and there were many who, although they did not think the matter stood thus, yet, that they might the more easily deter us, fired as we were with the zeal of learning, from study, gladly proclaimed what I have said about those orators—so that, if men without education had attained the highest prudence and an incredible eloquence, all our labour might seem vain, and the zeal of our father, an excellent and most prudent man, in educating us, might seem foolish.

As I set myself, brother Quintus, to record and to consign to this third book the conversation which Crassus held after the discourse of Antonius, a bitter recollection renewed in my mind its old care and distress. For that genius worthy of immortality, that humanity, that excellence of Lucius Crassus was suddenly extinguished by death scarcely ten days after the day contained in this book and the one before.

But this hope of my plans and reflections was disappointed both by the grievous troubles of the times common to all and by the various misfortunes of my own. For in that very place which seemed likely to be most full of quiet and tranquillity, there arose the greatest masses of vexations and the most turbulent storms; nor, for all our longing and yearning, was the fruit of leisure granted us, to cultivate among ourselves and to revive those arts to which we have been devoted from boyhood.

These men we then, as boys, used to refute by domestic witnesses—our father, and our kinsman Gaius Aculeo, and our uncle Lucius Cicero; for about Crassus our father, and Aculeo (with whom our maternal aunt was married, and whom Crassus loved most of all men), and our uncle, who had gone out with Antonius into Cilicia and had returned together with him, often told us many things about his zeal and learning; and since we were learning, together with our cousins, the sons of Aculeo, both those things which were approved by Crassus, and were being instructed by those teachers whom he employed, we also often perceived, when we were at his house—a thing which even as boys we could feel—that he both spoke Greek so well that he seemed to know no other language, and set before our teachers, in his questioning, and himself handled in all his conversation, such matters that nothing seemed new to him, nothing unheard of.

For when he had returned to Rome on the last day of the theatrical games, deeply stirred by that speech which was reported to have been delivered in the assembly by Philippus—who, it was agreed, had said that he must look for another counsel, since with that senate he could not conduct the public affairs—on the morning of the Ides of September both he and a crowded senate, summoned by Drusus, came into the senate-house; and there, when Drusus had complained much about Philippus, Crassus brought before the senate that very matter, namely that the consul had so heavily inveighed against that order in the assembly.

For in my early years I fell upon the very overthrow of the old order, and in my consulship I came into the midst of every conflict and crisis, and all this time since my consulship I have set myself against those waves which, having through my efforts been driven back from the general ruin, recoiled upon me alone. Yet even amid these harsh circumstances and these straits of time I shall obey our studies, and whatever leisure the malice of my enemies, the causes of my friends, or the commonwealth shall allow me, I shall devote above all to writing. As for you, brother, I shall fail neither your encouragement nor your request; for no one can prevail with me more than you, either by authority or by goodwill.

But about Antonius, although we had often heard from our most cultivated uncle in what manner he had given himself, whether at Athens or at Rhodes, to the conversations of the most learned men, yet I myself, as a youth, so far as the modesty of my entering years allowed, often inquired many things of him. What I write will assuredly not be new to you; for even then you used to hear from me that he had seemed to me, from many and various conversations, to be in no matter—at least in those arts of which I could form some judgement—unskilled or ignorant.

Here, as I have often seen agreed among the wisest of men, although it had nearly always befallen Crassus, whenever he had spoken with more than ordinary care, that he was thought never to have spoken better, yet by the common consent of all it was then so judged: that, while all others had always been surpassed by Crassus, on that day Crassus had been surpassed even by himself. For he lamented the misfortune and bereavement of the senate, whose patrimony of dignity was being plundered by the consul—who ought to be as it were a good parent or a faithful guardian—as though by some wicked brigand; nor indeed was it any wonder, if, having ruined the commonwealth by his own counsels, he now rejected the counsel of the senate from the commonwealth.

And so I must recall to memory a certain old recollection, not indeed fully worked out, but, as I think, suited to what you require, that you may learn what the most eloquent and most distinguished men have thought concerning the whole theory of speaking.

But this was the case with each of them: that Crassus did not so much wish to be thought not to have learned, as to despise those things, and to set the prudence of our own countrymen, in every kind, above the Greeks; while Antonius thought his speech would be more acceptable to this people if he were thought never to have learned at all; and so each thought he would be the weightier, if the one seemed to despise the Greeks, the other not even to know them.

Here, when he had applied, as it were, certain firebrands of words to a man both vehement and eloquent and pre-eminently bold in resisting, Philippus could not bear it, but blazed up violently, and, having taken pledges, set about to coerce Crassus. And in that very place many things were reported to have been said by Crassus with a more than human inspiration, when he denied that the man was a consul to him, to whom he himself was not a senator. 'Or do you,' he said, 'when you have reckoned the whole authority of the entire order as a pledge and have cut it to pieces in the sight of the Roman people, suppose that I am to be terrified by these pledges of yours? It is not those things you must cut down, if you wish to coerce Lucius Crassus: this tongue of mine must be cut out; and even when it is torn away, by my very breath my liberty shall rebuke your lust.'

For you wish—as you have often told me—since those things which fell from us as boys or mere youths, sketched and rough, out of our little notebooks, are scarcely worthy of this age of mine and of the experience I have gained from so many and so great cases such as I have described, that something more polished and more finished on these same subjects should be set forth by me. And you sometimes disagree with me on this matter in our discussions, because I hold that eloquence is bound up with the accomplishments of the most learned men, while you think it should be kept apart from the refinements of learning and placed in a certain kind of natural talent and practice. And indeed, as I have often considered the greatest men, those endowed with the highest gifts, it has seemed to me worth asking why it is that more men have been remarkable in all other pursuits than in speaking. For wherever you turn your mind and thought, you will see very many men outstanding in every kind of accomplishment, and that not in the lesser, but in well-nigh the greatest arts.

What their purpose was is nothing at all to the present time; but this belongs to the design of the present writing and occasion—that no one has ever been able to flourish and excel in eloquence, not only without the doctrine of speaking, but not even without all wisdom. For the other arts, generally, each maintains itself by itself; but to speak well, which is to speak knowingly and skilfully and elegantly, has no defined region within whose boundaries it is confined: all things whatsoever that can fall into the discussion of men must be spoken of well by him who professes that he can do this, or the name of eloquence must be abandoned.

It was agreed that very many things were then said by him with the most vehement straining of mind, of genius, of strength; and that the resolution—which the crowded senate followed—was uttered by him in words most elaborate and most weighty: that the Roman people might be satisfied that the senate had never failed the commonwealth either in counsel or in fidelity; and that he himself, as appears in the recorded decrees, was present at the drawing up of it.
For who is there who, if he should choose to measure the renown of famous men by the usefulness or the greatness of their deeds, would not set the general above the orator?

Wherefore for my part I confess that, both in our own state and in Greece itself, which always reckoned these things highest, there have been many of excellent talents and of great glory in speaking without the highest knowledge of all things; but that such an eloquence should arise as was in Crassus and Antonius, without a knowledge of all the things that pertained to so great a prudence, and to so great an abundance of speaking as was in them—this, I affirm, could not have been.

That was, as it were, the swan-song, the voice and oration of a divine man; and after his death we used to come into the senate-house as though expecting it, that we might gaze upon that very spot in which he had taken his last stand: for we heard that then, as he was speaking, his side had pained him and that much sweat had followed; from which, when he had shuddered with cold, he returned home with a fever, and on the seventh day was consumed by the pain in his side.
And yet who can doubt that, from this one commonwealth, we could produce almost countless leaders of war of the highest distinction, but in speaking scarcely a few of the first rank?

For this reason I did the more gladly commit to writing that conversation which they once held among themselves about these matters; both that that opinion which had always existed might be removed—that the one was not very learned, the other plainly unlearned; and that I might preserve in writing those things which I judged to have been said divinely by the greatest orators about eloquence, if in any way I could attain and embrace them; and, by Hercules, also that I might rescue their praise, now nearly fading, so far as I could, from the oblivion and the silence of men.

O the deceiving hope of men, the fragile fortune, and our vain strivings, which are often broken and fall to ruin in mid-course, or are overwhelmed in their very race before they can catch sight of the harbour! For so long as the life of Crassus was distracted by the labour of seeking office, so long he flourished more by his private services and the praise of his genius than by the fruit of high station or the dignity of public office; but that year which, with the consent of all, was first opening to him, now that he had finished the course of honours, the way to the highest authority—that year, by his death, overthrew all his hope and all the designs of his life.

Indeed, of those who by counsel and wisdom could govern and steer the commonwealth, there have been many in our own day, more in our fathers' memory, and still more among our ancestors; whereas of good orators there were none for a very long time, and scarcely one tolerable one was to be found in each generation. And lest anyone should suppose that this theory of speaking ought rather to be compared with other pursuits that are concerned with abstruse arts and a certain variety of learning, than with the renown of a general or the prudence of a good senator, let him turn his attention to those very kinds of arts and look around to see who have flourished in them and how many they are; thus he will most easily judge how small the number of orators is and always has been.

For if they could have been known from their own writings, perhaps I should have thought this less to be laboured at by me; but since the one had left not much that survived, and that itself written as a young man, and the other almost nothing written, I thought this was owed by me to the great talents of these men—that, while we still hold a living memory of them, I should, if I could, render it immortal.

This was grievous to his own people, bitter to his country, heavy to all good men; yet such disasters afterwards befell the commonwealth that to me it seems that life was not snatched from Lucius Crassus by the immortal gods, but rather that death was given to him as a gift. He did not see Italy ablaze with war, nor the senate burning with hatred, nor the leading men of the state arraigned for unspeakable crime, nor the mourning of his daughter, nor the exile of his son-in-law, nor the most bitter flight of Gaius Marius, nor, after Marius' return, that most cruel slaughter of all, nor, in short, that state disfigured in every kind of evil, in which he himself, when it was most flourishing, had far excelled all men.

For you are not unaware that what the Greeks call philosophy is judged by the most learned men to be the progenitress, as it were, and parent of all the praised arts; and in it it is difficult to count how many men there have been, of how great learning and of how great variety and richness in their studies, men who have toiled not separately upon some single subject, but have embraced everything within their reach, either by the investigation of knowledge or by the method of reasoning.

And I approach this with the greater hope of carrying it through, because I am not writing something about the eloquence of Servius Galba or Gaius Carbo, in which I might invent, if I wished anything, with no one's memory now refuting me; but I publish these things to be known by those who often heard the very men of whom I speak; so that we may commend two supreme men to those who have seen neither of them, with the memory of living and present men—men to whom both those orators were known—as witness.

And since I have touched in thought upon the power and the changefulness of fortune, my discourse shall not wander further afield, but shall be bounded almost by those very men who are contained in this conversation which I have undertaken to relate. For who would not justly call blessed that famous death of Lucius Crassus, which has often been bewailed by many, when he recalls the end of these very men who then spoke with him almost for the last time? For we hold in memory Quintus Catulus, a man pre-eminent in every praise, who, when he was begging not for an unimpaired fortune, but only for exile and flight, was compelled to deprive himself of his own life.

Who does not know in what obscurity of matters, and in how recondite, manifold, and subtle an art those move who are called mathematicians? Yet in this very kind so many men have attained perfection that scarcely anyone seems to have applied himself vigorously to that science without attaining what he wished. Who has given himself wholeheartedly to music, or to that study of letters which those profess who are called grammarians, without grasping by knowledge and understanding the well-nigh boundless range and substance of those arts?

Nor indeed, dearest and best of brothers, do I now pursue you with certain rhetorical books, which you think rustic, in order to instruct you; for what can be either more subtle or more ornate than your own speech? But whether by judgement, as you are wont to say, or whether—as that father of eloquence Isocrates himself wrote of himself—from a certain modesty and a kind of inborn timidity you have shrunk from speaking; or whether, as I myself am wont to jest, you thought one rhetorician enough, not only in one family, but well-nigh in the whole state, yet I do not think that these books will be to you of that kind which could deservedly be mocked because of the meagreness, in the good arts, of those who have disputed about the method of speaking; for nothing, at least to my mind, seems to have been omitted in the conversation of Crassus and Antonius that anyone of the highest talents, the keenest studies, the best learning, the greatest practice might think could have been known and grasped—a thing which you will most easily be able to judge, who wished to gain the prudence and method of speaking through yourself, but the practice through us.

Already on those very Rostra, on which he as consul had most steadfastly defended the commonwealth, and which as censor he had adorned with the spoils of his command, was placed the head of Marcus Antonius, by which the heads of many had been saved; nor indeed far from it lay the head of Gaius Julius, betrayed by the crime of an Etruscan host, together with the head of his brother Lucius Julius—so that he who did not see these things may seem both to have lived together with the commonwealth and to have been extinguished together with it. For he did not see his kinsman, that man of the greatest spirit, Publius Crassus, slain by his own hand, nor the image of Vesta sprinkled with the blood of his colleague the pontifex maximus; and for his grief—such was his disposition toward his country—the death of Gaius Carbo, his most bitter enemy, on that very same day, would have been a wicked thing.

This much, I think, I may truly say: that of all who have engaged in the most liberal studies and disciplines of these arts, the smallest supply has been of outstanding poets and orators; and within this very number, among whom some excellent man arises but very rarely, if you will diligently make the comparison from the abundance both of our own people and of the Greeks, far fewer orators will be found than good poets.

But that we may the more quickly complete this no slight task which we have undertaken, let us, leaving aside our own exhortation, come to the conversation and disputation of those whom we have set before us.

He did not see the horrible and pitiable misfortunes of those very young men who had then devoted themselves to Crassus: of whom Cotta, whom he had left flourishing, was a few days after the death of Crassus driven through hatred from his tribunate, and not many months from that time was cast out of the state; while Sulpicius, who had been in the same flame of hatred, set himself in his tribunate to strip of all dignity those with whom, as a private man, he had lived most closely; and from him, while he was blossoming to the highest glory of eloquence, life was snatched away by the sword, and a penalty for his rashness was exacted not without great evil to the commonwealth.

And this ought to seem the more wonderful, because the studies of the other arts are generally drawn from recondite and hidden springs, whereas all the theory of speaking lies open before us, is occupied with common usage, and dwells in the mouths and conversation of men—so that, while in other arts that excels most which is furthest removed from the understanding and perception of the unlearned, in speaking it is the greatest fault of all to depart from the common manner of discourse and from the practice of common sense.

On the next day, then, after those things had been done, at about the second hour, when Crassus was even then in bed, and Sulpicius was sitting by him, and Antonius was walking up and down with Cotta in the portico, suddenly thither came the old Quintus Catulus with his brother Gaius Julius. When Crassus heard this, he rose in some agitation, and all, wondering, suspected that there was some greater cause of their coming.

But you, Crassus, I judge to have been both adorned and extinguished by a divine counsel, alike in the flower of your life and in the opportune moment of your death; for either, by reason of the virtue and steadfastness of your spirit, you would have had to undergo the cruelty of the civil sword, or, if some fortune had delivered you from the horror of such a death, that same fortune would have compelled you to be a spectator of your country's funerals; and not only would the domination of the wicked have grieved you, but, because of the slaughter of citizens mingled with it, even the victory of the good would have been a sorrow to you.

Nor indeed can it truly be said either that more men devote themselves to this art than to the rest, or that they are moved to master it thoroughly by greater pleasure, or by richer hope, or by more ample rewards. And, to pass over Greece, which always wished to be foremost in eloquence, and that Athens, the discoverer of all learning, in which the supreme power of speaking was both invented and brought to perfection—even in this very city no studies have ever flourished more vigorously than those of eloquence.

When they had greeted one another in the friendliest way, as their intimacy bore, "What of you, pray?" said Crassus; "is there any news?" "Nothing at all," said Catulus; "for you see that it is the games; but—you may think us either silly," he said, "or troublesome—when Caesar came to me yesterday evening at my Tusculan villa from his own Tusculum, he told me that he had met Scaevola going from here, from whom he said he had heard certain wonderful things: that you, whom I have so often, by every means, in attempting to draw out to disputation, could not, had discoursed very much about eloquence with Antonius, and had disputed almost in the manner of the Greeks, as in a school:

To me indeed, brother Quintus, when I consider both the misfortunes of those of whom I spoke before, and the things which we ourselves, through our incredible and singular love for the commonwealth, have undergone and suffered, your judgement often seems true and wise—you who, on account of so many, so great, and so headlong disasters of the most illustrious men and the best citizens, have always called me back from all contention and conflict.

For after the dominion over all nations had been established, and a lasting peace had secured leisure, scarcely any young man eager for glory did not think that he must strive with all his zeal to speak well. And at first, ignorant of all method, since they thought there was no force in exercise and no precept of art, they attained only as much as they could by natural talent and reflection; but afterwards, having heard the Greek orators and become acquainted with their writings, and having employed teachers, our countrymen were inflamed with an incredible zeal for learning.

so my brother prevailed upon me—not myself too much averse from the desire of hearing, but, by Hercules, fearing lest we should intrude troublesomely upon you—to come hither with him; for he said Scaevola told him that a good part of the conversation had been put off to this day. If you think this too eager, you will attribute it to Caesar; if too familiar, to us both; we, at any rate, unless perchance we intrude troublesomely, are delighted to have come."

But since these things can now no longer remain whole for us, and since our highest labours are softened by being compensated with great glory, let us pass on to those consolations which can be not only pleasant to us when our troubles are appeased, but even wholesome while they still cling to us; and let us hand down to memory the remaining and almost the last discourse of Lucius Crassus, and pay him, if by no means equal to his genius, yet according to our zeal a deserved and due gratitude.

They were spurred on by the greatness, the variety, and the multitude of cases of every kind, so that to whatever learning each had attained by his own study there was added frequent practice, which surpassed the precepts of all teachers. And there were set before this study—as there are now too—the greatest rewards, whether for popularity, or for power, or for prestige; and indeed the talents of our countrymen, as we may judge from many things, have far surpassed those of all men of all nations.

Then Crassus said: "For my part, whatever cause had brought you hither, I should rejoice, since I see at my house men most dear and most friendly to me; but yet, to speak truly, I would rather any other had been the cause than that which you mention. For I, to speak as I feel, never pleased myself less than yesterday; and this happened to me more from good-nature than from any other fault of mine, who, while I humour these young men, forgot that I was an old man, and did what I had not done even as a young man—disputed about matters which are contained in some learning. But yet this fell out very opportunely for me, that, my part being now done, you have come to hear Antonius."

For there is none of us who, when he reads the wonderfully written books of Plato, in nearly all of which Socrates is portrayed, does not, although those writings are divine, yet suspect something greater concerning the man of whom they are written; and this same thing we ask, not indeed of you, who grant us everything of the highest, but of the rest who shall take these books into their hands: that they suspect something greater about Lucius Crassus than the measure of what is expressed by us.

For these reasons, who would not rightly wonder that, in all the record of ages, times, and states, so small a number of orators is found? But this thing is something greater than men suppose, and is gathered together from more arts and studies. For what else could one think to be the cause, amid the very great multitude of learners, the very great abundance of teachers, the most outstanding talents of men, the boundless variety of cases, and the most ample rewards set before eloquence, except a certain incredible greatness and difficulty of the thing itself?

Then Caesar said: "For my part, Crassus, I am so desirous of hearing you in that longer and continuous disputation, that, if that be less granted me, I should be content even with this daily conversation of yours; and so I shall try this—that my friend Sulpicius and Cotta may not seem to prevail more with you than I—and I shall assuredly entreat you to impart some of your sweetness to me too, and to Catulus; but if that be less pleasing to you, I shall not press you, nor allow it to happen that, while you fear lest you be silly, you should judge me to be so."

For we, who had not ourselves been present at the conversation, and to whom Gaius Cotta had handed down only the topics and sentiments of this discussion, have attempted to sketch in their conversation that very manner of speaking in which we had recognized each orator; so that if there shall be anyone who, led by the common opinion, thinks that Antonius was more meagre, or Crassus more full, than the way in which each of them has been brought in by us, he will be one of those who either never heard them or cannot judge; for each of them was, as I set forth before, both pre-eminent above all men in zeal and genius and learning, and perfect in his own kind—so that neither was this ornament of speech wanting in Antonius, nor did it overflow in Crassus.

For one must grasp a knowledge of very many matters, without which a fluency of words is empty and laughable; and the speech itself must be shaped not only by the choice but also by the arrangement of words; and all the movements of the mind which Nature has bestowed upon the race of men must be thoroughly understood, because the whole force and method of speaking must be exerted in soothing or in rousing the minds of those who listen. To this must be added a certain charm and wit and a culture worthy of a free man, and quickness and brevity both in reply and in attack, joined with a refined grace and urbanity. Moreover, one must hold the whole of antiquity and the store of precedents, nor should the knowledge of statutes and the civil law be neglected.

Then he said: "By Hercules, Caesar, of all Latin words I have always thought the force of this word the greatest; for he whom we call inept (ineptum) seems to me to have his name derived from this—that he is not fitted (aptus); and this, in the usage of our speech, has a very wide application; for he who either does not see what the occasion demands, or talks too much, or shows himself off, or has no regard for the dignity or convenience of those with whom he is, or, in short, is in any kind either uncouth or excessive, he is said to be inept.

So then, when they had departed before midday and rested a little, Cotta used to say that he himself had especially noticed this: that Crassus had spent all that midday time in the keenest and most intent reflection; and that he, who well knew Crassus' countenance when he was to speak, and the fixed gaze of his eyes in meditation, and had often seen it in the greatest causes, had then, on purpose, while the others were resting, come into that recess in which Crassus, with a couch set down, was reclining; and when he perceived that he was fixed in thought, he at once withdrew; and in that silence nearly two hours were spent. Then, when all had come to Crassus, the day now declining toward the afternoon, 'What is it, Crassus,' said Julius, 'shall we go and take our seats? Though we come to remind you, not to demand.'

For why should I say more about delivery itself? It must be controlled by the movement of the body, by gesture, by the expression of the face, by the modulation and variety of the voice; and how great this alone is in itself, the trifling art and the stage of actors declare; for although in it all labour at the management of countenance, voice, and movement, who does not know how few there are and have been whom we could watch with patience? What shall I say of that treasury of all things, the memory? Unless it be set as guardian over the matters discovered and thought out and over the words, we understand that all things, even though they have been most excellent in the orator, will perish.

With this fault that most learned nation of the Greeks is overflowing; and so, because the Greeks do not see the force of this evil, they have not even imposed a name upon the fault; for though you search through everything, you will not find how the Greeks call a man inept. But of all the kinds of ineptitude, which are countless, I scarcely know whether any is greater than this—as those men are wont, in whatever place, among whatever men it has seemed good, to dispute most subtly about matters either most difficult or not necessary. This we, against our will and protesting, were yesterday compelled by these young men to do."

Then Crassus: 'Do you think me so shameless as to suppose that I can owe you this service any longer, especially this one?' 'Where, then,' said he, 'is that place? Does the midst of the wood please you? For it is the most shady and cool.' 'Indeed,' said Crassus, 'for there is in that place a seat not unsuited to this conversation of ours.' When this same thing had pleased the rest, they went into the wood, and there, with great expectation of hearing, they sat down.

Wherefore let us cease to wonder what is the cause of the scarcity of eloquent men, since eloquence consists of all those things, in each one of which it is an immense labour to succeed; and let us rather exhort our children, and the others whose glory and dignity is dear to us, to embrace in their minds the greatness of the matter, and not to trust that they can attain what they seek by those precepts, teachers, or exercises which all employ, but by certain others.

Then Catulus said: "Not even the Greeks, Crassus, who in their own states were famous and great, just as you are, and as we all wish to be in our commonwealth, were like these Greeks who thrust themselves upon our ears; nor in their leisure did they shun conversations and disputations of this kind.

Then Crassus said: 'Both your authority and friendship, and the obliging temper of Antonius, took from me, in my best of causes, the liberty of refusing; although, in dividing our discussion, when he took for himself the matters which ought to be said by an orator, but left to me to explain in what manner those things ought to be adorned, he separated things which cannot be separated. For since all speech consists of matter and words, neither can the words have a place, if you take away the matter, nor the matter have light, if you remove the words.

And in my judgement no one will be able to be an orator perfect in every kind of praise unless he has acquired a knowledge of all great matters and arts; for the speech ought to flower forth and overflow from the knowledge of things. And unless the matter has been grasped and understood by the orator, this speech has a certain empty and almost childish manner of expression.

And if those seem to you inept who have no regard for time, place, and men—as they ought to seem—does, pray, either this place seem unsuitable, in which this very portico, where we now walk, and the wrestling-ground, and the seats in so many places of the gymnasia, in some way recall the memory of the Greeks' gymnasia and disputations? Or is the time importunate, in such great leisure, which is both rarely given and now given to us at the very moment of our wish? Or are the men averse from this kind of disputation, who are all such that we count life nothing without these studies?"

And to me indeed those men of old, who in their minds embraced something greater, seem to have seen much more than the sharpness of our genius can discern—those who said that all these things, both above and below, are one, and are bound together by one force and one harmony of nature; for there is no kind of thing which can either, torn away from the rest, stand of itself, or which, if the rest were to lack it, could preserve their own force and eternity.

Yet I would not lay so great a burden upon orators, especially our own, amid the great press of business of the city and of life, as to think it permissible for them to be ignorant of nothing—although the very meaning and profession of the orator, of speaking well, seems to undertake and promise this: that upon whatever subject may be set before him, he will speak with elegance and abundance.

"All those things," said Crassus, "I interpret in another way: for first I think that the Greeks themselves, Catulus, invented the wrestling-ground and the seats and the porticoes for the sake of exercise and delight, not of disputation; for the gymnasia were invented many ages before the philosophers began to chatter in them; and at this very time, when the philosophers hold all the gymnasia, yet their hearers would rather hear the discus than the philosopher; and as soon as it sounds, they all leave the philosopher, in the midst of his discourse, disputing about the greatest and weightiest matters, for the sake of the rubbing-down: thus they set the lightest delight before the weightiest usefulness, as they themselves declare.

But if this seems too great a system to be comprehended by the sense or thought of men, there is also that true saying of Plato, certainly not unheard by you, Catulus: that all the teaching of these liberal and humane arts is held together by a single bond of fellowship; for when once the power of that reason has been perceived, by which the causes and the issues of things are known, then a certain wonderful, as it were, consent and concord of all the branches of learning is found.

But because I do not doubt that to most men this seems immense and boundless, and because I see that the Greeks, men abounding not only in talent and learning but also in leisure and zeal, have already made a certain division of the arts, and that single men have not laboured at the whole field, but have set apart from the other branches of discourse that part of speaking which is concerned with the disputes of the courts and of deliberative bodies, and have left this one kind to the orator: I shall not embrace in these books more than what, after careful investigation and much debate, has been assigned to this kind by the well-nigh unanimous consent of the greatest men.

As for the leisure which you mention, I agree; but the fruit of leisure is not the straining of the mind, but its relaxation. Often I heard from my father-in-law, when he said that his father-in-law Laelius was almost always wont to take his country holidays with Scipio, and that they were wont to grow boys again incredibly, when they had flown out from the city into the country as from chains. I do not dare to say it of such men, but yet Scaevola is wont to relate that they used to gather shells and pebbles at Caieta and at Laurentum, and to descend to every relaxation and play of the mind.

But if this too seems to be loftier than that we, prostrate upon the ground, can look up to it, yet certainly that at least, which we have embraced, which we profess, which we have undertaken, we ought to know and to hold. For there is one eloquence—as both I said yesterday and Antonius signified in several places in his morning discourse—into whatever shores or regions of discussion it may be carried;

And I shall trace back, not from the cradle of our old childish learning, a certain sequence of precepts, but those things which I once heard were discussed in a debate among the most eloquent men of our nation, men first in every dignity—not that I despise what the Greek artists and teachers of speaking have left, but since those things lie open and are ready to hand for all, and cannot be set forth by any interpretation of mine either more elegantly or more plainly, you will grant me this indulgence, my brother, I think, that I should set the authority of those men, to whom the highest praise of speaking has been conceded by our countrymen, above the Greeks.

For the matter so stands that, just as we see birds fashion and build nests for the sake of their procreation and their advantage, but, when they have accomplished something, fly about freely, loosed from their work, here and there to ease their labour, so our minds, wearied with forensic business and city work, are eager and long to fly about free from care and toil.

for whether one speaks of the nature of the heavens or of the earth, whether of divine power or of human, whether from a lower place or from an equal or from a higher, whether to impel men or to teach or to deter or to rouse or to turn aside or to inflame or to soothe, whether to few or to many, whether among strangers or among one's own people or with oneself, the speech is divided into channels, not into separate springs; and wherever it goes, it is accompanied by the same equipment and adornment.

At the time, then, when the consul Philippus was inveighing very vehemently against the cause of the leading men, and the tribunate of Drusus, undertaken in defence of the authority of the senate, seemed already to be weakened and broken, I remember being told that during the days of the Roman Games Lucius Crassus betook himself, as it were to collect himself, to his estate at Tusculum. To the same place, it was said, came Quintus Mucius, who had been his father-in-law, and Marcus Antonius, a man both a partner in his political counsels and joined to Crassus in the closest intimacy.

And so what I said in the cause of Curius, against Scaevola, I said not otherwise than I felt: for, 'If,' I said, 'Scaevola, no will shall be rightly made except such as you have written, we citizens shall all come to you with our tablets, you alone shall write all our wills. What then?' I said; 'when will you do public business? When the business of friends? When your own? When, in short, will you do nothing?' Then I added this: 'For to me he does not seem to be free, who does not sometimes do nothing.' In which opinion, Catulus, I remain; and it delights me, when I have come hither, to do this very thing—nothing—and plainly to be idle.

But since we are now overborne by the opinions not only of the common crowd, but even of men slightly educated—who, since they cannot grasp whole what they cannot embrace, handle it more easily when it is pulled apart and, as it were, torn in pieces, and who, as it were, separate the body from the mind, so do they separate the words from the thoughts, though neither can come to pass without the destruction of both—I shall not take upon myself in my discourse more than is laid upon me; I shall only signify briefly that no ornament of words can be found except in well-shaped and well-expressed thoughts, nor is there any thought made brilliant without the light of words.

There had gone out with Crassus himself the young men, intimate friends especially of Drusus, in whom their elders at that time placed great hope for the maintenance of their own rank—Gaius Cotta, who was a candidate for the tribunate of the plebs, and Publius Sulpicius, who was thought likely to seek that same office next.

For as to your third addition—that you are those who would think life unpleasant without these studies—that not only does not exhort me to disputation, but even deters me. For as Gaius Lucilius, a learned and most urbane man, used to say of what he wrote, that he wished it to be read neither by the most unlearned nor by the most learned, because the one understood nothing, the other perhaps more than himself—about which he also wrote, 'I do not care to be read by Persius' (for this man was, as we knew, almost the most learned of all our countrymen) 'but I want Laelius Decumus'—whom we knew to be a good man and not unlettered, but nothing compared to Persius—so I, if now I must dispute about these our studies, should not indeed wish to do so before rustics, but much less before you; for I prefer that my speech be not understood than be censured."

But before I attempt to touch upon those things by which I think speech is adorned and illumined, I shall set forth briefly what I feel about the whole kind of speaking. There is no nature, as it seems to me, which does not have in its own kind a number of things unlike one another, which nevertheless are accounted worthy of a like praise; for we perceive many things with our ears which, although they delight us with their sounds, are yet often so various that the one you hear next seems the most pleasant; and with our eyes there are gathered almost innumerable pleasures, which so take us that they delight one and the same sense in unlike kinds; and the remaining senses are charmed by various pleasures, so that the judgement of the greatest excellence of sweetness is difficult.

On the first day these men talked much among themselves, right up to the close of day, about the times and about the whole state of the commonwealth, for the sake of which they had come; in which conversation Cotta used to relate that many things had been deplored and recalled, as if by prophecy, by those three men of consular rank, so that no evil afterwards befell the state which they had not, so long before, foreseen to be threatening.

Then Caesar said: "For my part, Catulus, I now seem to myself to have spent my labour well in coming hither; for this very refusal of disputation was itself a kind of disputation, to me at least most pleasant. But why do we hinder Antonius, whose part it is, I hear, to discourse about the whole of eloquence, and whom Cotta and Sulpicius have long been awaiting?"

And this same thing which is found in the natures of things can be transferred also to the arts: there is one art of sculpture, in which Myron, Polyclitus, and Lysippus were pre-eminent, who were all unlike one another, but in such a way nevertheless that you would not wish any of them to be unlike himself; there is one art and theory of painting, and yet Zeuxis, Aglaophon, and Apelles were most unlike one another, nor is there any of them to whom anything seems to be wanting in his art. And if this is to be wondered at, and yet is true, in these arts that are, as it were, mute, how much more admirable is it in oratory and in speech? Which, although it deals with the same thoughts and words, has the greatest dissimilarities; not in such a way that some are to be blamed, but that those who are agreed to be praiseworthy are nevertheless praised in unlike kinds.

And when this whole conversation was finished, there was such graciousness in Crassus that, when they had bathed and taken their places at table, all the gloom of the earlier conversation was dispelled, and there was such pleasantness in the man and so great a charm in his talk, that the day among them seemed to have been one of the senate-house, the dinner one of Tusculum.

"For my part," said Crassus, "I will neither allow Antonius to say a word, and I myself will be silent, unless I first obtain something from you"—"What, pray?" said Catulus. "That you stay here today." Then, when he hesitated, because he had promised his brother, "I," said Julius, "answer for both: so we will do; and indeed on that condition, even if you were to say not a word, you would keep me here."

And this may first be discerned in the poets, who have the closest kinship with orators: how unlike to one another are Ennius, Pacuvius, and Accius; how, among the Greeks, Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides—and yet to all almost equal praise is assigned in an unlike kind of writing!

But on the next day, when the elders had rested enough and a walk was proposed, then Scaevola, after they had taken two or three turns, said: "Why do we not imitate, Crassus, that Socrates who appears in Plato's Phaedrus? For this plane-tree of yours has put me in mind of him, spreading out with its broad branches to shade this spot no less than that one whose shade Socrates followed, which seems to me to have grown not so much from the little stream that is described as from Plato's discourse; and what he did with his very hard feet—throwing himself down upon the grass and so speaking those things which the philosophers say were uttered as if by inspiration—that may surely with more justice be granted to my feet."

Hereupon Catulus smiled, and at the same time said: "My hesitation is cut off, since I had given no orders at home, and he, at whose house I was to be, has so easily promised without my opinion." Then all turned their eyes upon Antonius, and he said: "Listen, then, listen; for you will hear a man instructed from the school and from a master and in Greek letters; and indeed I shall speak the more confidently, because Catulus has come as a hearer, to whom not only we of the Latin tongue, but even the Greeks themselves, are wont to concede the subtlety and elegance of their own language.

Look now at those men, and behold them, about whose faculty we are inquiring: Isocrates had sweetness, Lysias subtlety, Hyperides acuteness, Aeschines sonorousness, Demosthenes force. Which of them was not excellent? yet which was like any other than himself? Africanus had gravity, Laelius gentleness, Galba asperity; Carbo had a certain flowing and tuneful quality. Which of these was not the first in those times? and yet each was the first in his own kind.

Then Crassus said: "Nay rather, even more conveniently"; and he called for cushions, and they all sat down on those seats which were beneath the plane-tree. There, that the minds of all might be relaxed from the earlier conversation, Cotta used to relate that Crassus brought up a certain discussion about the study of speaking.

But because, nevertheless, this whole thing, whatever it is, whether art or zeal of speaking, can be nothing unless impudence be added, I will teach you, my pupils, what I myself never learned—what I think about every kind."

But why should I search out old examples, when I am permitted to use present and living ones? What was ever more pleasant to our ears than the speech of this Catulus? which is so pure that he seems almost the only one who speaks Latin, and yet so weighty that, amid his singular dignity, all humanity and charm is nevertheless present. Why say more? When I hear him, I am wont so to judge that, whatever you should add or change or take away, it would be more faulty and worse.

When he had thus begun—saying that Sulpicius and Cotta needed not exhortation but rather that both should be praised, since they had already attained such a faculty that they were not only set before their contemporaries but compared with their elders—"And indeed," he said, "nothing seems to me more excellent than to be able, by speaking, to hold the minds of men, to win over their wills, to drive them whither one will, and to lead them away whence one will. This one art has always flourished above all and always held sway in every free people, and most of all in peaceful and tranquil states.

When they had smiled at this, "The matter," he said, "seems to me to be excellent in respect of faculty, moderate in respect of art; for art belongs to those things which are known; but all the orator's action is contained in opinions, not in knowledge; for we both speak before those who do not know, and we say those things which we ourselves do not know; and so they at different times both feel and judge differently about the same matters, and we often plead contrary causes, not only so that Crassus speaks against me sometimes, or I against Crassus, when it is necessary that one of the two say what is false, but even so that each of us defends at different times different things about the same matter, when there cannot be more than one truth. As, then, in a matter of this kind, which rests on falsehood, which does not often arrive at knowledge, which hunts after the opinions and often the errors of men, so I will speak, if you think there is a cause why you should listen."

And what of our friend Caesar here? has he not brought in a certain new method of oratory and introduced a kind of speaking almost singular? Who ever, except this man, has handled tragic matters almost comically, sad matters with ease, severe matters cheerfully, forensic matters with an almost theatrical grace, and that in such a way that neither was the jest excluded by the greatness of the matters, nor the gravity lessened by the wit?

For what is so wonderful as that, out of the boundless multitude of men, there should arise one who, either alone or with very few, can do that which Nature has granted to all? Or what so pleasant to know and to hear as a speech adorned and polished with wise thoughts and weighty words? Or what so powerful and so magnificent as that the movements of the people, the consciences of judges, and the gravity of the senate should be swayed by the speech of one man? What, furthermore, is so kingly, so liberal, so munificent, as to bring help to suppliants, to raise up the afflicted, to give safety, to free men from dangers, to keep men within the state?

"We do indeed, and very greatly," said Catulus, "think so, and the more because you seem about to use no ostentation; for you have begun not gloriously, as you think, but rather from truth than from some kind of dignity."

Behold, present here, are two who are nearly of equal age, Sulpicius and Cotta. What is so unlike each other? what so excellent each in its own kind? The one polished and subtle, unfolding the matter in proper and apt words; he sticks always in his cause, and, when he has seen most keenly what is to be proved to the judge, he, leaving the other arguments aside, fixes his mind and his speech upon that one point; while Sulpicius, with a certain most courageous onset of spirit, with the fullest and greatest voice, with the utmost exertion of body and dignity of movement, has also such gravity and abundance of words that he seems alone to have been most fully equipped by nature for speaking.

And what is so necessary as to hold always those weapons by which you may either defend yourself, or challenge the wicked, or avenge yourself when provoked? Come now, that you may not always think of the forum, the benches, the rostra, and the senate-house, what can there be in leisure more pleasant, or more proper to humanity, than refined conversation, in no respect crude? For by this one thing we are pre-eminent above the very beasts, that we converse among ourselves and can express our thoughts in speech.

"As, then, I have confessed about the kind itself," said Antonius, "that it is no great art, so this I affirm—that certain very acute precepts can be given for handling the minds of men and for catching their goodwill. If anyone wishes to call the knowledge of this matter a certain great art, I will not contend; for since most men plead causes in the forum rashly and with no method, while some, by reason of practice or some habit, do it more skilfully, there is no doubt that, if anyone observes what it is whereby some speak better than others, he can note it: therefore he who shall have done this in the whole field will have found, if not plainly an art, yet a kind of quasi-art.

I return now to ourselves, since we have always been so paired that we are summoned, as it were, by the talk of men into a kind of judgement of comparison. What is so unlike as I in speaking and Antonius? Since he is such an orator that nothing can be more excellent than he, while I, although I am dissatisfied with myself, am yet for the most part joined with him in this comparison. Do you see what this manner of Antonius is? Bold, vehement, ardent in pleading, fortified beforehand and hedged about on every side of the case, keen, sharp, exact, lingering on each point in its turn, retiring honourably, pursuing fiercely, terrifying, supplicating, with the utmost variety of speech, with no satiety to our ears.

Wherefore who would not rightly wonder at this, and think that he must labour at it to the utmost—that in that one thing in which men are most pre-eminent over the beasts, he may surpass men themselves? And, to come now to those greatest matters, what other power could either gather scattered men into one place, or lead them from a wild and savage life to this human and civilized way of living, or, when states were already established, mark out laws, courts, and rights?

And would that, as I seem to myself to see those things in the forum and in causes, so now I could search them out for you—in what manner they may be discovered! But of myself I shall see; now I set forth this, of which I have persuaded myself: that, although it be not an art, yet nothing is more glorious than a perfect orator; for, to pass over the use of speaking, which holds sway in every peaceful and free state, there is so great a delight in the very faculty of speaking, that nothing more pleasant can be perceived either by the ears or the minds of men.

But we, whatever we are in speaking—since we seem to be of some account in your eyes—are yet certainly far distant from his kind; of what sort that is, it is not for me to say, because each man is least known to himself, and each judges most hardly of himself; but nevertheless the dissimilarity can be understood both from the moderation of my movement, and from this, that I am wont generally to end my speech upon the very tracks where I first set foot, and because somewhat greater labour and care torment me in the choosing of words, since I fear lest, if my speech be a little too plain, it may seem not worthy of the expectation and the silence.

And, not to pursue more things, which are well-nigh countless, let me comprehend it briefly: thus do I lay it down—that upon the moderation and wisdom of the perfect orator depend most of all not only his own dignity, but also the welfare of very many private persons and of the whole commonwealth. Wherefore go on as you are doing, young men, and apply yourselves with all your strength to this study in which you are engaged, that you may be able to be a glory to yourselves, a benefit to your friends, and an advantage to the commonwealth."

For what song can be found sweeter than a well-measured speech? What poem more fitting than the artistic rounding of words? What actor more pleasing in imitating the truth than the orator in upholding it? What is more subtle than frequent and acute thoughts? What more wonderful than a matter illustrated by the splendour of words? What more full than a speech heaped up with every kind of matter? Nor is there any matter which is not proper to the orator, provided it ought to be spoken of with elegance and weight.

But if among us who are present there are such great dissimilarities, such fixed qualities proper to each, and if in that variety the better is generally distinguished from the worse by faculty rather than by kind, and everything is praised which is perfect in its own kind—what think you, if we should wish to embrace all who anywhere are or have been orators, will it not come to pass that there are found almost as many kinds of speaking as there are orators? From which discussion of mine perhaps this objection may occur: if there are almost innumerable, as it were, forms and figures of speaking, unlike in appearance, praiseworthy in kind, then those things which differ among themselves cannot be formed by the same precepts and one method of instruction.

Then Scaevola said courteously, as was his manner: "In other respects I agree with Crassus, lest I should detract either from the art or the glory of my father-in-law Gaius Laelius, or of his son-in-law here; but those two points, Crassus, I fear I cannot concede to you: the one, that you said that states were both originally established and often preserved by orators; the other, that—setting aside the forum, the assembly, the courts, and the senate—you laid it down that the orator is perfect in every kind of discourse and of culture.

His it is, in giving counsel about the greatest matters, to set forth his opinion with dignity; his too is the rousing of a languishing people and the moderating of an unbridled one; by the same faculty both the fraud of men is summoned to destruction and integrity to safety. Who can exhort to virtue more ardently, who recall from vices more keenly, who censure the wicked more harshly, who praise the good more ornately, who break a passion more vehemently by accusing it? Who lighten grief more gently by consoling?

But this is not so; and it is to be most diligently observed by those who train and educate others, toward what each man's nature seems most to incline. For we see that from the same school, as it were, there have come forth disciples unlike one another and yet praiseworthy, when the instruction of the teacher was accommodated to the nature of each.

For who would grant you this, either that at the beginning the race of men, scattered over mountains and forests, hedged itself within towns and walls because it was driven thereto rather by the counsels of wise men than because it was charmed by the speech of eloquent men? Or, indeed, that the other advantages, whether in founding or in preserving states, were established not by wise and brave men, but by men eloquent and adorned in speech?

And history, indeed—the witness of times, the light of truth, the life of memory, the mistress of life, the messenger of antiquity—by what other voice than the orator's is it commended to immortality? For if there is any other art that professes a knowledge of either coining or choosing words; or if anyone but the orator is said to shape a speech and to vary and distinguish it as if by certain ornaments of words and thoughts; or if any method, whether of arguments, or of thoughts, or, in short, of arrangement and order, is handed down except by this one art—let us confess either that what this art professes is alien to it, or that it is common to it with some other art; but if in this one alone is that method and doctrine, then, even if those of other arts have spoken well, it is not on that account the less proper to this one alone;

Of which the most signal example—to pass over the other arts—is what Isocrates, that singular teacher, used to say: that he was wont to use spurs upon Ephorus, but, on the contrary, reins upon Theopompus; for the one, who exulted in a boldness of words, he restrained, while the other, who hesitated and was, as it were, bashful, he urged on. Nor did he make them like one another, but added something to the one, and pared something from the other, so that he might shape in each what the nature of each would allow.

Or do you really think that the famous Romulus assembled his shepherds and refugees, or arranged the marriages with the Sabines, or repressed the violence of his neighbours, by eloquence, and not by counsel and by his singular wisdom? What of Numa Pompilius? What of Servius Tullius? What of the other kings, by whom many excellent things were done for the establishment of the commonwealth—does there appear any trace of eloquence? And when the kings had been driven out—although we perceive that the very expulsion was accomplished by the mind, not the tongue, of Lucius Brutus—do we not see that all that followed was full of counsels, empty of words?

but as the orator can speak best about those matters which belong to the other arts, provided only he has learned them—as Crassus said yesterday—so men of the other arts speak more elegantly of their own matters, if they have learned anything from this art.

These things had to be premised by me, so that, if not all the things which I should set forth were suited to the zeal of every one of you and to that kind which each of you approves in speaking, you might yet perceive that the kind expressed by me was that which I myself most approve. Therefore these things which Antonius has explained are both to be done by the orator and to be spoken of in some way. What better manner of speaking is there, then—for of delivery I shall see afterwards—than that we should speak in Latin, plainly, with adornment, and aptly and suitably to whatever is being treated?

For my part, if I wished to use the examples both of our own state and of others, I could bring forward more harm done to public affairs by most eloquent men than help; but, to pass over the rest, it seems to me that the most eloquent men I ever heard, excepting you two, Crassus, were Tiberius and Gaius Sempronius, whose father, a prudent and weighty man, by no means eloquent, was at many times, and especially as censor, a saviour of the commonwealth. And he, not by any studied abundance of speech, but by a nod and a word, transferred the freedmen into the city tribes; and had he not done so, we should long since have had no commonwealth, which now we scarcely hold together. But his sons, eloquent and furnished with all the resources both of nature and of training for speaking, when they had received the state most flourishing both by their father's counsel and by the arms of their forefathers, by that noble pilot of states, as you call it, eloquence, brought the commonwealth to ruin.

For if some farmer about rustic matters, or even—as many do—some physician about diseases, or some painter about painting, has written or spoken eloquently, eloquence is not on that account to be reckoned of that art; in which, because there is great power in the talents of men, many even without instruction attain something of every kind and art; but, although what is proper to each can be judged from this—when you see what each art teaches—yet nothing can be more certain than this, that all the other arts can perform their function without eloquence, but the orator cannot obtain his name without it; so that the others, if they are eloquent, have something from him, but he, unless he has furnished himself with his own domestic stores, cannot seek the abundance of speaking from elsewhere."

And of those two which I named first, namely of pure and clear speech, I do not think a method is to be expected from me; for we do not attempt to teach a man to speak who does not know how to talk; nor to hope that he who cannot speak Latin will speak with adornment; nor indeed that he who does not say what we can understand can say what we may admire. Let us leave these things, then, which have an easy understanding and a necessary use. For the one is handed down by letters and by boyish instruction, and the other is employed for this reason, that it may be understood what each man says, which we see to be so necessary that yet nothing can be less than it.

What of the ancient laws and the customs of our ancestors? What of the auspices, over which you and I, Crassus, preside, to the great safety of the commonwealth? What of the rites and ceremonies? What of this civil law, which has long been cultivated in our family without any glory of eloquence—were any of these invented, or learned, or in any way handled by the class of orators?

Then Catulus said: "Although, Antonius, that course of your speech is by no means to be hindered by interruption, yet you will allow me, and will pardon me; 'for I cannot but cry out,' as that man says in the Trinummus: so well did you seem both to express subtly the power of the orator, and to praise it most copiously; which indeed it especially becomes the eloquent man to do—to praise eloquence; for he ought, in praising it, to employ that very thing which he praises. But go on further; for I agree with you that this whole thing—to speak eloquently—is yours, and that if anyone do this in another art, he uses a good thing borrowed from elsewhere, not proper or his own."

But all elegance of speech, although it is polished by the knowledge of letters, is yet increased by the reading of orators and poets; for those men of old, who could not yet adorn what they said, almost all spoke excellently; and those who have been accustomed to their language will not be able, even if they wish it, to speak otherwise than in Latin. Nor yet must we use those words which our own custom no longer uses, except sometimes, for the sake of adornment, sparingly, as I shall show; but of the customary words he will be able so to use them, as to use the choicest, who shall have been studiously and much versed in the old writings.

For my part I remember both Servius Galba, a man divinely gifted in speaking, and Marcus Aemilius Porcina, and Gaius Carbo himself, whom you struck down while still a youth—all of them ignorant of the laws, hesitant in the institutions of our ancestors, untrained in the civil law. And this generation of yours—except for you, Crassus, who, more by your own zeal than by any proper duty of orators, learned the civil law from us—is ignorant of the law, which is sometimes a cause for shame.

And Crassus said: "The night, Antonius, has polished you for us and made you a man; for in yesterday's conversation you had described to us an orator of some single function, as Caecilius says—some oarsman or porter, a man poor in culture and unrefined." Then Antonius said: "Yesterday I had set this before myself, that, if I refuted you, I should draw these pupils away from you; but now, with Catulus and Caesar listening, I think I ought not so much to fight with you as to say what I myself feel.

And, that we may speak Latin, we must take care not only that we utter such words as no one may justly censure, and that we so preserve them in their cases and tenses and gender and number that there be nothing disordered or discordant or out of place, but also the very tongue and breath and sound of the voice are to be regulated.

But as for that which at the close of your speech you assumed as if by your own right—that the orator can deal most copiously with every kind of discourse—this, were we not here in your own kingdom, I would not have allowed, and I would take the side of the many who would either contend with you by interdict or summon you to lay hands upon the property of others, since you have so rashly rushed into possessions that are not your own.
