With those, as I said, I delight myself, who have written either deeds or their own speeches, or who so speak that they seem to have wished to be familiar to us who are not most learned.

From this arose that divorce, as it were, of the tongue and the heart, an absurd thing surely, and useless and to be censured: that some should teach us to be wise, and others to speak. For since there were several who sprang in a manner from Socrates, because from his various and diverse discussions, diffused on every side, one had grasped one thing, another another, there were sown, as it were, families dissenting among themselves and much disjoined and unlike, although nevertheless all the philosophers both wished to be called Socratics and judged themselves to be such.

For if it is agreed that Philo the architect, who built the arsenal for the Athenians, gave the people a most eloquent account of his work, it is not to be thought that he was eloquent rather by the architect's skill than by the orator's; nor, if this Marcus Antonius had had to speak about the construction of ships on behalf of Hermodorus, would he, when he had learned the case from him, have failed to speak elegantly and copiously about another man's art; nor did Asclepiades, the physician and friend whom we employed, in that very thing—that he spoke elegantly and surpassed the other physicians—use the faculty of medicine, but of eloquence.

But I return thither: do you see how great a function of the orator history is? I scarcely know whether it be not the greatest, by the flood and the variety of the speech; and nowhere do I find it separately set forth in the precepts of the rhetoricians; for they lie before our eyes. For who does not know that the first law of history is that one dare say nothing false? Then that one dare say nothing untrue? That there be no suspicion of favour in writing? None of enmity?

And first, from Plato himself, Aristotle and Xenocrates, of whom the one obtained the name of the Peripatetics, the other of the Academy; then from Antisthenes, who in the Socratic conversation had most loved patience and endurance, came first the Cynics, then the Stoics; then from Aristippus, whom those discussions of pleasure rather delighted, flowed the Cyrenaic philosophy, which he and his successors defended without disguise, while these men who now measure all things by pleasure, since they do it more bashfully, neither satisfy dignity, which they do not despise, nor maintain pleasure, which they wish to embrace. There were also other kinds of philosophers, who all said that they were nearly Socratics—the Eretrians, the Erillians, the Megarians, the Pyrrhonians; but these have now long since been broken and extinguished by the force and discussions of these others.

And that saying of Socrates is more probable, yet not true—that all men are eloquent enough in that which they know; this is truer—that no one can be eloquent in that which he does not know, and that, even if he knows it most thoroughly but is ignorant of how to compose and polish a speech, he cannot speak eloquently even about that of which he has knowledge.

These foundations, of course, are known to all; but the very building-up rests upon facts and words: the system of facts demands the order of times, the description of regions; it requires also—since in great matters worthy of memory, first counsels, then deeds, afterward outcomes are looked for—both that it be signified, concerning counsels, what the writer approves, and that it be declared, in deeds, not only what was done or said, but also in what manner; and when the outcome is spoken of, that all the causes be unfolded, whether of chance or of wisdom or of rashness, and not only the deeds of the men themselves, but also, concerning those who excel in fame and name, the life and nature of each;

Of those, however, which remain, that philosophy which has undertaken the patronage of pleasure, even if it should seem true to anyone, is yet far from the man whom we are seeking, and whom we wish to be the author of public counsel, the leader in the governing of the state, and the chief of opinion and eloquence in the senate, among the people, and in public causes. Yet no injury shall be done by us to that philosophy; for it shall not be driven from the place to which it wishes to approach, but it shall rest in its own little gardens, where it will, where also, reclining softly and delicately, it calls us away from the Rostra, from the courts, from the senate-house—wisely, perhaps, especially in such a commonwealth as this.

Wherefore, if anyone wishes to define and embrace the universal and proper power of the orator, in my opinion that man will be an orator worthy of this so weighty a name who, on whatever subject may arise that must be unfolded in speech, shall speak prudently, in good order, elegantly, and from memory, with a certain dignity also of delivery.

but the system of words and the kind of speech must be a flowing and extended one, with a certain smoothness evenly streaming on, without this judicial harshness and without the forensic stings of epigrams. Do you see that of all these so great matters there are no precepts which are found in the arts of the rhetoricians? In the same silence many other functions of the orator have lain—exhortations, precepts, consolations, admonitions—all of which must be treated most eloquently, but have no place in these arts which have been handed down.

But I do not now inquire which philosophy is truest, but which is most closely joined to the orator; wherefore let us dismiss these men without any insult; for they are both good men and, since they so seem to themselves, happy; and let us only admonish them so far, that, even if it be most true, they should yet keep silent, as though it were a mystery, that thing which they assert—that it is not for the wise man to engage in the commonwealth; for if they shall persuade us and every best man of this, they themselves will not be able to be, what they most desire, at leisure.

But if to anyone it seems too unlimited that I have put it thus, "on whatever subject," let him cut away and prune from this as much as shall seem good to each; yet I shall hold to this—that, even if the orator be ignorant of those things which lie in the other arts and studies, and hold only what concerns disputes and the practice of the forum, yet, if he must speak on these very matters, when he has learned from those who are masters what belongs to each subject, the orator will speak much better even than those very men whose arts they are.

And in this kind there is also that boundless forest, in that most writers—as Crassus too showed—have given the orator two kinds for speaking: one about a fixed and definite cause, such as are those which are engaged in suits, in deliberations (let anyone add, if he will, also panegyrics); the other, which almost all writers call, but no one explains, the unlimited question of the kind, without time and without person. What this is and how great it is, when they speak of it, they do not seem to me to understand:

The Stoics, however, whom I by no means disapprove, I yet dismiss; nor do I fear that they will be angry, since they know not at all how to be angry; and I have this thanks to give them, that they alone of all men said that eloquence was a virtue and a wisdom. But assuredly there is in them something which is much at variance with this orator whom we are equipping; either because they say that all who are not wise are slaves, robbers, enemies, madmen, and yet that no one is wise: but it is very absurd to commit an assembly or a senate or any gathering of men to one to whom none of those present seems sane, none a citizen, none free.

Thus, if Sulpicius here must speak on military affairs, he will inquire of our kinsman Gaius Marius, and, when he has been informed, will deliver it so that he himself seems to know it almost better than Gaius Marius himself; if on the civil law, he will confer with you, and, a man most prudent and most skilled though you are, he will surpass you, in the art of speaking, in those very matters which he has learned from you.

for if it belongs to the orator to be able to speak on whatever matter is set unlimitedly, he will have to speak how great the magnitude of the sun is, what the shape of the earth; about mathematical, about musical matters he will not be able, having undertaken this burden, to refuse to speak; in short, to him who professes that it is his not only to speak about those controversies which are marked by times and persons—that is, about all forensic matters—but also about the unlimited questions of the kind, no kind of speech can be excepted.

There is added to this that they have also a kind of speech which is perhaps subtle and certainly acute, but, for an orator, meagre, unwonted, abhorrent to the ears of the multitude, obscure, empty, dry, and yet of such a sort that it can by no means be used before the multitude: for other things seem good and evil to the Stoics than to the rest of the citizens, or rather of the nations; the force of honour, of disgrace, of reward, of punishment is otherwise with them; whether truly or not is nothing to the present purpose; but if we should follow these, we could never set forth any matter by speaking.

But if there shall arise some matter in which he must speak about the nature, about the vices of men, about desires, about moderation, about self-restraint, about pain, about death, perhaps—if it shall seem good to him (although the orator ought to know these things)—he will confer with Sextus Pompeius, a man learned in philosophy; and this surely he will accomplish: that whatever subject he has learned from anyone, on that he will speak much more elegantly than that very man from whom he learned it.

But if we wish also to add to the orator that part of questions which is wandering and free and widely open—so that we should think the orator must speak about good or evil things, things to be sought or shunned, honourable or base, useful or useless, about virtue, justice, self-restraint, prudence, greatness of soul, liberality, piety, friendship, duty, good faith, and the other virtues and their contrary vices; and likewise about the commonwealth, about empire, about military affairs, about the discipline of the state, about the characters of men—let us assume that part too, but in such a way that it be circumscribed within moderate regions.

There remain the Peripatetics and the Academics; although the name of the Academics is one, the opinions are two; for Speusippus, the son of Plato's sister, and Xenocrates, who had heard Plato, and Polemo and Crantor, who had heard Xenocrates, dissented in no great matter from Aristotle, who had heard Plato along with them; in copiousness, perhaps, and variety of speaking they were not equal: Arcesilaus first, who had heard Polemo, snatched chiefly this from the various books of Plato and the Socratic conversations—that there is nothing certain which can be perceived either by the senses or by the mind; and they say that he, using a certain exquisite charm of speaking, scorned every judgement of mind and sense, and first instituted—although this was most Socratic—not to show what he himself felt, but to argue against that which each man had said he felt.

But if he will listen to me, since philosophy is divided into three parts—into the obscurity of nature, into the subtlety of reasoning, and into life and conduct—let us leave those first two and grant them to our indolence; but the third, which has always been the orator's, unless we hold to it, we shall leave the orator nothing in which he can be great.

For my part I think that all things which pertain to the practice of citizens, the custom of men, which are engaged in the habit of life, in the system of the commonwealth, in this civil society, in the common sense of man, in nature, in character, must be grasped by the orator; if not so that he may answer separately about these matters after the manner of the philosophers, yet certainly so that he may prudently weave them into a cause; but about these very matters that he should speak in such a way as those who established laws, statutes, and states spoke—simply and splendidly, without any train of disputations and without a meagre wrangling of words.

From this flowed this more recent Academy, in which arose, with a certain divine swiftness of genius and copiousness of speech, Carneades; of whom, although I have known many hearers at Athens, I can yet cite the most trustworthy authorities—both my father-in-law Scaevola, who heard him at Rome as a young man, and Quintus Metellus, son of Lucius, my friend, a most illustrious man, who said that he, when a young man, had for many days heard that man at Athens, then already affected by old age.

Wherefore this topic of life and conduct must be wholly mastered by the orator; the rest, even if he has not learned them, he will nevertheless be able, if ever there be need, to adorn in speech, provided they have been brought to him and delivered to him. For if it is agreed among the learned that a man ignorant of astronomy, Aratus, spoke of the heavens and the stars in most ornate and excellent verses; if a man wholly removed from the country, Nicander of Colophon, wrote excellently about rustic matters by a certain poetic, not rustic, faculty, why should not the orator speak most eloquently about those things which he has learned for a particular cause and occasion?

At this point, lest there be any wonder if no precepts about so many and so great matters are laid down by me, I lay it down thus: that, as in the other arts, when the most difficult things of each art have been handed down, the rest, because they are either easier or similar, need not be handed down; as in painting, he who has thoroughly learned to paint one form of man can paint of any form or age, even if he has not learned it, and there is no danger that he who paints a lion or a bull excellently cannot do the same with many other quadrupeds—and there is altogether no art in which everything that can be effected by that art is handed down by the teacher, but those who have learned the very kinds of the chief and definite matters attain the rest by themselves—

But these, as the divisions of the rivers from the Apennine, so were the partings of the branches of learning made from the common ridge of wisdom, so that the philosophers flowed down, as it were, into a certain Greek and harbour-filled upper sea, while the orators slipped down into this lower one, Tuscan and barbarous, full of rocks and perils, in which even Ulysses himself had wandered astray.

For the poet is closely akin to the orator, a little more bound by metre, but freer in the licence of words, and in many kinds of adornment a partner and well-nigh his equal; and in this at least almost the same, that he circumscribes and defines his right within no boundaries, so that he is free to range with that same faculty and abundance wherever he will.

similarly I think that in this—whether method or exercise—of speaking, he who has attained that power, of being able to move at his own pleasure the minds of those who hear with some power of deciding, whether about the commonwealth, or about his own matters, or about those against whom or on whose behalf he speaks—he will inquire no more, about that whole kind of the remaining speeches, what he should say, than that famous Polyclitus, when he was fashioning a Hercules, inquired how he should fashion the skin or the hydra, even though he had never learned to do these things separately."

Wherefore, if we are content with this eloquence and this orator, who knows either that he ought to deny what is charged, or, if you cannot do that, then to show that what the accused has done was either rightly done, or by another's fault, or by injury, or in accordance with law, or not against law, or through imprudence, or of necessity, or that it is not to be designated by that name by which it is charged, or that the matter was not carried on as it ought to have been and as was lawful—and if you think it enough to learn those things which these writers of the art teach, which Antonius nevertheless explained much more ornately than they are stated by them, and more fully—but if you are content with these, and with those things too which you wished to be said by me, then you drive the orator from a certain vast and immense field into a very narrow ring indeed.

For as to your saying, Scaevola, that you would not have endured it, except that you are in my kingdom, that I said the orator ought to be perfect in every kind of discourse and in every department of culture—by Hercules, I would never say this if I thought that the man I am imagining were myself.

Then Catulus said: "Excellently, Antonius, you seem to me to have set before our eyes what he ought to learn who is to be an orator, and what, even if he has not learned it, he would assume from what he has learned; for you have led the whole man into two kinds only of causes, and left the rest, countless, to exercise and likeness: but see lest in those two kinds you have the hydra and the skin, while the Hercules and other greater works are left in those matters which you pass over; for it seems to me no less a work to speak about the universal kinds of things than about the causes of individuals, and much greater even to speak about the nature of the gods than about the suits of men." "It is not so," said Antonius;

But if you wish to follow that ancient Pericles, or this man too, who is more familiar to us by reason of the multitude of his writings, Demosthenes; and if you have come to love that splendid and surpassing image of the perfect orator and his beauty—then you must comprehend either this Carneadean or that Aristotelian power.

But, as Gaius Lucilius used often to say—a man somewhat angry with you, and on that very account less my friend than he wished, yet learned and most urbane—so I think: that no one is to be reckoned in the number of orators who is not polished in all those arts which are worthy of a free man; which, even if we do not employ them in speaking, yet it appears and stands out whether we are ignorant of them or have learned them. As those who play at ball do not in the very game use the proper skill of the wrestling-school, but their very movement shows whether they have learned the palaestra or are ignorant of it; and as those who model anything, even though at the moment they make no use of painting, yet it is not obscure whether they know how to paint or not;

"for I will tell you, Catulus, not so much as a learned man as—what is greater—as one who has experience: the speaking about all other matters, believe me, is play to a man not dull, nor unexercised, nor without common letters and the more polished culture; in the contests of causes there is a certain great work, and I scarcely know whether of human works it be by far the greatest; in which the power of the orator is for the most part judged by the inexperienced by the outcome and the victory; where an armed adversary is at hand, who must both be struck and repelled; where often he who is to be the master of the matter is a stranger and angry, or even a friend of the adversary and an enemy to you; when he must be either taught or untaught, or repressed or roused, or in every way moderated by the speech to suit the occasion and the cause (in which often goodwill must be led to hatred, and hatred to goodwill); or, as by some engine, must now be turned to severity, now to mildness, now to sadness, now to gladness of mind;

For, as I said before, those men of old, down to Socrates, joined the knowledge and science of all things which pertained to the manners of men, to life, to virtue, to the commonwealth, with the theory of speaking; but afterwards, the philosophers, dissociated, as I have set forth, from Socrates and thereafter from all the Socratics likewise, despised eloquence, and the orators despised wisdom, and neither touched anything from the other's portion, except so far as the former borrowed from the latter, or these from those; from which they might have drawn indiscriminately, if they had wished to remain in their old community.

so in these very speeches of the courts, the assemblies, the senate, even though the other arts are not specifically employed, yet it is easily made plain whether he who speaks has merely been tossed about in this declamatory exercise, or has come to speaking equipped with all the liberal arts."

the weight of all thoughts, the weights of all words must be used; there must be added a delivery various, vehement, full of spirit, full of breath, full of grief, full of truth. In these works, if anyone has grasped that art, so that he can fashion the image of Minerva like Phidias, he will not indeed labour at how, like the same artist, he should learn to make those lesser works on the shield."

But as the old pontiffs, on account of the multitude of the sacrifices, wished there to be three epulones, although they themselves had been instituted by Numa to perform also that banquet-sacrifice of the games, so the Socratics separated the pleaders of causes from themselves and from the common name of philosophy, although the men of old had wished there to be a wonderful fellowship of speaking and of understanding.

Then Scaevola, smiling, said: "I will struggle no further with you, Crassus; for that very thing which you have said against me you have accomplished by a certain artifice, so that both you have conceded to me what I wished not to be the orator's, and you have somehow twisted those very things back again and made them over to the orator as his own.

Then Catulus said: "The greater and more wonderful you have made those things, the greater an expectation holds me, by what methods and by what precepts that so great a power is acquired; not that it now concerns me—for my age does not require it, and we have followed a certain other kind of speaking, who never wrested verdicts from the hands of the judges by a kind of force of speech, but rather, their minds being appeased, received only as much as they themselves allowed—but yet I ask these things of yours for no use of my own, led only by the zeal of knowing.

Since these things are so, I, for my part, will plead a little on my own behalf, and will ask of you that you account the things which I shall say to be said not about myself, but about the orator. For I am one who, although I was taught in boyhood with the highest zeal of my father, and brought to the forum only so much genius as I myself am aware of—not so much as perhaps I seem to you to have—cannot say that I learned these things which I now embrace just as I shall say they ought to be learned; inasmuch as I came earliest of all to public causes, and at the age of one-and-twenty summoned to trial a most noble and most eloquent man; to whom the forum was my school, my master was practice, and the laws and institutions of the Roman people and the custom of our ancestors.

When I came as praetor to Rhodes and conferred with that great teacher of this discipline, Apollonius, those things which I had received from Panaetius, he indeed laughed, as was his manner, at philosophy and despised it, and said many things not so weightily as wittily; but your speech was of such a kind that you despised no art or learning, but said that all are the companions and handmaids of the orator.

Nor do I need some Greek teacher to chant to me well-worn precepts, when he himself has never looked upon the forum, never upon any trial; as that Peripatetic Phormio is said to have done, when Hannibal, expelled from Carthage, had come to Ephesus to Antiochus as an exile, and, because his name had great glory among all, had been invited by his hosts to hear, if he wished, the man I have mentioned; and when he had said that he was not unwilling, the wordy man is said to have spoken some hours about the duty of a commander and about military affairs. Then, when the rest who had heard him were vehemently delighted, they asked of Hannibal what he himself judged of that philosopher: hereupon the Carthaginian is reported to have answered, not in the best Greek, but yet freely, that he had often seen many doting old men, but had seen no one who doted more than Phormio.

A little thirsting for those arts of which I speak, I tasted them, when I was quaestor in Asia, having got hold of a rhetorician from the Academy nearly of my own age, that Metrodorus of whose memory Antonius made mention; and departing thence, at Athens, where I should have lingered longer, had I not been angry with the Athenians because they would not repeat the mysteries, to which I had come two days too late; wherefore this, that I embrace so great a knowledge and force of learning, is not only not in my favour, but rather against me—for I am discussing not what I can do, but what the orator can do—and all these men who set forth the rhetorical arts I hold most ridiculous; for they write about the kinds of suits, and about exordia, and about narrations;

And if anyone has embraced all of these, and likewise has joined to them that faculty of most ornate speech, I cannot deny that he will be a man eminent and admirable; but if any such man existed, or ever did exist, or indeed could exist, you alone, assuredly, would be he, who, both in my judgement and in that of all men, have left scarcely any praise—I would say it with the leave of these gentlemen—to the other orators.

And, by Hercules, not without reason; for what could be done either more arrogant or more wordy than for a Greek, who had never seen an enemy, never a camp, never, in short, touched the least part of any public office, to give precepts about military affairs to Hannibal, who for so many years had contended with the Roman people, the conqueror of all nations, about empire? This all those who give precepts about the art of speaking seem to me to do; for what they themselves have not experienced, that they teach others; but in this perhaps they err less, that they try to teach not you, as that man Hannibal, but boys or youths."

but that power of eloquence is so great that it holds the origin, the force, and the changes of all things, of the virtues, of the duties, and of all that nature which contains the manners of men, their minds, and their life; the same eloquence describes manners, laws, and rights, governs the commonwealth, and speaks ornately and copiously of all things to whatever matter they pertain.

But if, while you yourself lack nothing of what concerns forensic and civil affairs that you do not know, you have nevertheless not embraced that knowledge which you join to the orator, let us see whether we be not assigning to him more than the truth and reality of the matter allows.'

"You err, Catulus," said Antonius; "for I myself have already fallen in with many a Phormio. For who is there of those Greeks who thinks any of us understands anything? And to me, indeed, they are not so troublesome; I easily bear and endure them all; for either they bring something which does not displease me, or they bring it about that I repent the less of not having learned; but I dismiss them not so insultingly as Hannibal dismissed that philosopher, and on that account I have perhaps even more trouble. But yet their doctrine, so far as I can judge, is very ridiculous:

In which kind we for our part are engaged so far as we can, so far as we have strength by genius, by our middling learning, by practice; nor yet do we much yield in disputation to those who have placed, as it were, the tent of their whole life in philosophy alone.

Hereupon Crassus said: 'Remember that I spoke not of my own, but of the orator's faculty; for what have we either learned, or been able to know, who came to action before we came to learning—whom the very business of affairs in the forum, in canvassing, in the commonwealth, in the affairs of friends, finished off before we could form any notion of such great matters?

for they divide the whole matter into two parts, into the controversy of the cause and into that of the question: they call a cause a matter placed in the dispute and controversy of defendants; but a question a matter placed in unlimited doubt; about the cause they give precepts; about the other part of speaking there is a wonderful silence.

For what can my friend Gaius Velleius bring forward, as to why pleasure is the highest good, which I could not maintain more copiously, if I wished, or refute, from those topics which Antonius set forth, by this exercise of speaking, in which Velleius is unskilled and in which each of us is versed? What is there that either Sextus Pompeius, or the two Balbi, or my friend Marcus Vigellius, who lived with Panaetius, the Stoic, could say about the virtue of men, in which disputation I, or any of you, ought to yield to them?

But if you think there is so much in us, who, even if we were not greatly lacking in talent, as you suppose, yet certainly lacked learning and leisure and, by Hercules, that keenest zeal for learning, what do you suppose, if to someone's talent, even greater, there should be added those things which I have not touched—what an orator he would be, and how great?'

Then they make, as it were, five members of eloquence: to find what you would say, to arrange what is found, then to adorn it with words, afterward to commit it to memory, then at the last to deliver and pronounce it; a thing surely not recondite; for who would not see this of his own accord—that no one can speak unless he have both what he would say, and in what words, and in what order he would say it, and remember these things? And I do not blame these things, but say that they are set before our eyes, as also those four, or five, or six, or even seven parts (since they are divided differently by different men), into which all speech is by these men distributed:

For philosophy is not like the rest of the arts: for what will he do in geometry who has not learned it? what in music? Either he must be silent, or not even be accounted sane. But these things which are in philosophy are dug out by the genius, for the eliciting of what is probable in each matter, by keen and sharp minds, and are polished by a practised speech. This our common orator, if he be less learned, yet, if he be practised in speaking, will by this very common practice belabour those men, and will not allow himself to be despised and looked down upon by them;
Then Antonius said: 'You prove to me, Crassus, what you say, nor do I doubt that a man will be much richer in speaking if he has comprehended the theory and nature of all things and arts;

for they bid us begin in such a way as to make the hearer well-disposed to us, and teachable, and attentive; then to narrate the matter, and so that the narrative be probable, that it be open, that it be brief; afterward to divide the cause or set it forth; to confirm our own points by arguments and reasons; then to refute the contrary; then some place at this point the conclusion of the speech and, as it were, the peroration, others bid us, before the peroration, digress for the sake of adorning or amplifying, and then conclude and round off.

but if there shall some day arise one who, after the manner of Aristotle, can speak on both sides of all matters, and in every cause, the precepts of that man being known, can unfold two contrary speeches—or who, in this manner of Arcesilaus and Carneades, can argue against everything that is proposed, and who shall join to that theory this practice and exercise of speaking—he will be the true, he the perfect, he the only orator. For neither without the forensic sinews can an orator be sufficiently vehement and weighty, nor without the variety of learning sufficiently polished and wise.

but, in the first place, that is difficult to do, especially in this life of ours and amid our occupations; and, in the second place, there is this also to be feared, that we may be drawn away from this practice and habit of popular and forensic speaking. For it seems to me that there is a certain other kind of speech belonging to those men of whom you spoke a little while ago, however elegantly and weightily they may speak either about the nature of things or about human affairs: it is a certain polished and luxuriant kind of words, suited more to the wrestling-school and the oil than to this civil throng and the forum.

Not even these things do I blame; for they are neatly distributed, but yet—a thing which was inevitable for men without experience of the truth—not skilfully: for those precepts which they wished to belong to introductions and narratives must be preserved throughout whole speeches;

Wherefore let us indeed allow that ancient Corax to hatch his own chicks in the nest, that they may fly forth as hateful and troublesome bawlers; and let us suffer some Pamphilus or other to paint so great a matter, as it were, in toy-pictures upon his tablets, like some childish playthings; and let us ourselves, in this short discussion of yesterday and today, explain the whole office of the orator—provided only that the matter be so great as to seem comprehended in all the books of the philosophers, which none of these men has ever touched.'

For I myself, who had touched Greek letters late and lightly, yet when, setting out as proconsul into Cilicia, I had come to Athens, stayed there several days then because of the difficulty of sailing; but, since I had daily with me the most learned men, almost those very same who were just now named by you, when somehow this had become noised abroad among them, that I, like you, was wont to engage in the greater cases, each as best he could discoursed about the duty and method of the orator.

for I can more easily make a judge well-disposed when I am in the course of my speech than when all is unheard; and teachable, not when I promise that I shall demonstrate, but then, when I teach and explain; and attentive we can make him in the whole action by rousing the minds of the judges, not by the first announcement.

Then Catulus said: 'By Hercules, Crassus, it is by no means to be wondered at that there is in you so great a force, or sweetness, or copiousness of speaking; whom indeed I formerly supposed to speak so by nature, that you seemed to me not only a most accomplished orator, but also a most wise man; now I understand that you have always counted those things even more important which looked toward wisdom, and that from these this copiousness of speaking has flowed. But yet, when I recall all the stages of your age, and when I consider your life and pursuits, I neither see at what time you learned these things, nor do I understand that you were greatly devoted to those studies, those men, those books. And yet I cannot determine whether I more wonder that you were able, amid such great occupations of yours, to learn thoroughly those things which you persuade me are the greatest helps, or, if you were not able, that you can speak in this manner.'

Of these, some, like that very Mnesarchus, said that those whom we call orators are nothing but a kind of hired labourers with a quick and practised tongue; that no one was an orator unless he were wise, and that eloquence itself, since it consists in the science of speaking well, is one single virtue, and that he who has one virtue has all, and that these are equal and on a par with one another; and so he who is eloquent has all the virtues and is wise. But this was a kind of thorny and meagre discourse, and far removed from our way of thinking.

But as to their bidding the narrative be probable and open and brief, they rightly admonish us: that they think these things to be more proper to the narrative than to the whole speech—in this they seem to me greatly to err; and altogether in this is all their error, that they think this to be a certain art not unlike the others, of such a kind as Crassus said yesterday could be composed about the civil law itself: that the kinds of matters should first be set forth—in which there is a fault if any kind is passed over; then the parts of the several kinds—in which both to omit some part and to have a superfluous one is faulty; then the definitions of all the words—in which neither ought anything to be absent nor to overflow.

Here Crassus said: 'I should wish you first to persuade yourself of this, Catulus: that I do not act much otherwise, when I discuss the orator, than I should do if I had to speak about the actor. For I should deny that he could give satisfaction in gesture, unless he had learned the palaestra, unless he had learned to dance; nor, when I said this, would it be necessary that I should be an actor, but perhaps a not foolish appraiser of another's art.

But Charmadas spoke much more richly on these same matters, not that he disclosed his own opinion—for this was the ancestral custom of the Academy, always to oppose all in disputation—but yet he chiefly signified this: that those who are called rhetoricians, and who hand down precepts of speaking, understand nothing at all, and that no one can attain the faculty of speaking unless he has learned the discoveries of the philosophers.

But if this can be attained in the civil law, if even in small or moderate matters by the more learned, I do not think the same can be done in so great and so boundless a matter as this; but if there are some who think so, they must be led to those who teach these things; they will attain everything already explained and polished; for there are countless books about these matters, neither hidden nor obscure: but let them see what they wish—whether they are going to take up arms for play or for fight; for fight and the battle-line require one thing, our play and exercise-ground another; and yet the very playful art of arms profits somewhat both the gladiator and the soldier; but a keen mind, present and acute and likewise versatile, makes men invincible.

Similarly now I speak about the orator at your impulse—the highest orator, of course; for always, whenever inquiry is made about any art or faculty, it is wont to be made about the absolute and perfect. Wherefore, if you now wish me to be an orator, even a fairly good one, or, in short, a good one, I will not resist; for why should I now be foolish? I know that I am so esteemed: but if it is so, yet certainly I am not the highest; for among men there is no thing more difficult, nor greater, nor which requires more helps of learning.

Against this disputed eloquent Athenians, men versed in public affairs and in cases, among whom was also that man who was lately at Rome, Menedemus, my guest. When he said that there was a certain prudence which was concerned with discerning the methods of establishing and governing commonwealths, there was roused that ready man, abounding in all learning and in a certain incredible variety and abundance of matter; he taught that all the parts of that very prudence must be sought from philosophy, and that those things which were established in the commonwealth concerning the immortal gods, concerning the discipline of youth, concerning justice, patience, temperance, and moderation in all things, and the rest, without which states could neither exist nor be well ordered, were nowhere to be found in the books of the rhetoricians;

Wherefore I will now so train the orator for you, if I can, that I may first foresee what he can effect: for let him be tinged with letters; let him have heard something, read something, received those very precepts; I will try what becomes him, what he can effect with his voice, his strength, his breath, his tongue. If I understand that he can attain to the highest, I will not only exhort him to labour, but, if he shall also seem to me to be a good man, I will entreat him; so great is the ornament I reckon there is in an excellent orator who is at the same time a good man, for the whole state; but if it shall seem, when he has done everything to the utmost, that he will nevertheless come only to the rank of moderate orators, I will permit him to do what he wishes; I will not be greatly troublesome; but if he shall plainly be unfit and absurd, I will admonish him to restrain himself or to transfer himself to another study;

And yet, since we must discuss the orator, I must of necessity speak of the highest orator; for the force and nature of a thing, unless it be set before the eyes in its perfection, cannot be understood of what sort and how great it is. But I confess, Catulus, that I neither today live among those books and with those men, nor indeed—which you have rightly remembered—ever had any time set apart for learning, nor gave so much time to learning as my boyish age and the forensic holidays allowed me.

and that if those rhetorical teachers embraced so great a power of the greatest matters in their art, he asked why their books were stuffed full of proems and epilogues and trifles of this sort—for so he called them—while not a letter was found in their books about founding states, about writing laws, about equity, about justice, about good faith, about breaking desires, about shaping the characters of men.

for neither is he who can do best to be in any way deserted by our exhortation, nor is he who can do something to be deterred: of which the one seems to me to be of a certain divinity; the other—either not to do what you cannot do best, or to do what you do not do worst—of humanity; but that third, to cry out contrary to what becomes one and to what one can do, is the mark of a man who, as you, Catulus, said of a certain bawler, gathers by his own domestic crying as many witnesses as possible of his own folly.

And, if you ask, Catulus, what I feel about that learning, I do not think that so much time is needful to an ingenious man, and to one who looks toward the forum, the senate-house, causes, the commonwealth, as those have taken to themselves for whom life failed while still learning: for all the arts are handled otherwise by those who transfer them to use, otherwise by those who, delighting in the very handling of the arts, are going to do nothing else in life. This master of the Samnite gladiators is now of extreme old age and practises daily, for he cares for nothing else: but Quintus Velocius had learned it in addition as a boy; yet, because he was fit for it and had thoroughly mastered it, he was, as it is in Lucilius, "though himself a good Samnite, in the school and with the foils sharp enough for anyone;" but he gave more pains to the forum, to his friends, to his household estate. Valerius sang daily, for he was an actor: what else should he do?

The precepts themselves he was wont so to mock, that he showed that those men were not only without that prudence which they claimed for themselves, but did not even understand this very method and way of speaking: for he thought that the chief thing for the orator was that he himself should appear to those before whom he pleaded such as he wished to be; that this was brought about by dignity of life, concerning which those rhetorical teachers had left nothing in their precepts; and that those who listened should be so affected in mind as the orator wished them to be affected; which likewise could in no way be done unless he who spoke had learned in how many ways, by what means, and by what kind of speech the minds of men are moved in each direction; but that these things were hidden away deep in the very midst of philosophy, which those rhetoricians had not touched even with the tips of their lips.

Of him, then, who shall be such that he must be exhorted and helped, let us so speak that we may hand down to him only those things which experience has taught us, so that, with us as guides, he may come whither we ourselves came without a guide, since we cannot teach him better things.

But Numerius Furius, our friend, sings when it suits him, for he is a head of a household, he is a Roman knight; as a boy he learned what had to be learned. The same principle holds for these greatest arts; day and night we used to see Quintus Tubero, a man of the highest virtue and prudence, giving his attention to philosophy; but his uncle Africanus you could hardly understand to be doing it, when nevertheless he was doing it. These things are easily learned, if you both take as much as is needful, and have one who can teach faithfully,

These things Menedemus tried to refute by examples rather than by arguments; for, reciting from memory many passages excellently written from the speeches of Demosthenes, he showed that that man was not ignorant, in moving the minds of judges or of the people in any direction by speaking, of the means by which he attained those things which the other denied that anyone could know without philosophy.

And, to begin with our friend, this Sulpicius, Catulus, I first heard as a very young man in a small cause, with his voice and form and movement of body and the other things apt for this function of which we are inquiring, but with a speech swift and impetuous, which was of his talent, and with words boiling over and a little too redundant, which was of his age. I did not despise it; for I wish fecundity to pour itself forth in a young man; for, as in vines, those things which have poured themselves forth too much are more easily checked than, if the stock have no strength, new shoots are roused up by cultivation; likewise I wish there to be in a young man that from which I may prune something; for there cannot be lasting sap in that which has too quickly run through to maturity.

and know also yourself how to learn; but if for your whole life you wish to do nothing else, the very handling and inquiry daily begets of itself something which you may track down with a slothful delight. But it is always pleasant to learn; as I, if I wished to play excellently at dice, or were held by the zeal of the ball-game, perhaps even though I could not attain it; but others, because they do these things excellently, take delight in them more vehemently than the matter demands—as Titius in the ball, Brulla in the dice.

To him Charmadas replied that he did not deny that Demosthenes had the highest prudence and the highest power of speaking, but that whether he had been able to do this by his own talent, or—what was agreed—had been a zealous hearer of Plato, the question was not what that man had been able to do, but what those rhetoricians taught.

I saw at once his natural quality, and I did not let the moment slip, and I exhorted him to think the forum his school for learning, and to choose for his master whomever he wished; me, indeed, if he would hear me, Lucius Crassus: which he eagerly caught at, and affirmed that he would so do, and even added—for the sake of compliment, of course—that I too should be his master. Scarcely a year had passed from this conversation of my exhortation, when he accused Gaius Norbanus, I defending: it is not credible what a difference there seemed to me between him who then was and him who had been a year before. Altogether nature itself was leading him toward that magnificent and splendid kind of Crassus, but that could not have profited him enough, unless he had bent himself with the same zeal and imitation, and had so accustomed himself to speak as to regard Crassus with his whole mind and his whole soul.

Wherefore there is no reason why anyone should dread the magnitude of the arts from this, that old men learn them; for either old men have approached them, or are detained in their studies even to old age, or are the slowest of learners; the matter, indeed, in my opinion, so stands that, unless each man could learn a thing quickly, he could never learn it thoroughly at all.'

Often, too, he was carried in his discourse to the point of arguing that there was no art of speaking at all; and when he had taught this by arguments—that we were so born that we could both flatter subtly those from whom anything had to be sought, and threateningly terrify our adversaries, and set forth a deed, and confirm what we maintained, and refute what was said against us, and, at the last, deprecate something and complain—in which things all the orator's faculty was concerned—and that practice and exercise sharpened the prudence of understanding and quickened the readiness of speech;

Therefore let this be first in my precepts—that we point out whom he should imitate; then let exercise be added, by which, in imitating, he may fashion and express him whom he has chosen, not as I have often known many imitators to do, who pursue in imitation either those things which are easy, or even those which are conspicuous and almost faulty.

'Now, now,' said Catulus, 'I understand, Crassus, what you say; and, by Hercules, I assent; I see well enough that you, a man most keen to learn thoroughly, had time enough to know those things which you speak of.' 'Do you persist,' said Crassus, 'in thinking that I say the things I say about myself, not about the matter? But now, if you please, let us return to our subject.' 'Indeed,' said Catulus, 'it pleases me.'

then, too, he relied upon a store of examples. For first, as if of set purpose, he used to say that no writer of an art had ever been even moderately eloquent, going back as far as some Corax and Tisias, who were agreed to have been the inventors and founders of that art; but he named certain countless men, most eloquent, who had neither learned those things nor cared at all to know them; among whom—whether mocking, or because he thought so and had so heard—he brought forward me, as one of that number, who had not learned those things and yet, as he himself said, could do something in speaking; in one of which I readily agreed with him, that I had learned nothing, but in the other I thought I was being mocked by him, or that he himself was mistaken.

Nothing is easier than to imitate someone's dress, or carriage, or movement; but if there be even something faulty, to take that and to be like in that fault is no great thing—as that man who, even now, his voice lost, rages in the commonwealth, Fufius, does not attain the sinews in speaking of Gaius Fimbria, which yet that man had, but imitates the distortion of the mouth and the broadness of the words; but yet that man neither knew how to choose whom he would most resemble, and in the very man he had chosen wished to imitate even the faults;

Then Crassus said: 'To what, then, does this so long and so deeply-fetched discourse look? These two parts, which remain to me—of illuminating speech and of crowning the whole of eloquence, of which the one demands that we speak ornately, the other aptly—have this power: that the speech may be as pleasant as possible, may flow as much as possible into the senses of those who hear, and may be furnished with as many things as possible;

He denied, indeed, that there was any art except such as is contained in things thoroughly known and clearly perceived, tending to one issue, and never deceiving; but all those things which are handled by orators are doubtful and uncertain, since they are both spoken by men who do not fully grasp them all, and heard by men to whom knowledge is not to be imparted, but only a brief, false, or at least obscure opinion.

but he who shall do as he ought must first be watchful in choosing; then, in him whom he has approved, must pursue most diligently those things which most excel. For what cause do you think there is why the several ages have brought forth almost several kinds of speaking? but this forensic, litigious, sharp instrument, drawn from the opinions of the crowd, is scanty and indeed beggarly; that again, which these men hand down who profess to be teachers of speaking, is not much greater than that common and forensic kind: we need apparatus and choice materials, gathered, fetched, and brought together from every side, as you, Caesar, must do for next year, as I laboured to do in my aedileship, because I did not think I could satisfy this people with everyday and homely materials.

In short, he then seemed to persuade me that there was no art of speaking at all, and that no one could speak either cleverly or copiously unless he had learned those things which were said in philosophy by the most learned men; in which Charmadas used vehemently to admire your talent, Crassus: that I seemed to him very easy in listening, you very combative in disputing.

The most ancient, of whom indeed the writings survive, are well-nigh Pericles and Alcibiades, and of the same age Thucydides—subtle, acute, brief, abounding more in thoughts than in words: it could not have happened that there should be one kind common to all, unless they set someone before themselves for imitation. These were followed by Critias, Theramenes, Lysias: many of Lysias's writings exist; some of Critias's; of Theramenes we hear; all even then retained that sap of Pericles, but were of a somewhat richer thread.

The choosing and arranging and rounding-off of words is a matter of easy method, or even of mere practice without method; but of matter there is a great forest, which, since the Greeks now no longer held it, and for that reason our youth nearly unlearned it in the very learning, even Latin teachers of speaking have, if you please, arisen within these two years; whom I, as censor, had removed by my edict—not because, as some said they alleged, I did not wish the genius of the young to be sharpened, but, on the contrary, I did not wish their genius to be blunted and their effrontery strengthened.

And so I myself, led by this same opinion, wrote even that in a certain little book which, unawares and against my will, slipped out and came into the hands of men—that I had known some men who were able speakers, but as yet no one eloquent; for I judged him an able speaker who could speak with sufficient acuteness and clarity before ordinary men according to the common opinion of mankind, but the eloquent man to be one who could in a more wonderful and magnificent way amplify and adorn whatever he wished, and could hold in his mind and memory all the sources of all things that pertain to speaking. And if this be difficult for us, who, before we entered upon learning, are overwhelmed by canvassing and the forum, yet let it be set down as resting in the nature of things:

Behold, then, there arose Isocrates, from whose school, as from the Trojan horse, none but leaders came forth; but of them some wished to be illustrious in the procession, some in the battle-line. And both those—Theopompus, Ephorus, Philistus, Naucrates, and many others—differ in their natures, but in their inclination are like both one another and their master; and those who betook themselves to causes, as Demosthenes, Hyperides, Lycurgus, Aeschines, Dinarchus, and several others, though they were not equal among themselves, yet were all engaged in the same kind of imitating the truth, and so long as the imitation of them remained, so long did that kind of speaking and the zeal for it live;

For among the Greeks, of whatever sort they were, I saw nevertheless that there was, besides this exercise of the tongue, some learning and some science worthy of humanity; but these new teachers I understood could teach nothing except to be bold, which, even when joined with good things, is of itself greatly to be shunned; since this one thing was being handed down, and since it was a school of effrontery, I thought it was the part of a censor to provide that it should not creep further.

for I, so far as I divine by conjecture, and seeing how great talents there are among our countrymen, do not despair that there will some day be someone who, with a keener zeal than we are or have been, and with greater and earlier leisure and capacity for learning, and with greater toil and industry, when he has given himself to hearing, reading, and writing, will come forth as such an orator as we seek, who may rightly be called not only an able speaker but also eloquent; who yet, in my opinion, either is here already, namely Crassus, or, if anyone of equal talent shall both have heard and read and written more than this man here, will be able to add some little to him.'

but after these were extinguished, and all memory of them was gradually obscured and vanished, certain other softer and more relaxed kinds of speaking flourished. At this point Sulpicius said: 'It has fallen out, Crassus, beyond my hope and Cotta's, but greatly to the wish of us both, that you should glide into this discussion; for to us, coming hither, it seemed pleasant enough if, while you talked of other matters, we might nevertheless catch from your conversation something worth remembering; but that you should come into the very inmost discussion of this whole study, or art, or faculty, seemed scarcely to be hoped for by us.

This likeness, then, whoever wishes to attain by imitation, let him pursue it both by frequent and great exercises and most of all by writing; which if our Sulpicius would do, his speech would be much more compressed; in which now sometimes—as rustics are wont to say of plants in their greatest luxuriance—there is a certain rankness, which must be cropped away by the pen."

Speech, then, is adorned first by its character and by, as it were, a certain colour and flavour of its own; for that it be weighty, that it be sweet, that it be learned, that it be liberal, that it be admirable, that it be polished, that it have as much of feeling and of grief as is needful—this does not belong to single joints; these things are regarded in the whole body. That, furthermore, it be besprinkled, as it were, with the flowers of words and thoughts, this ought not to be spread evenly through the whole speech, but so distinguished that there be, as it were, certain ornaments and lights disposed as in an adornment.

For I, who from my earliest years have been fired with zeal for you both, and indeed with love for Crassus, since I never departed from him, was never able to draw a word from him about the power and method of speaking, although I had tried both through myself and often through Drusus; in which matter you, Antonius—I will speak truly—never failed me when I asked or inquired anything, and very often taught me what you were wont to observe in speaking.

Hereupon Sulpicius said: "You admonish me rightly, and it is grateful to me; but I do not think that even you, Antonius, have done much writing." Then he said: "As though I did not give others precepts which I myself lack: but yet I am thought not even to keep accounts; however, in the one matter judgement can be made from my private estate, and in the other from what I say, however little that is, what I do.

A kind of speaking, therefore, is to be chosen which most holds those who hear, and which not only delights, but delights without satiety; for I do not now think it is to be expected of me that I should warn you to take care lest your speech be thin, lest it be uncultivated, lest it be common, lest it be obsolete; something else, greater, both your genius and your age urge me to.

Now, since each of you has opened up the approach to those very things which we seek, and since Crassus was the first to begin this conversation, grant us this favour, that you set forth in detail what you think concerning every kind of speaking; which, if it be obtained from you, I shall give great thanks, Crassus, to this wrestling-ground and your Tusculan villa, and I shall far prefer your suburban gymnasium here to that famous Academy and Lyceum.'

And yet we see that there are many who imitate no one, and by their own nature attain what they wish without the likeness of anyone; which can rightly be observed in you, Caesar and Cotta; of whom the one has attained a certain charm and wit unusual at least to our orators, the other a most acute and most subtle kind of speaking; nor indeed does your contemporary Gaius Curio—whose father was in my opinion the most eloquent of those times—seem to me to imitate anyone greatly; who yet, by the weight and elegance and abundance of his words, has expressed a certain form and figure of speaking of his own; which I was best able to judge in that cause which he spoke against me before the centumviri on behalf of the brothers Cossus; in which nothing was wanting to him that not only a copious but even a wise orator ought to have.

For it is hard to say what is the cause why those things which most strike our senses with pleasure and most keenly move us by their first appearance are also those from which we are most quickly estranged by a certain disgust and satiety. How much more florid in the beauty and variety of colours are most things in new pictures than in old ones! Which, nevertheless, even if at the first sight they take us, do not long delight us; whereas we are held, in old paintings, by that very roughness and antiquity.

Then Crassus said: 'Nay rather, Sulpicius, let us ask Antonius, who both can do what you require and is wont to do it, as I hear you say; for that I have shrunk from this whole kind of discourse, and have very often refused you when you wished and pressed it, you yourself said a little while ago—which I did not do from pride or inhumanity, nor because I did not wish to comply with your most right and excellent zeal, especially since I had recognized you above all men as most born and fitted for speaking, but, by Hercules, from my unfamiliarity with that kind of disputation and my ignorance of those things which are handed down as if in an art.'

But, to lead at length to causes that man whom we have set up—and to those indeed in which there is a little more business, of trials and suits—someone perhaps will have laughed at this precept; for it is not so much acute as necessary, and rather of a not foolish admonisher than of a learned master—this we shall enjoin upon him first: that whatever causes he is going to handle, he should learn them diligently and thoroughly.

How much softer and more delicate in singing are the modulations and false notes than the sure and severe ones! Against which, however, not only the austere, but, if they are too often repeated, the multitude itself protests. This may be seen in the rest of the senses also: that we are less long delighted by unguents seasoned with the highest and sharpest sweetness than by these of moderate scent, and that what is felt to smell of the earth is more praised than what is felt to smell of saffron; that in the very touch there is a measure both of softness and of smoothness. Nay, even taste, which is of all the senses the most given to pleasure, and which is moved beyond the rest by sweetness, how quickly does it scorn and spit out what is very sweet! Who can use a sweet drink or food for any length of time? whereas in both kinds those things which lightly move the sense with pleasure most easily escape satiety.

Then Cotta said: 'Since we have obtained what seemed to us most difficult—that you should speak at all about these matters, Crassus—from now on it will be our own fault if we let you go before you have explained all that we shall ask.'

This is not taught in the school; for easy causes are brought to boys; 'the law forbids a foreigner to ascend the wall; he ascended; he repelled the enemy: he is accused.' There is no trouble in learning a cause of this kind; rightly, then, do they give no precepts about learning the cause. But in the forum the documents, the testimonies, the agreements, the compacts, the stipulations, the relationships, the connections, the decrees, the responses, in short the whole life of those who are engaged in the cause, must be learned; by neglect of which things we see most causes—and especially private ones, for they are often much more obscure—lost.

So in all things satiety is the nearest neighbour to the greatest pleasures; at which we may the less wonder in speech, in which we can judge, both from poets and from orators, that a thing which is neat, distinct, ornate, festive, without intermission, without reprehension, without variety, however brightly painted in vivid colours, whether poetry or oratory, cannot be lasting in its power to please. And the more quickly is offence taken at the curls and rouge of the orator or the poet, because in too much pleasure the senses are sated by nature, not by the mind; in writings and in speeches not by the judgement of the ears only, but even more by that of the mind, are the rouged faults detected.

'Concerning those things, I suppose,' said Crassus, 'as is wont to be written in formal declarations of acceptance: "such as I shall know and shall be able." ' Then Cotta said: 'For as to what you shall not be able or shall not know, who of us is so impudent as to demand that he should know or be able?' 'On that condition, then,' said Crassus, 'provided I be allowed to deny that I can do what I shall not be able, and to confess that I do not know what I shall not know, you may inquire at your own pleasure.'

Thus some, while they wish their own labour to be thought great, so that they may seem to flit about the whole forum and to go from cause to cause, plead causes that they have not learned; in which there is indeed that great offence either of negligence, in matters undertaken, or of treachery, in matters accepted; but there is also that, greater than they suppose, that no one can speak otherwise than most disgracefully about a matter which he does not know: so, while they despise the censure of indolence, which is the greater, they incur even that which they themselves the more shun, of slowness.

Wherefore, "well and excellently" let it be said to us as often as you please; but "prettily and festively" I would not have said too often; though I should wish that very exclamation "it could not be better" to be frequent; yet let that admiration and highest praise in speaking have nevertheless some shade and recess, that thereby what is illuminated may seem the more to stand out and be eminent.

'And so,' said Sulpicius, 'this is what we ask of you, on which Antonius just now set forth his view: do you think there is any art of speaking?' 'What?' said Crassus, 'do you now set before me, as before some idle and chattering little Greek, perhaps even learned and erudite, a little question on which I am to speak at my own pleasure? For when do you suppose I have cared for or thought about these things, and have not rather always laughed at the impudence of those men who, when they had sat down in a school, in a great crowd of men, bade anyone ask a question, if any wished to inquire anything?

For my part I am wont to take pains that each one should himself teach me about his own matter, and that no one else be present, that he may speak the more freely, and to plead the adversary's cause, that he may plead his own and bring out into the open whatever he has thought about his case: and so, when he has departed, I alone sustain three persons with the greatest equanimity of mind—my own, the adversary's, the judge's. Whatever point is such that it has more of help than of harm, this I judge must be spoken; where I find more of evil than of good, that I wholly reject and cast out.
