for a copiousness of matter begets a copiousness of words; and, if there is honour in the very matters of which one speaks, there arises from the matter a certain natural splendour in the words. Let only the man who shall speak or write be liberally trained by education and boyish learning, and burn with zeal, and be aided by nature, and, exercised in the indefinite debates of the universal kinds, have chosen the most ornate writers and orators to know and to imitate—and assuredly that man will by no means inquire of these masters how he should construct and illuminate his words; so easily, in the abundance of matter, does nature itself, if only it be exercised, glide of itself to the ornaments of speech, without a guide.'

But as to that which was said by you, that there are very many things which, unless the orator has them from nature, he would not be much helped by a master, I greatly agree with you, and in this respect I have approved most highly that supreme teacher, Apollonius of Alabanda, who, though he taught for pay, yet would not allow those whom he judged unable to turn out orators to waste their labour with him, but dismissed them, and was wont to urge and exhort each to that art for which he thought him fitted.

Then Catulus said: "I, indeed, am wont to admire this most of all in you—that, although you are most unlike one another in speaking, yet each of you so speaks that nothing seems to him to have been denied by nature or not conferred by learning; wherefore, Crassus, you will not deprive us of your sweetness, but, if anything has been omitted or left by Antonius, will set it forth; nor of you, Antonius, if you shall not have said something, shall we suppose that you could not, rather than that you preferred it to be said by Crassus."

Here Catulus said: 'Immortal gods, what a variety of matters, what force, what copiousness, Crassus, have you embraced, and from what narrow straits have you dared to lead the orator out and to place him in the kingdom of his ancestors! For we have received that those ancient teachers and authors of speaking thought no kind of discussion foreign to themselves, and were always versed in every method of speech;

For it is enough, in mastering the other arts, only to be like a man, and to be able to grasp in the mind and keep in the memory that which is handed down or even drummed in, even if one is somewhat slow; there is no requirement of nimbleness of tongue, of swiftness of words, in short, of those things which we cannot fashion for ourselves—face, expression, voice;

Hereupon Crassus said: "Why do you not, Antonius, omit those things which you have proposed, which none of these desire—from what topics those things which must be said in causes may be found; which, although they are said by you in a certain new and excellent way, are yet both easier in fact and common in the precepts; bring forth to us whence you draw those things which you most often handle, and always divinely."

of whom Elian Hippias, when he had come to Olympia at that great quinquennial celebration of the games, boasted, almost in the hearing of all Greece, that there was nothing in any art, of all things, which he himself did not know; and that he held not only these arts in which the liberal and ingenuous studies are contained—geometry, music, the knowledge of letters and of poets, and those things which are said about the natures of things, about the manners of men, about commonwealths—but that he had made with his own hand the ring which he had, the cloak in which he was clad, and the shoes with which he was shod.

but in the orator the acuteness of the dialecticians, the thoughts of the philosophers, the words almost of the poets, the memory of the jurisconsults, the voice of the tragedians, the gesture well-nigh of the greatest actors, must be sought; wherefore nothing rarer can be found in the race of men than a perfect orator; for those things which, if the artists of single arts have moderately attained them singly, are approved, unless they are all present in the highest degree in the orator, cannot be approved.'

"I will bring them forth, indeed," said he; "and that I may the more easily exact from you what I seek, I will refuse you nothing that you ask of me. Of my whole method in speaking, and of that very faculty which Crassus just now extolled to heaven in words, there are three things, as I said before: one of winning over men, another of teaching them, the third of stirring them up.

To be sure, he indeed went too far; but from this very thing the conjecture is easy how much those orators claimed for themselves of the most excellent arts, who did not reject even the meaner ones. What shall I say of Prodicus of Ceos, of Thrasymachus of Chalcedon, of Protagoras of Abdera? each one of whom, for those times, both discoursed and wrote very much about the nature of things.

Then Crassus said: 'And yet see, in a very slight and trifling art, how much more diligence is bestowed than in this matter which is agreed to be the greatest: for often I am wont to hear Roscius say that he has so far been able to find no pupil whom he could approve—not because there were not some who were tolerable, but because, if there were only some little fault, he himself could not bear it; for nothing is so conspicuous, nor so lasting in the memory, as that in which you have given offence.

Of these three parts the first requires gentleness of speech, the second acuteness, the third force; for it is necessary that he who is to adjudge the cause to us either incline toward us by an inclination of will, or be led by the arguments of the defence, or be compelled by an emotion of the mind. But since that part in which the unfolding and defence of the matters themselves is placed seems to contain all the doctrine, as it were, of this kind, of it we will speak first, and will say a few things; for there are few things which we seem to have, now handled by practice and as it were noted in the mind.

That very Gorgias of Leontini, to whom, as a patron, the orator yielded to the philosopher, as Plato would have it—who either was never conquered by Socrates, and that conversation of Plato is not true; or, if he was conquered, then doubtless Socrates was the more eloquent and the more fluent, and, as you call him, the more copious and the better orator—but he, in that very book of Plato, professes that he will speak most copiously about any matter whatever that is brought into debate and question; and he first of all dared in an assembly to demand on what subject each man wished to hear; to whom so great an honour was paid by Greece that to him alone of all men a statue not gilded, but golden, was set up at Delphi.

And so, that we may direct the orator's praise to this likeness of this actor, do you see how nothing is done by him except perfectly, nothing except with the highest grace, nothing except so as is becoming and such as moves and delights all? And so he has long since attained this—that whoever excels in any art is called the Roscius of his kind. This perfection and completeness, which I desire in the orator, and from which I myself am far removed, I demand impudently; for I wish indulgence for myself, but I do not myself grant it to others; for him who cannot, who does faultily, who, in short, is unbecoming, I think must be thrust down, as Apollonius bade, to that which he can do.'

And to you, Crassus, wisely admonishing, we will gladly assent—that we should leave aside the defences of particular causes which the masters are wont to hand down to boys, but should open up those heads whence all disputation is drawn for every cause and every speech. For neither, as often as some word must be written by us, must the letters of that word be sought out by thought; nor, as often as a cause must be pleaded, must we revolve back to the arguments set apart for that cause, but must have certain topics which, as letters for writing a word, so may at once occur for unfolding a cause.

But these whom I have named, and many besides, the highest teachers of speaking, existed at one time; from which it can be understood that the matter so stands as you, Crassus, say, and that the name of orator flourished among the ancients in Greece with a certain greater copiousness or glory.

'Do you, then,' said Sulpicius, 'bid me, or this Cotta here, learn the civil law or military affairs? For who can attain to those supreme things, perfect in every kind?' Then he said: 'I have indeed set forth all these things because I have recognized in you a certain excellent and remarkable natural aptitude for speaking; and I have fitted my discourse not so much to deter those who could not, as to whet you, who could; and although I have perceived in each of you the highest talent and zeal, yet those things which are placed in outward appearance, of which I have perhaps said more than the Greeks are wont to say, in you, Sulpicius, are divine;

But these topics can at length profit only that orator who is versed either in the practice of affairs, which age finally brings, or in the hearing and reflection which zeal and diligence have outrun in advance of age. For if you bring me a man however learned, however keen and acute in thinking, however ready in delivery, if he be at the same time a stranger to the custom of the state, to its precedents, its institutions, its characters and the inclinations of his fellow-citizens, those topics from which arguments are drawn will profit him little: I need a worked-over mind, as a field not once ploughed but ploughed again, that it may bring forth better and larger crops; and the working-over is practice, hearing, reading, letters.

And on this account I the more doubt whether more of praise is to be assigned to you, or of blame to the Greeks: since you, born in another tongue and amid other manners, in a most busy state, distracted either by the affairs of private men, almost all of them, or by the administration of the whole world and the governance of the highest command, have nevertheless comprehended so great a force and knowledge of matters, and joined all of it with the science and exercise of one who is to prevail in the state by counsel and oratory; while they, born amid letters and ardent for these studies, but melting away in leisure, have not only acquired nothing, but have not even preserved what was left and handed down and their own.'

for I think I have heard no one more fit either in the movement of the body or in the very carriage and form, nor of fuller or sweeter voice; and those to whom these things have been given less by nature can yet attain this—to use what they have moderately and skilfully, and so as not to be unbecoming. For this is most of all to be avoided, and on this one point it is least easy to give precepts, not only for me, who speak of these matters like a single head of a household, but even for that very Roscius, whom I often hear say that the chief point of the art is to be becoming, which yet is the one thing that cannot be handed down by art.

And first let him see the nature of the cause, which is never hidden—whether it is asked whether a thing was done, or of what kind it is, or what name it has; which being perceived, there at once occurs, by a certain natural prudence—not by those subtractions which those men teach—what makes the cause, that is, that which, being removed, the controversy cannot stand; then what comes into judgement: which those men bid us seek thus: 'Opimius killed Gracchus. What makes the cause? That he did it for the commonwealth's sake, when, by a decree of the senate, he had called to arms. Take this away, there will be no cause. But Decius denies that this very thing was lawful against the laws. It will come, then, into judgement whether it was lawful, by a decree of the senate, for the sake of saving the commonwealth.' These things, indeed, are plain and set in vulgar prudence; but those things must be sought which both the accuser and the defender ought to bring forward as arguments looking to that which comes into judgement.

Then Crassus said: 'Not in this one matter alone, Catulus, but in many others besides, the magnitudes of the arts have been diminished by the distribution of the parts and by separation. Or do you suppose that, when there was that famous Hippocrates of Cos, there were then other physicians who healed diseases, others who healed wounds, others who healed the eyes? Was geometry, when Euclid or Archimedes handled it, was music when Damon or Aristoxenus handled it, were letters themselves when Aristophanes or Callimachus handled them, so torn in pieces that no one embraced the whole kind, and that one set apart for himself one part, another another, in which to labour?

But, if you please, let us turn the conversation elsewhere, and talk for once in our own manner, not the rhetorical.' 'By no means,' said Cotta; 'for now we must entreat you, since you keep us in this study and do not dismiss us to another art, to explain to us, whatever it is, that power you have in speaking—for we are not too greedy; we are content with that moderate eloquence of yours—and we ask this of you (that we may attain no more than that little which you have attained in speaking), since you say that those things which are to be sought from nature are not too much lacking to us, what besides you think must be acquired.'

And here that must be seen in which is the greatest error of those masters to whom we send our children—not that this, indeed, greatly pertains to speaking, but that you may see what kind this is of those who seem learned to themselves. It is dull and unpolished: for in dividing the modes of speeches they set up two kinds of causes: one they call that in which, without persons and times, it is inquired about the universal kind; the other, that which is defined by fixed persons and times; ignorant that all controversies are referred to the force and nature of the universal kind;

For my part I have often heard this from my father and from my father-in-law: that our own men too, who wished to excel in the glory of wisdom, were wont to embrace all things which at least this state then knew. They remembered Sextus Aelius; but Manius Manilius we ourselves even saw walking across the forum; which was a sign that he who did this offered to all his fellow-citizens the abundance of his counsel; to whom of old, both as they thus walked and as they sat at home in their chairs, men came in such wise as to consult them not only about the civil law, but also about the marrying of a daughter, the buying of a farm, the tilling of a field, in short about every duty or business.

Then Crassus, smiling, said: 'What do you suppose, Cotta, except zeal and a certain ardour of love? Without which, as nothing distinguished in life can be achieved by anyone, so certainly this which you seek will never be attained by any. And indeed I do not see that you need be exhorted to this, you who, since you are troublesome even to me, I understand to be already burning too much with desire.

for in that very cause of which I spoke before, the person of Opimius pertains nothing to the orator's topics, nothing that of Decius; about the universal kind itself there is an unlimited question—whether he seems liable to punishment who has slain a citizen, by a decree of the senate, for the sake of preserving the fatherland, when this was not lawful by the laws; in short, there is no cause in which that which comes into judgement is inquired about by the persons of the defendants and not by the universal doubt of the kinds themselves.

This was the wisdom of that ancient Publius Crassus, this of Tiberius Coruncanius, this of the great-grandfather of my son-in-law, Scipio, a most prudent man—all of whom were pontiffs maximi, so that to them reference was made about all matters divine and human; and the same men in the senate and before the people and in the causes of their friends and at home and in war showed forth their counsel and their fidelity.

But assuredly studies avail nothing toward reaching any goal, unless you have learned that which will carry and lead you to that which you aim at. Wherefore, since you lay upon me a somewhat lighter burden, and inquire of me not about the orator's art, but about this faculty of mine, however small it be, I will set forth to you a certain method of my own practice, not very recondite, nor very difficult, nor magnificent, nor weighty, which I once was wont to use, when, as a young man, it was permitted me to engage in that study.'

Nay even, in those very cases where it is disputed about the fact—whether Decius took moneys against the laws—the arguments both of the charges and of the defence ought to be referred to the kind and the universal nature: because he is extravagant, to luxury; because greedy of another's property, to avarice; because seditious, to turbulent and bad citizens; because he is accused by many, to the kind of witnesses; and on the contrary, what is said for the defendant, all must necessarily be revolved from the time and the man to the common heads of things and kinds.

For what was wanting to Marcus Cato, besides this most polished learning, transmarine and foreign? Did he, because he had learned the civil law, not plead causes? or, because he was able to plead, did he neglect the knowledge of law? In both kinds he both laboured and excelled. Was he, on account of this favour gathered from the affairs of private men, the slower in undertaking the commonwealth? No one was braver before the people, no one a better senator; and the same man was easily the best general; in short, nothing in this state in those times could be known or learned which he did not both investigate and know, and then also set down in writing.

Then Sulpicius said: 'O day longed for by us, Cotta! For that which I could never attain by entreaties, nor by waylaying, nor by spying—to see, or even to suspect from his copyist and reader Diphilus, what Crassus did for the sake of meditating or speaking—that I hope we have attained, and shall now learn all from himself which we have long desired.'

And these, perhaps, to a man not quickly grasping in mind all things that are in the nature of things, may seem very many, which come into judgement when it is inquired about the fact; but yet the multitude is of charges and of defences, not unlimited of topics.

Now, on the contrary, most men come to the obtaining of honours and to the governing of the commonwealth bare and unarmed, furnished with no knowledge of matters, with no science. But if anyone, one out of many, excels, he gives himself airs, if he brings one single thing—either warlike valour, or some military experience, which indeed have now grown obsolete; or knowledge of the law, and not even of the whole of it; for the pontifical law, which is connected with it, no one learns; or eloquence, which they think placed in shouting and in the running of words; but of the fellowship and kinship of all the good arts, in short of the very virtues themselves, they know nothing.

Then Crassus said: 'And yet I think, Sulpicius, when you have heard, you will not so much admire these things which I shall say, as judge then, when you desired to hear them, that there was no reason why you desired them; for I shall say nothing recondite, nothing worthy of your expectation, nothing either unheard by you or new to anyone. For, to begin with—a thing worthy of a man freeborn and liberally educated—I shall not deny that I have learned those common and well-worn precepts: first, that it is the duty of the orator to speak in a manner adapted to persuading;

But those things which, when it is not disputed about the fact, are inquired of what kind they are—if you count them from the defendants, they are both countless and obscure; if from the matters, they are both quite moderate and clear; for if we place Mancinus's cause in Mancinus alone, as often as a man whom the pater patratus has surrendered shall not have been received, so often a new cause will arise; but if that controversy makes the cause—whether he whom the pater patratus has surrendered, if he be not received, seems to have the right of return—then the name of Mancinus pertains nothing to the art of speaking nor to the arguments of Mancinus's defence;

But, to bring my discourse back to the Greeks—whom we cannot do without in this kind of conversation, for, as examples of virtue are to be sought from our own men, so of learning from them—seven men are said to have existed at one time who both were held and were called wise: all these, except Thales of Miletus, presided over their own states. Who in those same times is recorded to have been more learned, or whose eloquence more furnished with letters, than Pisistratus'? who is said to have been the first to arrange the books of Homer, formerly confused, in the order in which we now have them. He indeed was not useful to his fellow-citizens, but he so flourished in eloquence that he excelled in letters and learning.
next, that all speech is either about an inquiry into a matter unlimited, without designation of persons and times, or about a matter placed in fixed persons and times;

and, if besides the dignity or unworthiness of the man brings anything, it is outside the question, and yet that very speech must necessarily be referred to the disputation of the universal kind. These things I do not dispute with the purpose of refuting learned men; although they are to be censured who, in defining the kind, describe these causes as placed in persons and times; for although times and persons come in, yet it must be understood that the causes depend not on these, but on the kind of the question.

What of Pericles? of whose force of speaking we have so received it, that, when he spoke against the will of the Athenians, more severely, for the safety of his country, yet that very thing which he said against the popular men seemed to all popular and pleasant; on whose lips the old comic poets, even when they spoke ill of him (which was then permitted to be done at Athens), said that charm had dwelt, and that there was in him so great a force that he left, as it were, certain stings in the minds of those who had heard him. But this man no declaimer had taught to bark at the water-clock, but, as we have received, that famous Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, a man supreme in the knowledge of the greatest matters: and so this man, excelling in learning, in counsel, in eloquence, presided over Athens for forty years, both in civil affairs and at the same time in war.

and that in both cases, whatever comes into controversy, in it the question is wont to be either whether a thing was done, or, if it was done, of what kind it is, or even by what name it is called, or, what some add, whether it seems to have been rightly done;

But this is nothing to me; for we ought to have no contest with those men; it is enough only that it be understood that they have not even attained this, which in so great leisure, even without this forensic exercise, they could have effected—to distinguish the kinds of things and to set them forth a little more subtly.

What of Critias? what of Alcibiades? not good indeed to their own states, but certainly learned and eloquent—were they not trained in the Socratic discussions? Who polished Dion of Syracuse with all the branches of learning? Was it not Plato? And the same man, a master not only of his tongue but also of his mind and his virtue, impelled, equipped, and armed him for the liberating of his country. Did Plato, then, instruct this Dion in other arts, Isocrates that most illustrious man Timotheus, the son of Conon a most excellent general—himself a supreme general and a most learned man—in others? or that Pythagorean Lysis the Theban Epaminondas, perhaps the one supreme man of all Greece, in others? or Xenophon Agesilaus? or Philolaus Archytas of Tarentum? or Pythagoras himself all that ancient Greece of Italy, which was once called Magna?

that controversies arise also from the interpretation of a writing, in which either something is written ambiguously, or contradictorily, or so that the writing dissents from the intention; and that to all these parts there are subjoined certain proper arguments.

But this, as I said, is nothing to me; that is to me, and much more to you, our Cotta and Sulpicius: in the way in which those men's arts now stand, the multitude of causes is to be dreaded; for it is unlimited, if it is placed in persons—as many men, so many causes; but if it is referred to the universal questions of the kinds, it is so moderate and few that all diligent and mindful and sober orators ought to have them run through in mind and, I may almost say, conned by heart; unless perchance you think that Lucius Crassus learned the cause from Manius Curius, and for that reason brought forward many points, why, though no posthumous son had been born, Curius ought nevertheless to be the heir of Coponius:

For my part I do not think so; for I see thus: that there was one single learning of all things which were worthy of a learned man and of one who wished to excel in the commonwealth; and that those who had received it, if they had been likewise strong in genius for delivery, and had given themselves also to speaking, nature not resisting, had excelled in eloquence.

But of cases which are separated from the general inquiry, that some are concerned with trials, some with deliberations; that there is also a third kind, which is placed in praising or blaming men; and that there are certain topics which we use in trials, in which equity is sought; others in deliberations, which are all directed to the advantage of those to whom we give counsel; others likewise in panegyrics, in which all things are referred to the dignity of the persons;

the name of Coponius or Curius pertained nothing to the abundance of arguments, nor to the force and nature of the cause; the whole question was in the universal kind of the matter and the business, not in the time and the names: when it is so written, 'if a son be born to me, and he die before, etc., then let that man be my heir,' whether he seems to be heir who is appointed heir, the son being dead—the question of perpetual law and of the universal kind requires not the names of men, but the method of speaking and the sources of arguments.

And so Aristotle himself, when he saw that Isocrates flourished in the nobility of his disciples, because he had transferred his discussions from forensic and civil causes to an empty elegance of language, suddenly changed almost the whole form of his teaching, and uttered a certain verse of Philoctetes a little altered: for he says it is base for him to be silent, while he suffers barbarians—the other, while he suffers Isocrates—to speak; and so he adorned and illuminated all that learning, and joined the knowledge of things with the exercise of speech. Nor indeed did this escape that most wise king Philip, who summoned this man as a teacher for his son Alexander, that from the same man he might receive both precepts of action and of speaking.

and that, since all the power and faculty of the orator is distributed into five parts—that he ought first to find what he should say; then to dispose and arrange what he has found, not only in order but also with a certain weight and judgement; then to clothe and adorn these things with speech; afterward to guard them with memory; and finally to deliver them with dignity and grace.

In which even these our jurisconsults hinder us from learning and deter us; for I see that in the books of Cato and of Brutus it is generally reported by name what each man answered to some man or woman about a point of law; I suppose so that we might think that the cause of consultation or doubt was in the men, not in the matter; so that, because men were countless, we, disheartened, might cast away the wish to learn together with the hope of learning thoroughly. But these things Crassus will some day unfold for us and set forth, described by kinds; for—lest perchance you do not know—yesterday he promised us this, Catulus, that he would gather the civil law, which is now diffused and scattered, into fixed kinds, and reduce it to an easy art."

Now if anyone wishes to call that philosopher who hands down to us copiousness of matter and of speech an orator, he may, so far as I am concerned; or if he prefers to call this orator, whom I say has wisdom joined to eloquence, a philosopher, I will not hinder it; provided only this be agreed: that neither the speechlessness of him who knows a matter but cannot explain it by speaking, nor the ignorance of him to whom matter is wanting but words are not lacking, is to be praised; of which, if one or the other were to be chosen, I for my part should prefer an inarticulate prudence to a talkative folly; but if we inquire what one thing excels above all, the palm must be given to the learned orator;

I had learned and received this also: that, before we speak of the matter, we should at the outset conciliate the minds of those who listen; then set forth the matter; afterward establish the controversy; then confirm that which we maintain; afterward refute what was said against us; and at the end of the speech amplify and exalt those things which were in our favour, and weaken and break those which were on the side of our adversaries.

"And indeed," said Catulus, "that is by no means difficult for Crassus, who both learned what could be learned of the law, and what was wanting to those who taught him, he himself will supply, so that he can either aptly arrange or ornately illustrate what is in the law." "Therefore," said Antonius, "we shall learn those things from Crassus then, when he has betaken himself, as he intends, from the crowd and the benches into leisure and the chair."

whom, if they suffer to be also a philosopher, the controversy is removed; but if they shall sever them, they will be the lower in this, that in the perfect orator is contained all their science, while in the knowledge of the philosophers eloquence is not necessarily contained; which, however much it be despised by them, must nevertheless be seen to add a certain crown to their arts.' When Crassus had said these things, both he himself was silent for a little while, and there was silence on the part of the rest.

I had also heard those things which are handed down about the ornaments of the speech itself, in which it is enjoined: first, that we speak purely and in good Latin; then plainly and clearly; then with elegance; afterward fittingly and, as it were, becomingly to the dignity of the subject; and I had learned the precepts of each particular.

"This indeed I have often heard from him," said Catulus, "when he said it was now fixed for him to retire from the courts and causes; but, as I am wont myself to say to him, it will not be allowed; for neither will he suffer his aid often to be implored in vain by good men, nor will the state bear it with an even mind, which, if it lacks the voice of Lucius Crassus, will think itself robbed of a certain ornament." "Why, by Hercules," said Antonius, "if these things have been truly said by Catulus, you must live with me in the same mill, Crassus; and let us yield that yawning and drowsy wisdom to the leisure of the Scaevolae and the other blessed ones."

Then Cotta said: 'For my part, Crassus, I cannot complain that you seem to me to have discussed something other than that which you had undertaken; for you have brought forward somewhat more than was assigned and announced to you by us; but certainly, as your parts were that you should speak about the illuminating of speech, and you had yourself already entered upon it and had distributed all the praise of speech into four parts, when, about the first two, you had spoken sufficiently for us indeed, but, as you yourself said, quickly and scantily, you had made two remaining for yourself—in what manner we might speak first ornately, then aptly:

Nay, even those things which were most proper to nature, yet I had seen that art was applied to these very things; for of delivery and of memory I had tasted certain brief precepts, but with much exercise. For in these matters, generally, all the teaching of those artists is concerned; and if I should say that this gives me no help, I should lie; for it has certain things, as it were, for reminding the orator to what he should refer each thing, and looking to which he may stray less from whatever he has set before himself.

Hereupon Crassus smiled gently and said: "Only weave to the end, Antonius, what you have begun; but that yawning wisdom, as soon as I have fled to it, will claim me into liberty." "Of this topic, which I have just begun, this is the end," said Antonius; "since it has been understood that not in the countless persons of men nor in the unlimited variety of times, but in the kinds and natures of causes, are all things placed which are called into doubt, but that the kinds are defined not only in number but also in fewness, so that those who were zealous of speaking might grasp the material of speech which belonged to each kind, described in all its topics, furnished and adorned—I mean in facts and thoughts.

when you had entered upon this, suddenly, as it were, a certain tide of your genius snatched you far from the land and drew you away into the deep, almost out of the sight of us all; for, having embraced all knowledge of things, you did not indeed hand it down to us—for there was not time so short for that—but among these I know not what you have accomplished; me at least you have driven wholly into the Academy. In which I should wish that to be true which you have often laid down—that it is not necessary to spend one's age, and that he can discern all those things who has only looked upon them; but even if it is sometimes thicker going, or if I am the slower, assuredly I shall never rest nor be wearied before I have grasped those ambiguous ways and methods of theirs, of disputing both for all things and against all things.'

But I understand this power to be in all the precepts, not that orators, by following them, have attained the praise of eloquence, but that certain men have observed and collected those things which eloquent men did of their own accord; so that eloquence has not arisen from art, but art from eloquence; which yet, as I said before, I do not cast out; for it is, even if less necessary for speaking well, yet not ungentlemanly for knowing;

These by their own force will bring forth words, which always seem to me at least sufficiently adorned, if they are of such a kind that the matter itself seems to have brought them forth; and if you ask the truth, what seems true to me at least—for I can affirm nothing else but my own opinion and view—this equipment of causes and of the universal kinds we ought to bring into the forum, and not, as each matter is brought to us, then at last to search out the topics from which we may dig out arguments; which indeed can be thoroughly handled, with zeal applied and practice, by all who have but moderately considered them; but yet the mind must be referred to those heads and to those topics, which I have now often named, from which all things invented are drawn for every speech; and this whole thing, whether of art or of observation or of habit, is to know the regions within which you may hunt out and track down what you seek:

Then Caesar said: 'One thing out of your discourse, Crassus, has especially moved me—that you denied that one who had not quickly learned a thing could ever learn it thoroughly at all; so that it is not difficult for me to make the trial, and either at once to grasp those things which you with your words have lifted to the sky, or, if I shall not be able, not to waste time, since I can nevertheless be content with these our own attainments.'

and a certain exercise must be undertaken by you—although you indeed have long been in the course: but for those who are entering the lists, and who can even now, by a kind of play exercise, learn beforehand and practise those things which must be done in the forum as in the battle-line.'

when you have hedged about in thought all that region, if only you have become thoroughly versed in the practice of affairs, nothing will escape you, and everything that is in the matter will occur and fall in your way. 'This very thing,' said Sulpicius, 'we wish to know; and yet those things which you have briefly run through about the art, we long to hear, although they are not unheard by us either; but those things presently; now we ask what you think about the exercise itself.'

diligence, I say, which in all matters, as in defending causes, avails most. This must be especially cultivated by us; this must always be applied; there is nothing which it does not attain: that the cause be thoroughly known, which I said at the outset, is of diligence; that we listen attentively to the adversary, and catch not only his thoughts but even all his words, in short perceive all his looks, which generally indicate the feelings of the mind, is of diligence;

Then Crassus said: 'You ask for common things, Sulpicius, and not unknown to you: for who has not taught, instituted, even left in writing, about that kind? But I will humour you, and will briefly set forth to you only those things which are known to me; I shall think, however, that we must return to those who are the authors and inventors of these, to be sure minute, matters.

'For my part I approve those things,' said Crassus, 'which you are wont to do—that, some cause being set down very like those cases which are brought into the forum, you should speak as nearly as possible adapted to the truth; but most men in this only exercise the voice—and that not skilfully—and their lungs, and quicken the swiftness of the tongue, and delight in the abundance of words; in which they are deceived by that which they have heard, that men, by speaking, are wont to make themselves able to speak;

yet to do this dissemblingly, lest he seem to himself to gain anything, is of prudence; then that the mind be revolved in those topics which I shall set forth a little later, that it may thoroughly insinuate itself into the cause, that it be intent with care and reflection, is of diligence; that to these things it apply, as a kind of light, the memory, the voice, the strength, is of diligence.

All speech, then, is made up of words; of which we must first see the principle singly, then in combination. For there is a certain adornment of speech which is from single words; another, which consists of words joined together. Therefore we use words either those which are proper and are, as it were, the fixed names of things, born almost together with the things themselves; or those which are transferred and placed, as it were, in another's place; or those which we coin and make ourselves.

for that is also truly said, that men most easily attain, by speaking badly, to speak badly. Wherefore in those very exercises, although it is useful also to speak often on the sudden, yet it is more useful, when time has been taken for thinking, to speak in a more prepared and careful way. But the chief thing is that which—to speak truly—we do least (for it is a matter of great labour, which most of us shun), to write as much as possible. The pen is the best and most excellent former and master of speaking; and not without reason; for if meditation and reflection easily surpass a sudden and chance speech, this very speech will assuredly be surpassed by diligent and careful writing.

Between talent indeed and diligence very little room is left for art: art shows only where you should seek, and where that is which you are eager to find; the rest are in care, attention of mind, reflection, vigilance, assiduity, labour; I will embrace it in one word, which we have now often used—diligence; in which one virtue all the remaining virtues are contained.

In proper words, then, is that praise of the orator, that he shun the abject and obsolete, and use the choice and brilliant, in which there seems to be something full and sonorous. But in this kind of proper words a certain selection is to be made, and that is to be weighed by a certain judgement of the ears; in which the habit also of speaking well avails most.

For all the topics, whether of art or of a certain talent and prudence, which only inhere in the matter about which we write, present themselves and meet us as we search and contemplate with the whole edge of our talent; and all the thoughts and all the words which are most brilliant of each kind must of necessity come under and succeed beneath the point of the pen; then the very arrangement and shaping of words is perfected in writing, in a certain oratorical, not poetic, rhythm and measure.

For we see how the philosophers abound in abundance of speech, who—as I think, but you, Catulus, know these things better—give no precepts of speaking, nor on that account the less undertake, whatever matter is proposed, to speak about it copiously and abundantly."

And so this, which is commonly said about orators by the unskilled, "this man uses good words," or "someone uses words not good," is not weighed by any art, but is judged by a certain, as it were, natural sense; in which there is no great praise in avoiding a fault, though it is a great thing; but yet this is, as it were, a certain ground and foundation—the use and supply of good words.

These are the things which produce applause and admiration for good orators; and no one will attain them unless he has written much and long, even if he has exercised himself most vehemently in those sudden speeches; and he who comes to speaking from the habit of writing brings this faculty, that, even if he speaks on the sudden, yet those things which are said seem like things written; and even, if at any time in speaking he has brought something written, when he has departed from it, the rest of the speech will follow in like manner;

Then Catulus said: "It is, Antonius, as you say, that most philosophers hand down no precepts of speaking and yet have ready what to say about each thing; but Aristotle, the man whom I most admire, set down certain topics, from which the whole way of every argument might be found, not only for the disputation of philosophers, but also for this speaking which we use in causes; from which man, indeed, Antonius, your speech has not for a long time strayed, whether by a likeness to that divine talent you fall into the same footsteps, or whether you have even read and learned those very things—which to me at least seems more probable; for I see that you have given more labour to Greek matters than we had supposed."

But what the orator himself may build, and in what he may add art, this it seems we must inquire. There are, then, three things in a single word which the orator may bring to the illuminating and adorning of speech: either an unusual word, or a coined one, or a transferred one.

as in a swiftly moving ship, when the rowers have backed water, the ship herself nevertheless keeps her motion and course, though the impulse and the stroke of the oars have ceased, so in a continuous speech, when the written matter fails, the rest of the speech nevertheless keeps an equal course, set in motion by the likeness and force of what was written.

Then he said: "The truth you shall hear from me, Catulus: I always thought the orator would be more pleasant and more acceptable to this people who should give, first, as little indication as possible of any art, and then none of Greek matters: and I likewise thought it was the mark of a beast, not a man, when the Greeks were undertaking, professing, treating such great matters, and were promising to give men the method both of seeing the most obscure things and of living well and speaking copiously, not to lend an ear; and, if you did not dare to hear them openly, lest you diminish your authority among your fellow-citizens, yet by listening on the side to catch their voices and to attend from afar to what they related. And so I did, Catulus, and I tasted, in summary, the causes and the very kinds of all those men."

Unusual words are generally those that are antique and, by reason of antiquity, now long since disused from the practice of daily speech; which are freer for the license of poets than for ours; but yet rarely some poetic word has dignity even in oratory. For I would not shun to say, as Caelius does, "at what season the Carthaginian came into Italy," nor "offspring," or "progeny," or "to declare," or "to name," or, as you are wont, Catulus, "I did not deem" or "I supposed"; or many other words, which, placed in their proper places, often make speech seem grander and more antique.

But in my daily exercises I, as a young man, used especially to set before myself that exercise which I knew our famous enemy Gaius Carbo was wont to use—that either, certain verses being set before me, the weightiest possible, or some speech being read, to such an end as I could grasp by memory, I should recite that very matter which I had read in other words, chosen as best I could; but afterward I noticed that there was this fault in this practice, that those words which were most proper to each thing, and most ornate and best, had been forestalled either by Ennius, if I exercised myself on his verses, or by Gracchus, if I had set before myself his speech: so that, if I used the same words, it was no profit; if others, it was even a hindrance, since I was accustoming myself to use less suitable ones.

"By Hercules," said Catulus, "very timidly, as if toward some rock of lust, did you put in your mind to philosophy, which this state has never spurned; for Italy was once full of Pythagoreans, then when that great Greece was in this nation; from which some even report that Numa Pompilius, our king, was a Pythagorean, who lived very many years before Pythagoras himself; on which account he must be held the greater man, since he knew that wisdom of establishing a state almost two centuries before the Greeks perceived that it was born; and certainly this state has produced none more famous, or weightier in authority, or more polished in culture than Publius Africanus, Gaius Laelius, Lucius Furius, who always had openly with them most learned men from Greece.

Words are coined, again, which are begotten and made by the speaker himself, either by the joining of words, as these: "then terror, when I was unsouled, expectorates all wisdom from me;" "do you not wish me to . . . the wile-speaking malices of this man"—for you see that both "wile-speaking" and "expectorates" are words made by joining, not born; but often even without joining words are coined, as "that deserted old man," as "the begetting gods," as "to grow bent with the abundance of berries."

Afterward it pleased me, and I used this method as a young man, to expound the Greek speeches of the greatest orators; and by reading these I attained this—that, when I rendered into Latin those things which I had read in Greek, I not only used the best words, and yet such as were usual, but also expressed by imitation certain words which were new to us, provided only they were suitable.

And I often heard this from them, when they said that the Athenians had done a most acceptable thing both to themselves and to many of the leading men of the state, in that, when they were sending ambassadors to the senate about their greatest affairs, they had sent the three most noble philosophers of that age—Carneades and Critolaus and Diogenes; and so, while they were at Rome, they were frequently heard both by themselves and by others; whom, when you had as authorities, Antonius, I wonder why you have declared, like that Zethus of Pacuvius, almost war upon philosophy."

That third mode, of transferring a word, is widely extended; which necessity begot, compelled by poverty and want, but afterwards pleasantness and delight made common. For as clothing, devised first for the purpose of repelling cold, afterwards began to be employed also for the adornment and dignity of the body, so the transference of a word was instituted by reason of poverty, but made frequent for the sake of delight. For "the vine buds," "there is luxuriance in the grass," "joyful crops"—even rustics say. For what can scarcely be declared by a proper word, when it is said by a transferred one, the likeness of that thing which we have set down by an alien word illuminates what we wish to be understood.

Now the movements and exercises of the voice and the breath and the whole body and of the very tongue need not so much art as labour; in which matters one must take careful account whom we imitate, whom we wish to be like. Not only orators must be regarded by us, but also actors, lest by bad habit we come to some deformity and depravity.

"By no means," said Antonius; "and I have so resolved rather to philosophize, as Neoptolemus in Ennius does, 'in a few things; for altogether it does not please me.' But yet this is my opinion, which I seemed to have set forth: I do not disapprove of those studies, provided only they be moderate; but I think the reputation of those studies and the suspicion of art, among those who judge causes, is adverse to the orator; for it diminishes both the authority of the orator and the credit of the speech.

These transferences, then, are, as it were, borrowings, when you take from elsewhere what you have not; those a little bolder, which do not indicate poverty, but fetch some splendour for the speech; of which what reason of finding, or what kinds, shall I set before you?

The memory, too, must be exercised by learning by heart, word for word, as many as possible both of our own writings and of others'; and in that exercise it does not altogether displease me to employ, if you have grown accustomed to it, that system of places and images which is handed down in the art. Then the speaking must be led forth from this domestic and shadowy exercise into the midst of the line of battle, into the dust, into the clamour, into the camp and the forensic array; the gaze of men must be faced and the powers of talent put to the test, and that secluded preparation must be brought forth into the light of truth.

But, that the speech may be called back whither it has digressed, of those three most famous philosophers whom you said came to Rome, do you not see that Diogenes was the one who said that he handed down the art of reasoning well and of distinguishing the true and the false, which he called by the Greek word dialectic? In this art, if indeed it be an art, there is no precept how the truth may be found, but only how it may be judged;

. . . but those things ought to be transferred which either make a matter clearer, as all these: "the sea bristles up; the darkness is redoubled, and the blackness of night and storm-cloud blinds; the flame flashes amid the clouds, the sky trembles with thunder; hail, mingled with abundant rain, suddenly rushing headlong falls; from every side all the winds burst forth, savage whirlwinds arise, the sea boils with surge"—almost all of which, that they might be clearer, are said by words transferred through likeness;

The poets, too, must be read, the histories learned, the teachers and writers of all good arts chosen and turned over, and, for the sake of exercise, praised, interpreted, corrected, censured; and one must dispute about every matter on both sides, and whatever in each matter can seem probable must be drawn out and brought to light;

for both everything that we utter in such a way that we say it either is or is not, and, if it be simply stated, the dialecticians undertake to judge whether it be true or false; and, if it be uttered in combination and other things be joined to it, they judge whether they are rightly joined and whether the sum of each particular reasoning is true; and at the last they prick themselves with their own subtleties, and by much questioning find out not only those things which they themselves can no longer untie, but even those by which things already begun and rather woven are well-nigh unwoven again.

or whereby a whole matter is the more signified, whether of some deed or of some design, as that man who, indicating by the very likeness, with two transferred words, one concealing on purpose, lest what was being done could be understood: "since he clothes himself round about with words, hedges himself with guile." Sometimes also brevity is achieved by transference, as that, "if the weapon has fled from the hand": the imprudence of a weapon thrown could not be set forth more briefly by proper words than it is signified by one transferred.

the civil law must be thoroughly learned, the statutes known, all antiquity understood, the usage of the senate, the discipline of the commonwealth, the rights of allies, the treaties, the agreements, the policy of empire must be known; and a certain charm of wit must also be sipped from every kind of urbanity, with which, as with salt, all the speech may be sprinkled. Here, then, this Stoic helps us nothing, since he does not teach in what manner I may find what to say; and the same even hinders, because he both discovers many things which he says can in no way be untied, and brings a kind of speech that is not liquid, not flowing and streaming, but meagre, dry, concise and minute, which if anyone shall approve, he will so approve it as yet to confess that it is not suited to the orator; for this speech of ours must be accommodated to the ears of the multitude, to delight their minds, to impel them, to prove those things which are weighed not in the goldsmith's balance, but in a certain popular scale;

In this kind it very often seems to me a thing to be wondered at, what it is that all men are more delighted by transferred and alien words than by proper and their own. For if a thing has not its own name and proper appellation, as "foot" in a ship, as "nexum," which is transacted by the balance, as "divorce" in a wife, necessity compels one to take from elsewhere what one has not; but, in the greatest abundance of one's own words, men are nevertheless delighted far more by alien ones, if they are transferred with reason.

When Crassus had said this, silence followed; but although it seemed to those who were present that enough had been said for what was proposed, yet they felt that he had brought it to a close much more quickly than they themselves wished. Then Scaevola said: 'What is it, Cotta? Why are you silent? Does nothing come into your mind that you might further ask of Crassus?'

wherefore we dismiss that whole art, which is too dumb in devising arguments, too talkative in judging them. That Critolaus, whom you mention as having come with Diogenes, I think could have profited this our study more; for he was of that Aristotle, from whose discoveries I seem to you not to wander far. And between this Aristotle—both that book of whom I read, in which he set forth the arts of speaking of all his predecessors, and those in which he himself said certain things of his own about the same art—and those true masters of this art, this seemed to me to be the difference, that he with the same edge of mind with which he had seen the force and nature of all things, looked also upon these things which pertained to the art of speaking, which he despised; but those who thought this alone worth cultivating dwelt in handling this one method, not with the same prudence as he, but with greater practice and zeal in this one kind.

This happens, I believe, either because it is a certain sign of genius to leap over the things placed before the feet and to take others fetched from far off; or because the hearer is led elsewhere in thought, and yet does not stray, which is the greatest delight; or because in single words a thing and a whole likeness is achieved; or because every transference which is taken with reason is applied to the very senses, especially to the eyes, which is the keenest sense.

'That very thing, by Hercules,' he said, 'I am attending to: for so great was the rush of words and so did the speech fly forth, that I caught sight of its force and impulse, but scarcely saw its footsteps and approach; and, as if I had come into some rich and well-stocked house, where the tapestry was not unrolled nor the plate set out, nor the pictures and statues openly placed, but all these many and magnificent things were heaped up and stored away; so just now, in the speech of Crassus, I perceived the riches and the ornaments of his talent through certain wrappings and coverings, but, when I desired to contemplate them, I scarcely had the power of looking; and so I can neither say that I am wholly ignorant of what he possesses, nor that I plainly know and have seen it.'

But Carneades's incredible power of speaking and his versatility would be very much to be wished for by us—a man who in those disputations of his never defended a thing which he did not make probable, never attacked one which he did not overthrow. But this is something greater than is to be demanded from those who hand down and teach these things.

For both "the odour of urbanity" and "the softness of humanity" and "the murmur of the sea" and "the sweetness of speech" are drawn from the other senses; but those of the eyes are much keener, which place almost in the sight of the mind those things which we cannot discern and see. For there is nothing in the nature of things whose name and appellation we cannot use in other matters. For whence a likeness can be drawn—and it can be drawn from all things—from the same source one word, which contains the likeness, being transferred, will bring light to the speech.

'Why, then, do you not do the same,' said Scaevola, 'as you would do if you had come into some house or villa full of ornaments? If these were set aside, as you say, you, being very desirous of seeing them, would not hesitate to ask the master to order them brought out, especially if he were a friend: likewise now you will ask of Crassus to bring into the light that abundance of his ornaments, which, heaped up in one place, we have glimpsed only in passing, as through a lattice, and to set each thing in its own place.'

But I, for my part, if I now wished to train someone altogether raw for speaking, would rather hand him over to those assiduous men beating the same anvil day and night in one task, who would insert into his mouth all the most minute particles and all the smallest morsels chewed up, as nurses do for infant boys; but if it be one who seems to me both liberally instructed in learning and already imbued with some practice and to be of a sufficiently keen talent, thither I would hurry him, where he might be held not by some secluded little stream, but whence the whole river bursts forth; one who may point out to him the seats and, as it were, dwelling-places of all arguments, and briefly illustrate them and define them in words.

In which kind, first, dissimilarity is to be shunned: "the huge arches of the sky"; though Ennius brought a "sphere" upon the stage, as it is said, yet in a sphere the likeness of an arch cannot be contained. "Live, Ulysses, while you may; with your eyes snatch the last radiant light!"—he did not say "seek," nor "take"—for that would have had the delay of one hoping to live longer—but "snatch": this word is fitted to that

'I, indeed,' said Cotta, 'ask this of you, Scaevola—for shame restrains me and this Sulpicius here from inquiring of a man the most weighty of all, who has always despised this kind of discussion, these things which to him perhaps seem the elements of boys—but do you grant us this favour, Scaevola, and bring it about that Crassus should expand and unfold for us those things which he has compressed and very narrowly crammed into his speech.'

For what is there in which he can stick fast who has seen that everything which is taken in a speech, either for proving or for refuting, is either taken from its own matter by its own force and nature, or assumed from without? from its own force, when either the whole matter, what it is, is inquired, or a part of it, or the name which it has, or something which touches that matter; but from without, when those things are gathered which are outside and do not inhere in the nature of the matter.

which he had said before, "while you may." Then it must be seen that the likeness be not fetched from too far: I would more willingly say "the Syrtis" of a patrimony, the "rock"; "the Charybdis" of goods, rather "the whirlpool"; for the eyes of the mind are more easily borne to those things which are seen than to those which are heard; and since this is, as it were, the highest praise in transferring words, that what is transferred strike the sense, all baseness of those things is to be shunned, to which the likeness will draw the minds of those who hear.

'I, by Hercules,' said Mucius, 'wished this before more for your sake than for my own; for I did not so greatly desire this discussion from Crassus as I delight in his speaking in cases; but now, Crassus, I too ask you, for my own sake also, that, since we have so much leisure as has not fallen to us for a long time, you would not be reluctant to build up that work which you have begun: for I see the form of the whole undertaking to be better and greater than I had supposed, which I greatly approve.'

If the whole matter is inquired, the force must be unfolded by a universal definition, thus: 'if majesty is the greatness and dignity of the state, he diminishes it who has handed over an army to the enemies of the Roman people, not he who has handed over him who did this to the power of the Roman people.'

I would not have it said that the commonwealth was "castrated" by the death of Africanus; I would not have Glaucia called "the dung of the senate-house"; though there be a likeness, yet in each there is a deformed thought of likeness; I would not have it greater than the matter requires: "the tempest of a revel"; or less: "the revel of a tempest"; I would not have the word that is transferred narrower than that proper and its own word would have been: "what is it, pray? Why do you nod me away from approaching you?"—it were better to say "forbid," "prohibit," "frighten away"; since the other had said, "there on the spot, lest my contagion or my shadow harm the good . . ."

'Truly,' said Crassus, 'I cannot sufficiently wonder that you too, Scaevola, desire these things, which I neither hold so well as those who teach them, nor are they of such a kind that, if I held them perfectly, they would be worthy of your wisdom and your ears.' 'Do you say so?' said he: 'if you think that these common and well-worn matters are scarcely to be heard at my age, can we even neglect those things which you said the orator ought to know—about the natures of men, about characters, about those methods by which the minds of men are both roused and restrained, about history, about antiquity, about the administration of the commonwealth, in short, about our very own civil law? For I knew that all this knowledge and store of matters was in your prudence; but in the orator's equipment I had never seen such elegant furniture.'

But if a part, by partition, in this manner: 'either the senate had to be obeyed about the safety of the commonwealth, or another counsel had to be devised, or it had to be done of one's own accord; another counsel is proud, one's own is arrogant; the counsel of the senate, therefore, had to be used.' If from the name, as Carbo: 'if he is a consul who consults for his fatherland, what else did Opimius do?'

And also, if you fear lest the transference may seem a little too harsh, it is often to be softened by a word set before it; as if of old, Marcus Cato being dead, anyone should say the senate was left an "orphan," it is a little hard; but if "an orphan, so to speak," it is somewhat milder: for the transference ought to be modest, so that it may seem to have been led into another's place, not to have burst in, and to have come on sufferance, not by force.

'Can you, then,' said Crassus, 'to pass over other things countless and immense, and to come to your very civil law, call those men orators whom Publius Scaevola waited for many hours, both laughing and chafing, when he was hastening to the Campus, while Hypsaeus, with the loudest voice and in very many words, contended with the praetor Marcus Crassus that the man he was defending might be allowed to lose his case, and Gnaeus Octavius, a man of consular rank, in a speech no less long refused that the adversary should lose his case, and that the man for whom he himself was speaking should be freed from the disgraceful verdict of an action of guardianship and from all annoyance by the folly of his adversary?'

But if from that which touches the matter, there are several seats and topics of arguments; for we shall seek both conjuncts, and kinds, and the parts subjected to the kinds, and likenesses, and unlikenesses, and contraries, and consequents, and consentaneous things, and, as it were, antecedents, and repugnant things; and we shall track out the causes of things, and those things which have arisen from causes; and we shall seek the greater, the equal, the lesser.

There is no mode, however, more florid in single words, nor which brings more light to a speech; for that which flows from this kind is not in one transferred word, but is connected from several joined together, so that one thing is said and another to be understood: "Nor will I suffer myself to strike a second time, as once the fleet of the Achaeans, upon one rock." And that: "you err, you err; for, as you exult and presume upon yourself, the strong reins of the laws shall restrain you and set you under the yoke of command."

'I, indeed,' said he—'for I remember that Mucius told me of it'—'should scarcely think those men worthy not only of the name of orator, but even of the forum.' 'And yet,' said Crassus, 'those advocates lacked neither eloquence, nor method, nor abundance of speaking, but knowledge of the civil law: for the one, by suing under the law, claimed more than the law in the Twelve Tables permitted, and, when he had obtained it, would lose his case; the other thought it unfair that more should be claimed against him than was in the action, and did not understand that, if it were so conducted, his adversary would lose the suit.

From conjuncts arguments are drawn thus: 'if the highest praise is to be given to piety, you ought to be moved when you see Quintus Metellus mourn so piously.'
