the feigned introduction of persons, even the weightiest light of amplification; description, the introduction of error, the impulse to mirth, anticipation; then those two things which most move, likeness and example; partition, interruption, contrast, reticence, recommendation; a certain free, even unbridled, utterance for the sake of amplification; anger, rebuke, promise, deprecation, entreaty, a brief turning-aside from the proposition—not like that former digression—justification, conciliation, wounding, wish, and execration. With these lights, well-nigh, thoughts illuminate speech.

'What if,' said Crassus, 'since I, that I might the more easily keep you with me, have rather complied with your wish than with my own habit or nature, we ask of Antonius that he should set forth and declare to us those mysteries of speaking which he keeps to himself and has not yet brought forth, out of which he just now complained that a little book had slipped from him?' 'As you think best,' said Sulpicius; 'for from Antonius's speaking we shall perceive also what you understand.'

For my part I am wont first to consider whether the cause demands it; for neither in small matters are these torches of speaking to be applied, nor before men so disposed that we can avail nothing toward bending their minds by speech, lest we be thought worthy either of ridicule or of hatred, if we either act tragedies in trifles or attempt to tear up those things which cannot be moved.

But of the speech itself, as of arms, there is both a menacing, as it were, and a kind of thrust for use, and a handling for grace itself. For both the doubling of words sometimes has force, at other times charm, and a word a little changed and turned aside, and the frequent repetition of the same word, now from the beginning, now its turning to the end, and an onset upon the same words, and a concourse, and a joining, and a progression, and a certain distinguishing of the same word more often placed, and a recalling of the word, and those which similarly end, or which fall similarly, or which are matched, equal to equal, or which are similar among themselves.

'I ask of you, then, Antonius,' said Crassus, 'since this burden is laid upon us, men of this age, by the studies of these young men, that you set forth what you think on those matters which you see are asked of you.' 'I plainly see and feel that I am caught,' said Antonius, 'not only because those things are asked of me of which I am ignorant and unaccustomed, but because that which in causes I am very wont to avoid—lest I should follow you, Crassus—these gentlemen now do not allow me to avoid;

Now, since these things are for the most part especially to be worked upon by speech in the minds of the judges, or of whoever they shall be before whom we plead—love, hatred, anger, envy, pity, hope, gladness, fear, vexation: we feel that love is won, if we seem to defend, in justice, that which is useful to the very men before whom we plead, or if we labour on behalf of good men or at least of those who are good and useful to them; for this matter wins love the more, that defence of virtue, affection; and it profits more, if a hope of future usefulness is set forth, than the recalling of a past benefit.

There is also a certain gradation, and a turning-about, and a neat transposition of words, and the contrary, and the dissolute, and declination, and reprehension, and exclamation, and diminution, and that which is placed in many cases, and that which, drawn from single matters set forth, is referred to single ones, and a reason subjoined to the proposition, and likewise a reason supplied in things distributed, and concession, and again another doubt, and something unforeseen, and enumeration, and another correction, and dispersion, and the continued, and the interrupted, and image, and an answer to one's own self, and change, and disjunction, and order, and relation, and digression, and circumscription.

but I will enter upon those things which you wish the more boldly, because I hope the same will happen to me in this discussion as is wont in speaking, that no ornate speech be expected: for I am not going to speak about an art which I never learned, but about my own habit; and those very things which I set down in my notebook are of such a kind, not handed down to me by any teaching, but practised in the use of affairs and in causes; which, if they shall not be approved by you, most learned men, accuse your own unfairness, who have asked of me those things which I do not know; praise my readiness, since, led not by my own judgement but by your zeal, I shall answer not unwillingly.'

One must strive to show that in the matter which you defend there is either dignity or usefulness, and that he to whom you would win this love has referred nothing to his own advantage and has done nothing at all for his own sake; for men's own advantages are envied, but their zeal for serving others is favoured.

For these things, well-nigh, and things like these—or even more than these can be—are such as illuminate speech by thoughts and by the shapings of words.' 'These indeed,' said Cotta, 'I see, Crassus, that you have poured out without definitions and without examples, because you think they are known to us.' 'For my part,' said Crassus, 'I did not think those things which I said above to be new to you either, but I obeyed the wish of you all.

Then Crassus said: 'Only go on, Antonius; for there is no danger that you should say anything except so prudently that none of us would repent of having urged you to this conversation.' 'I will indeed go on,' he said, 'and will do that which I think ought to be done at the beginning of all discussions—that it should be explained what that is about which the discussion is held, lest the speech be compelled to wander and stray, if those who disagree with one another do not understand that same thing about which it is treated.

And at this point one must see, lest those whom we wish to be loved for their benefactions, we seem to extol too much their praise and glory, which is wont most of all to be envied; and from these same topics we shall learn both to build up hatred against others and to remove it from ourselves and ours; and these same kinds must be handled in either rousing or appeasing anger; for if you magnify that which is pernicious or useless to the very men who hear, hatred is created; but if that which is against good men, or against those whom each least ought to have so treated, or against the commonwealth, then is roused, if not so bitter a hatred, yet an offence not unlike envy or hatred;

But concerning these matters that sun there has admonished me to be the briefer, which, itself now sinking, has compelled me too to roll out these things almost headlong. But yet the demonstration and the teaching of this kind is itself common; the practice, however, is the weightiest and, in this whole study of speaking, the most difficult.

For if it were perchance asked what is the art of the general, I should think it must first be settled who the general is; and when he had been established as a certain manager of the conduct of war, then we should add about the army, about the camp, about marches, about the joining of battle, about the storming of towns, about supplies, about laying and avoiding ambushes, about the other matters which are proper to the conducting of war; and those who were masters in mind and knowledge of these things, those I should call generals, and I should use the examples of the Africani and the Maximi, and I should name Epaminondas and Hannibal and men of that kind.

likewise fear is struck in either from their own dangers or from common ones: the former, that proper one, is more inward; but this common one too must be brought to the same likeness. Equal and one method is of hope, gladness, vexation; but I scarcely know whether of all the movements envy be by far the keenest, nor is less of strength needed in repressing it than in rousing it. But men envy most their equals or inferiors, when they feel themselves left behind, and grieve that those others have flown ahead; but the superior too are often vehemently envied, and the more if they boast themselves too intolerably and pass beyond the equality of common right by the eminence of their dignity or fortune; which if they must be inflamed, it must especially be said that they were not gained by virtue, then even by vices and faults, then, if they are more honourable and weighty, yet that those merits are not so great as the insolence and disdain of the man.

Wherefore, since concerning all the adornment of speech the topics are all, if not laid open, at least pointed out, let us now see what is apt—that is, what is most becoming in speech. Although this indeed is plain, that one single kind of speech does not suit every cause, nor every hearer, nor every person, nor every occasion; for both capital cases require a certain sound of words, and another sound is required by private and small matters;

But if we were inquiring who he is who has brought his experience and knowledge and zeal to the governing of the commonwealth, I should define it thus: that he who held and used those things by which the advantage of the commonwealth is procured and increased should be reckoned the director of the commonwealth and the author of public counsel; and I should proclaim that famous Publius Lentulus the leader, and Tiberius Gracchus the father, and Quintus Metellus, and Publius Africanus, and Gaius Laelius, and countless others both from our own state and from others.

But for appeasing it, it must be said that those things were gained by great labour, by great dangers, and were conferred not for his own advantage but for that of others; and that he, if he seems to have gained any glory, yet, although that be not an unfair wage of danger, is not delighted by it, and casts it all off and lays it down; and altogether it must be brought about—since most men are envious, and this is the most common and perpetual fault, and a pre-eminent and flourishing fortune is envied—that this opinion be diminished and that fortune, eminent in reputation, seem mingled with labours and miseries.

and one kind of speaking deliberations demand, another encomiums, another trials, another conversations, another consolation, another rebuke, another disputation, another history. It matters too who hear—the senate, or the people, or the judges; whether many or few or single; and of what sort; the very orators too, of what age, honour, authority they are, must be considered; the time, of peace or of war, of haste or of leisure.

But if it were asked who is truly named a jurisconsult, I should say he who is skilled in the laws and in that custom which private men use in the state, both for giving opinions, and for conducting cases, and for taking precaution; and from that class I should name Sextus Aelius, Manius Manilius, Publius Mucius. And, to come now to the lighter studies of the arts, if the musician, the grammarian, the poet be sought, I could similarly explain what each of them professes and what no more is to be demanded of each. Of the philosopher himself, finally, who alone professes well-nigh everything about his own power and wisdom, there is yet a certain description—that he who studies to know the force, nature, and causes of all things divine and human, and to hold and follow the whole method of living well, should be called by this name.

Now pity is moved, if he who hears can be brought to refer those things which are bewailed of another to his own affairs, which he has either borne bitterly or fears, so that, looking at another, he frequently returns to himself; and while the single cases of human miseries are gravely received, if they are spoken of mournfully, then afflicted and prostrate virtue is most lamentable. And as that other part of the speech, which by the commendation of uprightness ought to preserve the appearance of a good man, must be gentle, as I have often now said, and lowered, so this, which is undertaken by the orator to change the minds and to bend them by every method, must be intent and vehement.

And so in this place there is nothing at all that seems able to be taught, except that we should choose the figure of speech—the fuller, the slenderer, and likewise that middle one—accommodated to what we shall be treating. It will generally be permitted to use the same ornaments at one time more vigorously, at another more subduedly; and to be able, in every matter, to do what is becoming is of art and of nature, to know what is becoming on each occasion is of prudence.

But the orator, since we are inquiring about him, I for my part do not make the same as Crassus, who seemed to me to comprehend all knowledge of all things and arts in the one office and name of orator; but I think him to be one who can use words pleasant to hear and thoughts adapted to proving in forensic and common causes: this man I call an orator, and I wish him besides to be furnished with voice and delivery and a certain charm.

But there is a certain likeness, difficult to distinguish, in these two kinds, of which we wish one to be gentle, the other vehement; for both from that gentleness, by which we win those who hear, something ought to flow into this keenest force by which we rouse the same men, and from this force something of spirit must sometimes be breathed into that gentleness; nor is there any speech more tempered than that in which the harshness of contention is seasoned by the humanity of the orator himself, while the remission of gentleness is firmed by a certain weight and contention.

But all these things are even as they are delivered. Delivery, I say, in speaking alone holds sway; without this the highest orator can be of no account, while a middling one furnished with this can often surpass the highest. To this Demosthenes is said to have given the first place, when he was asked what was first in speaking; to this the second, to this the third; whence even better seems to me that saying of Aeschines; who, when on account of the disgrace of the trial he had withdrawn from Athens and betaken himself to Rhodes, being asked by the Rhodians, is reported to have read that excellent speech which he had delivered against Ctesiphon, in opposition to Demosthenes; and when it had been read through, he was asked on the next day to read also that which had been delivered on the other side by Demosthenes, on behalf of Ctesiphon: which, when he had read it with a most sweet and mighty voice, all marvelling, "How much more," said he, "would you marvel, if you had heard the man himself!" by which he sufficiently signified how much there is in delivery, since he thought that the same speech would be another thing, the deliverer being changed.

But our friend Crassus seemed to me to describe the orator's faculty not by the bounds of that art, but by the well-nigh boundless limits of his own talent; for he handed over to the orator, by his opinion, the helm of governing states, in which it seemed very wonderful to me, Scaevola, that you conceded this to him, since the senate has very often assented to you when speaking briefly and unpolishedly on the greatest matters. But Marcus Scaurus—whom I hear to be not far off in the country at his own place—a man most skilled in governing the commonwealth, if he shall hear this authority of weight and counsel claimed by you, Crassus, because you say it is proper to the orator, will, I believe, come hither at once and terrify this loquacity of ours by his very look and aspect; who, although in speaking he is by no means to be despised, yet relies upon prudence in great matters rather than upon the art of speaking.

But in either kind of speaking, both that in which force and contention is sought, and this which is accommodated to life and character, both the beginnings ought to be slow and likewise the endings spun out and prolonged. For neither should one leap at once into that kind of speech—for it is wholly removed from the cause, and men first desire to hear that very thing which is proper to their judgement—nor, when you have entered upon that method, should one quickly depart;

What was there in Gracchus—whom you better remember, Catulus—which, when I was a boy, was so greatly extolled? "Whither shall I betake myself, wretched man? Whither shall I turn? To the Capitol? But it is wet with my brother's blood. Or home? That I may see my mother, wretched, lamenting and cast down?" Which were so delivered by him with the eyes, the voice, the gesture, that even his enemies could not restrain their tears. These things I say at greater length, because this whole kind the orators—who are the actors of the very truth—have abandoned; while the imitators of truth, the actors of the stage, have seized upon it.

Nor indeed, if anyone can do both, is either that author of public counsel and good senator on that very account an orator, or is this fluent and eloquent man, if he is likewise excellent in the management of the state, on that account possessed of that knowledge of speaking through abundance of speech: those faculties are far distant from one another, and are widely diverse and distinct; nor by the same method and way did Marcus Cato, Publius Africanus, Quintus Metellus, Gaius Laelius, who were all eloquent, adorn their own speech and the dignity of the commonwealth. For it is not forbidden either by the nature of things or by any law or custom that single men should not be allowed to know more than single arts.

for not, as an argument, as soon as it is set down, is caught up, and a second and third is demanded, so can you, as soon as you have introduced it, move pity or envy or anger: the very reasoning confirms an argument, and as soon as it is sent forth, it cleaves; but that kind of speech requires not the instruction of the judge, but rather his disturbance, which no one can attain except by much and various and copious speech, and a like contention of delivery;

And without doubt in every matter truth surpasses imitation; but if it could of itself effect enough in delivery, we should assuredly have no need of art; but because the emotion of the mind, which is chiefly to be declared or imitated in delivery, is often so disturbed that it is obscured and almost overwhelmed, those things which obscure it are to be shaken off, and those which are eminent and ready are to be taken.

Wherefore not, if Pericles was most eloquent at Athens, and the same man was for very many years the leader of public counsel in that state, are both faculties on that account to be thought to belong to the same man and the same art; nor, if Publius Crassus was at once eloquent and skilled in law, is on that account a knowledge of the civil law inherent in the faculty of speaking.

wherefore those who speak either briefly or in a lowered way can instruct the judge, but cannot move him, in which is everything. Now this is plain, that the faculty for opposite sides of all matters is supplied from the same topics. But an argument must be resisted either by reproving those things which are taken for proving it, or by demonstrating that what they wish to conclude does not follow from the premises nor is a consequence; or, if you do not so refute it, something must be brought for the contrary side, which is either weightier or equally weighty.

For every motion of the mind has from nature its own countenance and sound and gesture; and the whole body of a man, and all his countenance and all his voices, like the strings in a lyre, so sound as they have been struck by the motion of the mind. For the voices, like strings, are stretched, which answer to each touch—sharp, grave, quick, slow, great, small; among all which, however, there is in each kind a middling tone; and from these too have flowed yet more kinds—smooth, rough, contracted, diffused, with breath sustained or interrupted, broken, split, with a bent sound attenuated, inflated;

For if, as each man, excelling in some art and faculty, has also taken to himself another art, he will bring it about that what he knows besides should seem to be a certain part of that in which he excels, then by that reasoning we may say that to play well at ball and at the twelve-line game is proper to the civil law, since Publius Mucius did both excellently; and by the same reasoning those whom the Greeks call natural philosophers might be called poets, because the natural philosopher Empedocles made an excellent poem. But not even the philosophers themselves, who wish all things to be their own as if their own property and to be possessed by themselves, dare to say that geometry or music belongs to the philosopher, because all confess that Plato was most outstanding in those arts.

But those things which are done either gently, for winning over, or vehemently, for moving, must be taken away by contrary emotions, so that goodwill be removed by hatred, envy by pity. But sweet, and often very useful, is jesting and wit; which, even if all other things can be handed down by art, are at least proper to nature and certainly require no art: in which you, in my opinion, Caesar, far excel others; on which account you can even more be either a witness to me that there is no art of wit, or, if there is any, you above all can teach it to us.

for there is none of these kinds which is not handled by art and moderation. These are set before the actor, as colours before the painter, to vary. For anger takes to itself one kind of voice, sharp, excited, frequently broken off: "my brother himself urges me, wretched, to give my children to the jaws . . ." and those things which you brought forward a while ago, Antonius—"have you dared to sever them from yourself . . ."—and "will anyone heed this? bind ye . . ."—and almost the whole Atreus. Commiseration and grief take another, flexible, full, interrupted, with a tearful voice: "whither now shall I turn? what journey shall I begin to enter? to my father's house? or to the daughters of Pelias?" and that—"O father, O fatherland, O house of Priam!" and what follows—"all these I saw set on fire, and Priam's life reft from him by violence."

And if it now pleases us to subject all the arts to the orator, it is more tolerable to say it rather thus: that, since the faculty of speaking ought not to be meagre and bare, but sprinkled and varied with a certain pleasant variety of many things, it belongs to a good orator to have heard much, to have seen much, to have run over much in mind and thought, much also in reading, yet not to have possessed these as his own but to have tasted them as another's; for I confess that he must be a man clever and in no respect a novice or untrained, nor a stranger and guest in pleading.

'For my part,' said he, 'I think it easier to dispute about any matter by a man not unurbane than about wit itself. And so, when I had seen certain Greek books inscribed "about things laughable," I had come into some hope that I could learn something from them; but I found many laughable and salty sayings of the Greeks—for both the Sicilians excel in this kind, and the Rhodians and the Byzantines, and beyond the rest the Attics; but those who tried to deliver a certain method and art of this matter turned out so saltless that nothing of theirs is laughed at except their very saltlessness;

Fear takes another, low, hesitating, cast down: "in many ways am I beset—by disease, by exile, and by want; then terror, when I am unsouled, expectorates all wisdom from me; my mother threatens a terrible torment of my life and death; than which there is no one of so firm a spirit and of so great confidence but that his blood flees back in terror and he grows pale with fear." Force takes another, strained, vehement, threatening with a certain incitation of weight: "again Thyestes comes to assail Atreus, again now attacks me and rouses me from my quiet; a greater mass, a greater evil, must be stirred up by me, wherewith I may crush and curb his bitter heart." Pleasure takes another, poured out, gentle, tender, gladdened and relaxed: "but when she brought the garland to bind the nuptials, she bore it to you, when she feigned to give it eagerly to herself, then, playfully, learnedly and daintily, she brought it to you." Trouble takes another, without commiseration, weighty and overspread with a single pressure and tone: "at what season Paris joined Helen in unwedded wedlock, I then was with child, with the months already fulfilled for bringing forth; at the same time Hecuba bore Polydorus in her last childbirth."

Nor indeed, Crassus, am I disturbed by those tragedies of yours, which the philosophers are especially wont to use, in that you said that no one can either inflame the minds of those who listen by speaking, or extinguish them when inflamed—wherein the force and greatness of the orator is most discerned—unless he has thoroughly examined the nature and characters and reasonings of men, in which philosophy must necessarily be grasped by the orator; in which study we see whole lives of men most talented and most leisured worn away. The abundance and greatness of whose knowledge and art I not only do not despise, but even vehemently admire; yet for us, who are engaged in this populace and forum, it is enough to know and to say about the movements of the mind those things which are not at variance with the characters of men.

wherefore to me at least this matter seems in no way able to be handed down by teaching. For since there are two kinds of wit, one diffused evenly through all the discourse, the other very acute and brief, the former was called by the ancients banter (cavillatio), this other railing (dicacitas). Each thing has a light name. No wonder; for this whole thing—to move laughter—is light.

For what great and weighty orator, when he wished to make the judge angry with his adversary, ever hesitated for this reason, that he did not know what anger was—whether a heat of the mind or a desire of avenging pain? Who, when he wished to stir up and excite the other movements of the mind in the judges or the people by speaking, said those things which are wont to be said by the philosophers? Some of whom deny that there ought to be any movements at all in the mind, and say that those who stir them up in the minds of judges commit a nefarious crime; others, who wish to be more tolerable and to approach nearer to the truth of life, say that the movements ought to be very moderate and rather slight.

But yet, as you say, Antonius, I have seen much profit very often gained in causes by charm and wit. But since in that kind of continuous pleasantry art is not required—for nature fashions and creates men as imitators and witty narrators, with countenance and voice and the very kind of speech helping—then indeed in this other kind of railing what place has art, when the witty saying ought to be sent forth and to cleave before it can seem to have been able even to be thought of?

But all these movements gesture ought to follow—not this stage-gesture expressing the words, but declaring the whole matter and meaning not by demonstration but by signification, with this strong and manly bending of the sides, drawn not from the stage and the actors, but from arms or even from the palaestra; the hand, again, less expressive, following the words with the fingers, not expressing them; the arm thrown out somewhat far, as a certain weapon of speech; the stamping of the foot in contentions, either at the beginning or at the ending of them.

But the orator makes all these things, which are thought in the common course of life evil and troublesome and to be avoided, by his words much greater and more bitter; and likewise those things which commonly seem desirable and to be wished for, he amplifies and adorns by speaking; nor does he wish to seem so wise among the foolish that those who listen should either think him silly and a little Greek, or, even if they greatly approve his talent, admire the orator's wisdom but be vexed that they themselves are fools;

For what could this my brother be helped by art, when, asked by Philippus what he was barking at, he answered that he saw a thief? What in his whole speech could Crassus, whether before the centumviri against Scaevola, or against the accuser Brutus, when he spoke on behalf of Gnaeus Plancius? For that which you, Antonius, attribute to me, must by the opinion of all be conceded to Crassus; for scarcely anyone besides him will be found excelling in either kind of charm: both that which is in the continuity of discourse, and this which is in quickness and in a saying.

But all is in the countenance; and in that itself the dominion belongs wholly to the eyes; wherefore our old men did the better, who did not greatly praise even Roscius when masked; for all delivery is of the mind, and the countenance is the image of the mind, the eyes its indicators: for this is the one part of the body which can effect as many significations as there are movements of the mind; nor indeed is there anyone who can effect the same with eyes closed. Theophrastus indeed says that a certain Tauriscus, an actor, was wont to say that he who, in acting, delivered his lines gazing at any one fixed thing, performed with his back turned.

but he so ranges through their minds, so handles the feelings and minds of men, that he does not need the descriptions of the philosophers, nor inquire in his speech whether that highest good is in the mind or in the body, whether it is defined by virtue or by pleasure, whether these can be joined and coupled together; or indeed whether, as it has seemed to some, nothing certain can be known, nothing clearly comprehended and perceived; of which matters I confess that there is a great and manifold discipline, and many copious and various theories.

For that whole continuous Curian defence against Scaevola overflowed with a certain hilarity and jesting; it had not those brief sayings; for he spared the dignity of his adversary, in which he preserved his own; which is most difficult for witty and railing men—to have regard to men and times, and to hold back those things which occur when they can be said most saltily; and so some witty men interpret this very thing not without point;

Wherefore there is great moderation of the eyes; for the appearance of the mouth is not to be too much changed, lest we be carried off either to absurdities or to some distortion; it is the eyes, by whose now intensity, now relaxation, now glance, now mirth, we may signify the motions of our minds aptly with the very kind of speech; for delivery is, as it were, the speech of the body, and therefore ought the more to agree with the mind; and the eyes nature has given us, as to a horse or a lion their mane, their tail, their ears, to declare the motions of the mind.

But something else, far different, Crassus, do we seek: we need a keen man, clever both by nature and by practice, who shrewdly investigates what his fellow-citizens, and those men whom he wishes to persuade of something by speaking, think, feel, suppose, expect; he ought to hold the pulse of every kind, age, and order, and to taste the minds and feelings of those before whom he is pleading or will plead;

for they say that Ennius says that a wise man can more easily keep down a flame in his burning mouth than hold back good sayings—these good sayings, of course, which are salty; for these sayings are now called by their own proper name. But as Crassus held back these against Scaevola, and in that other kind, in which there were no stings of insult, eluded that cause and disputation, so against Brutus, whom he hated and whom he judged worthy of insult, he fought with either kind.

Wherefore in this delivery of ours, next after the voice, the countenance prevails; but that is governed by the eyes. And in all these things which belong to delivery there is a certain force given by nature; wherefore by this even the unskilled, by this the common crowd, by this in short barbarians are most moved: for words move no one save him who is joined by the fellowship of the same tongue, and keen thoughts often fly past the perception of men not keen; delivery, which bears before it the motion of the mind, moves all men; for by the same motions of the mind all men are stirred, and they recognize them in others by the same marks and betray them in their own selves.

but let him reserve the books of the philosophers for himself, for the rest and leisure of a Tusculan villa such as this, lest, if ever he must speak about justice and good faith, he borrow from Plato; who, when he thought these things must be expressed in words, fashioned a certain new state in his books; so far did those things which he thought must be said about justice depart from the custom of life and the manners of states.

How many things he said about the baths which that man had lately sold, how many about his lost patrimony! And those brief sayings—when that man said he was sweating without a cause, 'no wonder,' he said, 'for you have just come out of the baths.' There were countless others, but no less pleasant was that continuous one: for when Brutus had raised up two readers, and given to the one Crassus's speech about the colony of Narbo to read, to the other that about the Servilian law, and had set side by side passages contradictory to one another about the commonwealth, our friend here most wittily gave the three little books of Brutus's father about the civil law to three men to read.

But to the use and praise of delivery, without doubt, the voice holds the greatest part; which first is to be wished for by us; then, of whatever sort it shall be, it is to be cherished; concerning which that matter—in what manner the voice is to be tended—is nothing now to this kind of precept-giving: for my part, however, I think very much that it is to be tended; but this seems not abhorrent from the office of this our discourse, that, as I said a little before, in very many things that which is most useful, that, by some means or other, is also most becoming. For toward maintaining the voice nothing is more useful than frequent change; nothing more pernicious than straining poured out without intermission.

But if these things were approved among peoples and in states, who would have conceded to you, Crassus, a most distinguished and eminent man and the leader of the state, to say in the greatest assembly of your fellow-citizens those things which you said? 'Rescue us from our miseries, rescue us from the jaws of those whose cruelty cannot be sated except by our blood; do not suffer us to be slaves to anyone except to you all together, to whom we both can and ought to be.' I pass over the miseries, in which, as they say, a brave man cannot be; I pass over the jaws from which you wish to be rescued, lest your blood be drained by an unjust trial, which they deny can happen to a wise man: but to be a slave—did you dare to say that not only you, but the whole senate, whose cause you were then pleading?

From the first book: 'It chanced that we were in the Privernate country.' 'Brutus, your father testifies that he left you the Privernate estate.' Then from the second book: 'We were at Alba, I and my son Marcus.' 'A wise man, evidently among the first of our state, knew this whirlpool; he feared lest, when the son should have nothing, nothing should be thought left to him.' Then from the third book, in which he made an end of writing—for so many are the genuine books of Brutus, as I heard Scaevola say—'We chanced to sit down at Tibur, I and my son Marcus.' 'Where are these estates, Brutus, which your father left you, recorded in public documents? And had he not had you already grown up,' he said, 'he would have composed a fourth book and left it written that he had even bathed in the baths with his son.'

What is more apt, for our ears and for the sweetness of delivery, than alternation and variety and change? And so the same Gracchus—as you can hear, Catulus, from Licinius your client, a lettered man, whom that man kept by him as a slave at hand—was wont, when he addressed the assembly, to have a skilled man with a little ivory pipe, who stood secretly behind him, to sound quickly that note by which he might either rouse him when slack or recall him from straining.' 'I have heard it, by Hercules,' said Catulus, 'and have often marvelled at the man's diligence, and likewise at his learning and knowledge.'

Can virtue, Crassus, be a slave, according to those authorities whose precepts you embrace by the orator's faculty? Which is both always and alone free, and which, even if bodies be captured by arms or bound by chains, yet ought to keep its own right and the unpunished liberty of all things. But as to what you added—that the senate not only can but even ought to be a slave to the people—what philosopher so soft, so languid, so enervated, so referring all things to the pleasure and pain of the body, could approve this, that the senate should be a slave to the people, to whom the people itself had handed over the power of moderating and governing itself, like a kind of reins?

Who, then, is there who would not confess that Brutus was no less refuted by this charm and these jests than by those tragedies which the same man acted, when by chance, in the same cause, the old woman Junia was being carried out for burial? By the immortal gods, what a thing was that, how great a force! how unexpected! how sudden! when, his eyes fixed, his whole gesture threatening him, with the highest weight and quickness of words: 'Brutus, why do you sit? What do you wish that old woman to announce to your father? What to all those whose images you see borne? What to your ancestors? What to Lucius Brutus, who freed this people from kingly domination? What do you do? To what matter, to what glory, to what virtue are you devoted? To increasing your patrimony? But that is not the mark of nobility.

'For my part,' said Crassus, 'I have indeed, and I grieve that those men fell into such guilt in the commonwealth; although such a web is being woven, and such a method of living is being shown to posterity in the state, that we may now desire to have men like those citizens whom our fathers did not endure.' 'Cease, I beseech you, Crassus,' said Julius, 'that discourse of yours, and bring yourself back to the pipe of Gracchus; the method of which I do not yet plainly understand.'

And so, although I thought these things had been said by you divinely, Publius Rutilius Rufus, a learned man and devoted to philosophy, said that they had been spoken not only ill-suitedly, but even basely and disgracefully; and the same man was wont very gravely to censure Servius Galba—a man whom he said he well remembered—because he, when Lucius Scribonius was bringing an inquiry against him, had roused the pity of the people, although Marcus Cato, the grave and bitter enemy of Galba, had spoken harshly and vehemently before the Roman people, which speech he himself set forth in his Origins.

But suppose it were, nothing is left; lusts have squandered it all. Or to the civil law? It is your father's. But it will say that you, when you were selling the house, did not even except for yourself your father's chair among the fixtures and movables. Or to military affairs? You who have never seen a camp! Or to eloquence? Which is not in you, and whatever there is of voice and tongue, you have bestowed it all upon that most disgraceful trade of calumny! Do you dare to look upon the light? You to gaze on these men? You to be in the forum, you in the sight of the citizens? You not to shudder at that dead woman, you not at the very images? Whom you have left yourself no place not only to imitate, but not even to set up.'

'In every voice,' said Crassus, 'there is a certain middle, but proper to each voice: from this to ascend the voice by degrees is both pleasant—for to shout from the beginning is a rustic thing—and that same is salutary for strengthening the voice; then there is a certain extreme of straining, which yet is more inward than the sharpest shouting, to which the pipe will not suffer you to proceed, and will recall you even from the very straining; there is likewise, on the contrary, a certain deepest point in relaxation, to which one descends, as it were, by degrees of sounds. This variety, and this course through all the sounds of the voice, will both protect itself and bring sweetness to delivery. But you will leave the piper at home, and carry with you to the forum the sense of this habit.

Rutilius, then, censured Galba, because he had himself lifted up well-nigh upon his shoulders the ward son of his kinsman Gaius Sulpicius Galus, that he might by the recollection and memory of his most distinguished father move the people to weeping; and had commended his own two little sons to the guardianship of the people, and had said that, as if making a will in readiness for battle without scales and tablets, he appointed the Roman people guardian for the orphanhood of those boys. And so, although Galba was then pressed both by the envy and the hatred of the people, Rutilius said he was freed by these tragedies; which I see is likewise written in Cato, that, unless he had used boys and tears, he would have suffered punishment. These things Rutilius greatly censured, and said that exile or even death was to be preferred to this humiliation.

But these things were tragic and divine; while witty and urbane things were countless even from one assembly; for there was never a greater contention, nor before the people a weightier speech, than that of this man against his colleague lately in the censorship, nor one more seasoned with charm and pleasantry. Wherefore, Antonius, I agree with you in both points—that wit often greatly profits in speaking, and that it can in no way be handed down by art: this indeed I wonder at, that you have attributed so much to us in that kind and have not borne off the palm of this matter too to Crassus.'

I have set forth what I could, not as I wished, but as the straits of time have compelled me; for it is a wise thing to lay the blame upon time, when, even if you wished it, you could not bring forward more.' 'But indeed,' said Catulus, 'you have gathered all things together, as far as I can judge, so divinely, that you seem not to have taken them from the Greeks, but to be able to teach these very things to the Greeks themselves; and I for my part rejoice that I have been made a partaker of this discourse; and I should wish that my son-in-law, your companion, Hortensius, had been present; who indeed I am confident will be pre-eminent in all those praises which you have embraced in your speech.'

Nor indeed did he only say this, but he himself both felt and did it: for, though that man was, as you know, an example of innocence, and there was no one in the state either more upright or more holy than he, he not only was unwilling to be a suppliant to the judges, but would not have his cause pleaded even more ornately or freely than the simple plan of truth bore. He assigned a small part of the pleading to this Cotta, a most eloquent young man, the son of his sister; Quintus Mucius also pleaded that cause in some part, in his own manner, without any ornament, purely and clearly.

Then Antonius said: 'I should indeed have so done, were it not that sometimes I envy this Crassus a little; for to be ever so witty and salty is not in itself too much to be envied; but since he is of all men the most graceful and most urbane, and at the same time both is and seems the most weighty and severe—which has befallen him alone—it seemed to me scarcely to be borne.' Hereupon, when Crassus himself had smiled, 'And yet,' said Antonius, 'though you denied, Julius, that there is an art of wit, you opened up something which seemed to need a precept: for you said that regard ought to be had for the men, the matter, the time, lest the jest detract anything from weightiness; which indeed is wont above all to be observed by Crassus. But this is a precept for omitting wit, when there is no need of it; we, however, are inquiring how we may use it, when there is need—as against an adversary, and especially if his folly can be made sport of; against a witness who is foolish, eager, frivolous, if men seem likely to listen readily.

And Crassus said: 'Do you say he will be? I for my part judge that he is so already, and judged it then, when, in my consulship, he defended in the senate the cause of Africa, and lately even more, when he spoke on behalf of the king of Bithynia. Wherefore you see rightly, Catulus; for I perceive that nothing is wanting to that young man, either from nature or from learning:

But if you had then spoken, Crassus—you who a little while ago said that the orator must seek aid for his abundance of speaking from those disputations which the philosophers use—and if it had been permitted you to speak on behalf of Publius Rutilius not after the manner of the philosophers, but in your own, however wicked those men had been—as in fact they were pestilent citizens and worthy of punishment—yet the force of your speech would have torn out all their wickedness from the very depths of men's minds. Now such a man has been lost, while the cause is pleaded as if the matter were being conducted in that fictitious state of Plato. No one of the advocates groaned, no one cried out, nothing grieved anyone, no one complained, no one implored the commonwealth, no one supplicated; in short, no one stamped his foot in that trial, I suppose, lest it should be reported to the Stoics.

Altogether those things are more acceptable which we say when provoked than those which we say first; for both the quickness of talent is greater, which appears in answering, and answering is the mark of good-nature; for we seem as though we would have been quiet, had we not been provoked—as in that very assembly nothing was said by this man, which at least seemed wittily said, which he did not say when challenged in answer; but there was so great weight in Domitius, so great authority, that what was thrown out by him seemed rather to be relieved by charm than to be broken by contention.'

on which account it is the more for you, Cotta, and for you, Sulpicius, to be watchful and to labour; for he grows up no middling orator, as it were, into your generation, but one of most keen genius and of burning zeal and of excellent learning and of singular memory; whom, although I favour him, yet I wish to excel his own age—but that he should outrun you, who are so much his elders, is scarcely honourable.' 'But now let us rise,' said he, 'and refresh ourselves, and at length relax our minds and our care from this strain of disputation.'

A Roman man and of consular rank imitated that old Socrates, who, when he was the wisest of all and had lived most holily, so spoke for himself in a capital trial that he seemed not a suppliant or a defendant, but the master or lord of the judges. Nay even, when the most eloquent orator Lysias had brought him a written speech, which, if it seemed good to him, he might learn by heart, that he might use it for himself in the trial, he read it not unwillingly and said it was suitably written; 'but,' he said, 'as, if you had brought me Sicyonian shoes, I would not use them, although they were handy and fitted to the foot, because they were not manly,' so that speech seemed to him eloquent and oratorical, but not brave and manly. Therefore he too was condemned; and not only by the first votes, by which the judges only decided whether to condemn or acquit, but also by those which they had to give a second time according to the laws;

Then Sulpicius said: 'What then? Shall we suffer Caesar—who, although he concedes wit to Crassus, yet labours much more at that study himself—not to unfold for us this whole kind of jesting, what it is and whence it is drawn, especially since he confesses that there is so great a force and usefulness in salt and urbanity?' 'What if,' said Julius, 'I agree with Antonius saying that there is no art of salt?'

for at Athens, when a defendant had been condemned, if the offence were not capital, there was, as it were, an assessment of the penalty; and when the verdict was being given to the judges, the defendant was asked what penalty he confessed he had most deserved. When Socrates was asked this, he answered that he had deserved to be honoured with the most ample honours and rewards, and that daily sustenance should be provided for him at public expense in the Prytaneum, which is held the greatest honour among the Greeks.

When Sulpicius had fallen silent at this, 'As though indeed,' said Crassus, 'there were any art of these very things of which Antonius has now long been speaking: there is a certain observation, as he himself said, of those things which avail in speaking; which, if it could make men eloquent, who would not be eloquent? For who could not learn these things either easily or at least in some way? But I think there is this force and this usefulness in these precepts, not that we be led by art to find what we should say, but that we may either be confident that those things which we attain by nature, by zeal, by exercise, are right, or understand that they are faulty, when we have learned to what they should be referred.

By this answer the judges were so inflamed that they condemned to death the most innocent of men; who, indeed, if he had been acquitted—which, by Hercules, even if it concerns us not at all, yet on account of the greatness of his talent I should wish—in what way could we endure those philosophers who now, when that man was condemned for no other fault except his ignorance of speaking, nevertheless say that the precepts of speaking ought to be sought from them? With whom I do not contend which is better or truer: I only say that this is one thing and that another, and that this can be supreme without that.

Wherefore, Caesar, I too ask this of you, that, if it seems good to you, you dispute about this whole kind of jesting what you think, lest perchance some part of speaking, since you so wished, seem to have been omitted in such an assembly and in so careful a discourse.' 'For my part,' said he, 'since you exact the contribution from a guest, Crassus, I will not bring it about that, if I shrink away, I give you some cause for refusing. Although I am often wont to wonder at the impudence of those who act gesture on the stage with Roscius looking on; for who can move himself, whose faults that man does not see? So I now, with Crassus listening, will first speak about wit, and will teach—a pig teaching the orator, as they say—him whom, when Catulus lately heard him, he said that others ought to be hay.'

For as to your having so vehemently embraced the civil law, Crassus, I see what you have done; even when you were speaking, I saw it: first, you devoted yourself to Scaevola, whom we all ought most deservedly to love for his singular sweetness; whose art, when you saw it was undowered and unadorned, you enriched and adorned it with the dowry of words; then, because you had spent more labour and toil upon it, since you had at home both the encourager and the master of that study, you feared, unless you exalted that art by your speech, lest you should have wasted your pains.

Then he said: 'Catulus was jesting, especially since he himself so speaks that he seems to be fed on ambrosia. But let us hear you, Caesar, that we may see the rest of Antonius.' And Antonius said: 'Very few things indeed remain to me; but yet, now wearied with the labour and the journey of my disputation, I will rest in Caesar's discourse as in a very opportune lodging.' 'And yet,' said Julius, 'you will say my hospitality is not too liberal; for I will thrust you and cast you out into the road as soon as you have tasted ever so little.

But I do not contend even with that art. Let it be as great as you wish it to be—for without controversy it is both great and widely extends and concerns many and has always been in the highest honour, and the most distinguished citizens even today preside over its study—but see, Crassus, lest, while you wish to adorn the knowledge of the civil law with a new and foreign ornament, you also despoil and strip it of its own granted and acknowledged ornament.

And, lest I detain you longer, I will very briefly set forth what I think about that whole kind. About laughter there are five things to be inquired: one, what it is; second, whence it is; third, whether it belongs to the orator to wish to move laughter; fourth, how far; fifth, what are the kinds of the ridiculous. And as for that first—what laughter itself is, in what way it is roused, where it is, in what manner it arises and so suddenly bursts forth that, wishing to hold it, we cannot, and how at the same moment it seizes the sides, the mouth, the veins, the eyes, the countenance—let Democritus see to that; for it does not pertain to this discourse, and, if it did pertain, I should yet not be ashamed to be ignorant of that which not even those knew who professed it.

For if you said that he who is a jurisconsult is therefore an orator, and likewise that he who is an orator is the same a jurisconsult, you would establish two noble arts, equal to one another and partners of the same dignity. But now you confess that the jurisconsult can exist without this eloquence about which we are inquiring, and that there have been very many such; but you deny that the orator can exist unless he has taken on that knowledge. Thus to you the jurisconsult is in himself nothing but a kind of cautious and shrewd quibbler, a crier of actions, a chanter of formulae, a catcher of syllables; but because the orator often uses the aid of law in causes, you have therefore joined that knowledge of law to eloquence as a little handmaid and attendant.

But the place and region, as it were, of the ridiculous—for that is next inquired—is contained in a certain baseness and deformity; for these things are laughed at, either alone or chiefly, which mark and designate some baseness, not basely. But—to come to that third point—it is plainly the orator's to move laughter; either because the very hilarity wins goodwill toward him by whom it has been roused; or because all admire the acuteness often placed in a single word, especially of one answering, sometimes also of one provoking; or because it breaks the adversary, hinders him, makes light of him, deters him, refutes him; or because it signifies that the orator himself is a polished man, that he is learned, that he is urbane; most of all because it mitigates and relaxes sadness and severity, and often loosens by a jest and laughter odious matters which are not easily dissolved by arguments.

But as for your having wondered at the impudence of those advocates who either, when they were ignorant of small things, professed great ones, or dared to handle in causes those things which were greatest in the civil law, when they did not know them and had never learned them—of both things the defence is easy and ready. For neither is it to be wondered at that he who does not know by what words a coemption is made should be able to defend the cause of that woman who has made a coemption; nor, if the science of steering a small ship and a great one is the same, can it be that he who does not know by what words an inheritance ought to be divided cannot conduct a cause for the dividing of an estate.

But how far the ridiculous is to be handled by the orator must be most diligently seen—which we had placed in the fourth place of inquiry. For neither conspicuous wickedness, joined with crime, nor again conspicuous misery, is laughed at when assailed: men wish the criminal to be wounded by some greater force than the ridiculous; they do not wish the wretched to be mocked, unless perchance they boast themselves; but most of all must the affection of men be spared, lest you rashly speak against those who are loved.

For as to your having brought forward the greatest centumviral causes as resting on law, which, pray, of those causes was there that could not have been most ornately pleaded by an eloquent man unskilled in law? In all which causes—as in that very cause of Manius Curius, which was lately pleaded by you, and in the dispute of Gaius Hostilius Mancinus, and in the case of that boy who had been born of another wife, no notice of divorce having been sent to the former—there was the highest disagreement about the law among the most skilled men: I ask, then, what knowledge of law helped the orator in these causes, when this jurisconsult here was about to come off the inferior, who was sustained not by his own art, but by another's—that is, not by knowledge of law, but by eloquence.

This moderation, then, must first be applied in jesting; and so those things are most easily made sport of which are worthy neither of great hatred nor of the greatest pity; wherefore all the material of the ridiculous is in those vices which are in the life of men who are neither beloved nor calamitous nor those who seem to be hurried off to punishment for a crime; and these things, prettily handled, are laughed at.

For my part, I have often heard this: that when Publius Crassus was a candidate for the aedileship, and the elder and now consular Servius Galba accompanied him, because he had betrothed Crassus's daughter to his son Gaius, a certain countryman came up to Crassus to consult him; and when he had drawn Crassus aside and laid his case before him, and had carried off an answer truer than suited to his own purpose, when Galba saw him downcast, he called him by name and asked on what matter he had consulted Crassus; and when he had heard it, and saw the man disturbed,

There is also in deformity and the vices of the body a pretty enough material for jesting; but we ask the same thing which in other matters is most to be asked—how far; in which not only is this enjoined, that nothing be said saltlessly, but also, even if you could say something most ridiculously, both must be avoided by the orator, lest the jest be either scurrile or mimic. What things of this kind are we shall the more easily understand when we come to the very kinds of the ridiculous. For there are two kinds of wit, of which one is handled by a thing, the other by a saying:

'with an anxious and preoccupied mind,' he said, 'I see Crassus answered you,' and then he himself took Crassus by the hand and said, 'Hark you, what came into your mind to answer thus?' Then that most skilled man confidently affirmed that the matter was as he had answered, and that there could be no doubt; but Galba, sporting variously and copiously, brought forward many comparisons and said many things for equity against law; and Crassus—though Crassus was in the number of the eloquent, but in no way Galba's equal—since he could not be his match in disputing, took refuge in authorities, and produced what he himself had said, written both in the books of his brother Publius Mucius and in the commentaries of Sextus Aelius, and yet conceded that Galba's argument seemed to him probable and well-nigh true.

by a thing, when sometimes something is narrated as a kind of little tale, as once you, Crassus, against Memmius, that he had eaten Largus's arm, when he had quarrelled with him at Tarracina about a sweetheart: a salty narrative, and yet feigned by yourself; you added a close: that all Tarracina then had inscribed on every wall the letters L. L. L. M. M.; when you asked what that was, a certain old townsman told you,

And yet those causes which are of such a kind that there can be no doubt about their law are not at all wont to be brought into court. Does anyone claim an inheritance under that will which a head of a family made before a son was born to him? No one; because it is agreed that a will is broken by the subsequent birth of an heir; therefore in this kind of law there are no trials: the orator, then, may with impunity be ignorant of all this part of uncontroverted law, which part is without doubt by far the greatest;

'Biting Memmius mangles Largus's arm (Lacerat Lacertum Largi Mordax Memmius).' You perceive how witty this kind is, how elegant, how oratorical, whether you have something true that you can narrate—which yet must be sprinkled with little lies—or whether you feign. But the virtue of this kind is, that you so set forth the deeds that the characters of him about whom you narrate, his speech, his looks, may all be expressed, so that to those who hear those things seem then to be done and to happen.

but in that law which is disputed among the most skilled, it is not difficult for the orator to find some authority for whatever side he shall defend; from whom, when he has received the javelins fitted with thongs, he will himself hurl them with the arms and strength of an orator. Unless indeed—I would say it with the good leave of this excellent man—you, Crassus, defended the cause of Manius Curius by the little books or precepts of your father-in-law Scaevola, and did not snatch up the patronage of equity and the defence of wills and of the wishes of the dead.

In a thing there is likewise the ridiculous which is wont to be taken from a certain distorted imitation, as the same Crassus: 'By your nobility, by your family!' What else was there in which the assembly laughed, except that imitation of countenance and voice? But when he said, 'By your statues!' and with arm extended even added something a little of gesture, we laughed more vehemently. Of this kind is that Roscian imitation of an old man: 'These things, Antipho, I sow for you, he says; it is old age, when I hear it.' And yet this whole thing is so ridiculous by its very kind, that it must be handled most cautiously; for it belongs to mimes and to mimics, if the imitation is excessive, as does obscenity. The orator ought to steal the imitation, so that he who hears may imagine more than he sees; let him likewise display his own ingenuousness and modesty by avoiding baseness of words and obscenity of things.

And in my opinion—for I often heard you and was present—you won over much the greater part of the verdicts by your wit and charm and most polished pleasantries, when you both mocked that excessive subtlety and wondered at the talent of Scaevola, who had discovered that one must be born before one dies; and when you gathered many things both from the laws and from decrees of the senate and from life and common speech, not only acutely but also ridiculously and wittily, where, if we followed the words and not the substance, nothing could be made out: and so the trial was full of merriment and gladness; in which what your practice of the civil law profited you, I do not understand; your excellent power of speaking, joined with the highest gaiety and grace, profited you.

These two, then, are the kinds of that ridiculous which is placed in a thing, which are proper to continuous wit, in which the characters of men are described and so portrayed that, either by some thing narrated, they are understood what they are, or, by an imitation briefly thrown in, are detected in some conspicuous vice fit for mockery.

That very Mucius, the defender of his father's law and, as it were, the champion of his own patrimony, what did he bring forward in that cause, when he spoke against you, that seemed drawn from the civil law? What law did he recite? What did he open up by speaking that had been too hidden for the unskilled? Surely all his speech was concerned with this—to maintain that the written word ought to have the most weight; but in this kind all boys are exercised under their masters, when in causes of this sort they are taught to defend now the written word, now equity.

But in a saying the ridiculous is that which is moved by a certain acuteness of a word or thought; but as in that former kind, whether of narration or of imitation, the likeness of mimes and mimics is to be avoided, so in this the scurrile railing of the orator must be greatly shunned. How, then, shall we distinguish your friend Granius, or my friend Vargula, from Crassus, from Catulus, from the rest? By Hercules, it does not come into my mind: for they are railing men; than Granius indeed no one is more railing. This, I suppose, first—that, as often as a saying can be said, we should not think it necessary to say it.

And, I suppose, in that cause of the soldier, if you had defended either the heir or the soldier, you would have had recourse to the Hostilian actions, not to your own force and oratorical faculty: but you, indeed, even if you were defending the will, would so plead that all the law of all wills would seem to rest upon that trial; or if you were pleading the soldier's cause, you would, as you are wont, by speaking have raised his father from the dead; you would have set him before our eyes; he would have embraced his son and, weeping, commended him to the centumviri; you would, by Hercules, have compelled the very stones to weep and lament, so that all that 'as the tongue shall have pronounced' would seem written not in the Twelve Tables, which you prefer to all libraries, but in a schoolmaster's lay.

A tiny witness came forward. 'May I question him?' said Philippus. Then the examiner, in haste, 'Only briefly.' Hereupon he, 'You will not complain: I shall question a very tiny one.' Ridiculous. But the judge Lucius Aurifex was sitting, himself shorter even than the witness: all the laughter was turned upon the judge; the whole thing seemed scurrile and ridiculous. Therefore those things which can fall upon men whom you would not wish, however pretty they be, are yet by their very kind scurrile;

For as to your accusing the indolence of young men, who do not first learn that art, the easiest of all—how easy it is, let those see who walk about so puffed up with the arrogance of that art, as if it were the most difficult of all; and then let yourself also see, who say that that art is easy, which you grant is not yet an art at all, but will some day, if anyone shall have learned another art, so that he can make this an art, then become an art; then, that it is full of delight—in which all remit to you that pleasure and suffer themselves to be deprived of it; nor is there anyone of them who, if something must now be learned by heart, would not prefer to learn the Teucer of Pacuvius than the Manilian laws of selling things for sale;

as that Appius, who wishes to be railing—and, by Hercules, is so—but sometimes sinks into this scurrile vice. 'I shall dine,' he said, 'at your house,' to this one-eyed friend of mine, Gaius Sextius; 'for I see there is room for one.' This is scurrile, both because he provoked without cause, and yet said that which would fit all one-eyed men; such things, because they are thought premeditated, are less laughed at: that of Sextius was excellent and extempore: 'Wash your hands,' he said, 'and dine.' A regard, then, for the time, and a moderation and temperance of the railing itself, and a rarity of sayings, will distinguish the orator from the buffoon; and that we speak with a cause, not that we may seem ridiculous, but that we may accomplish something, while they do it all day and without cause. For what did Vargula gain, when the candidate Aulus Sempronius had embraced him together with his brother Marcus, in saying, 'Boy, drive off the flies'? He sought a laugh, which in my opinion is the very slightest fruit of talent. We shall, then, moderate the time of speaking by prudence and weightiness; of which would that we had some art! But nature is mistress.

then, as to your thinking that out of love of country we ought to know the inventions of our ancestors, do you not see that the old laws have either grown old by their very antiquity, or have been abolished by new laws? But as to your thinking that men become good by the civil law, because by the laws both rewards are set before the virtues and punishments before the vices, for my part I used to think that virtue was imparted to men—if indeed it can be imparted by method—by instructing and persuading, not by threats and force and fear. For that very thing, indeed, how good it is to beware of evil, we can know even without the knowledge of law.

said he, 'and dine.' A regard, then, for the time, and a moderation and temperance of the railing itself, and a rarity of sayings, will distinguish the orator from the buffoon; and the fact that we speak with a cause, not that we may seem ridiculous but that we may accomplish something, while they do it all day and without cause. For what did Vargula gain, when the candidate Aulus Sempronius had embraced him together with his brother Marcus, in saying, 'Boy, drive off the flies'? He sought a laugh, which in my opinion is the very slightest fruit of talent. We shall, then, moderate the time of speaking by prudence and weightiness; of which would that we had some art! But nature is mistress.

But of myself, to whom alone you concede that I can satisfy causes without any knowledge of law, I answer you this, Crassus: that I never learned the civil law, nor yet ever, in those causes which I could defend in court, missed that knowledge; for it is one thing to be the artist of a certain kind and art, another to be in the common life and ordinary intercourse of men neither dull nor untrained.

Now let us set forth in summary the very kinds which most move laughter. Let this, then, be the first division: that what is wittily said has its wit sometimes in the thing, sometimes in the word; but that men are most delighted when the laughter is moved by thing and word conjoined. But remember this, that whatever topics I shall touch, whence the ridiculous is drawn, from those same topics weighty thoughts too can generally be drawn: so much only is the difference, that weightiness is placed in honourable and serious matters, jesting in slightly base and as it were deformed ones—as by the same words we can both praise a thrifty servant and, if he is worthless, jest. That old Neronian saying about a thievish servant is ridiculous: that he was the only one in whose house nothing was either sealed or shut up—which same thing is wont to be said of a good servant.

Which of us is free to go over our farms or to visit our country property either for the sake of profit or of delight? Yet no one lives so without eyes, so without mind, as to be wholly ignorant of what sowing and harvest are, what the pruning of trees and vines is, at what time of year or in what manner these things are done. If, then, some farm must be inspected, or something be entrusted to a steward about the cultivation of the land, or commanded to a bailiff, must the books of Mago the Carthaginian be thoroughly learned? Or can we be content with this common understanding? Why, then, can we not, in the civil law also—especially since we are worn out in causes and business and in the forum—be sufficiently instructed at least to this extent, that we do not seem to be foreigners and strangers in our own country?

But this is by the same words; all things are from the same topics. For as for what Spurius Carvilius's mother said—when he was lamed grievously from a wound received for the commonwealth, and on that account was ashamed to go out in public—'why do you not go out, my Spurius? As often as you take a step, so often let your virtues come into your mind,' that is noble and weighty: but what Glaucia said to the limping Calvinus, 'where is that old saying—"does he limp? Nay, this man halts!"'—that is ridiculous; and each is drawn from that which could be observed in lameness. 'What is more sluggish (ignavius) than this Navius?' said Scipio severely; but to a man of bad smell, 'I see I am being surrounded (circumventum) by you,' said Philippus rather ridiculously: but either kind is contained by the likeness of a word changed in a letter.

And if now some obscurer cause be brought to us, it would, I suppose, be difficult to confer with Scaevola here; although those very persons whose business it is bring to us everything consulted and inquired into. Or indeed, if there is a controversy about the matter itself, about boundaries, when we have come upon the spot, about deeds and accounts, do we necessarily learn thoroughly intricate and often difficult matters; but if statutes or the responses of skilled men must be learned, do we fear that, if from our youth we have less studied the civil law, we cannot learn these things? Does, then, the knowledge of the civil law profit the orator nothing? I cannot deny that any knowledge profits, especially him whose eloquence ought to be adorned with abundance of matter; but those things which are necessary for the orator are many and great and difficult, so that I would not wish to distract his industry into more studies.

Things said from ambiguity are thought even most pointed, but they are engaged not always in jesting, often even in weightiness. To that elder Africanus, adjusting a wreath to his head at a banquet, when it kept breaking, Publius Licinius Varus said: 'Do not wonder if it does not fit; for the head is big': both praiseworthy and honourable; but of the same kind is 'for Calvus it is enough that he says too little (parum).' Not to be long: there is no kind of jest from which serious and weighty things too may not be taken.

Who would deny that the orator needs, in this oratorical movement and posture, the gesture and grace of Roscius? Yet no one would advise young men zealous for speaking to labour in learning gesture after the manner of actors. What is so necessary to the orator as the voice? Yet, on my authority, no one zealous for speaking will, after the manner of the Greek tragedians, be a slave to the voice—men who both for several years declaim sitting, and daily, before they deliver, raise their voice gradually as they lie down, and the same, when they have pleaded, sitting, bring it back from the sharpest tone all the way to the deepest, and, as it were, gather it up. If we wished to do this, those whose causes we had undertaken would be condemned before we had recited, as often as is prescribed, the Paean or the hymn.

And this also must be noticed, that not all ridiculous things are witty. For what can be so ridiculous as a buffoon (sannio)? But he is laughed at by his very mouth, countenance, voice, in short by his very body; I can call him salty, and so, not that I should wish an orator to be of that kind, but a mime. Wherefore the first kind, which most of all moves laughter, is not ours: the morose, the superstitious, the suspicious, the boastful, the foolish: these very natures are laughed at, which characters we are wont to make sport of, not to sustain.

But if in gesture, which much helps the orator, and in voice, which alone most commends or sustains eloquence, we are not allowed to labour, and can only attain in each as much as the space of our daily task in this battle-line allows us, how much less must we descend to the occupation of thoroughly learning the civil law? Which can both be grasped in summary without instruction, and has this unlikeness to those other things, that voice and gesture cannot be taken up suddenly and snatched from elsewhere, while the usefulness of the law can be drawn out for any cause, however suddenly, either from the skilled or from books.

The second kind is in imitation, exceedingly ridiculous, but we are allowed to use it only stealthily, if ever, and in passing; otherwise it is by no means liberal; the third, the distortion of the mouth, is not worthy of us; the fourth, obscenity, is not only not worthy of the forum, but scarcely of the banquet of free men. So many things, then, being subtracted from this oratorical topic, the remaining wit is that which seems to be placed either in a thing, as I divided before, or in a word; for what, in whatever words you say it, is yet witty, is contained in the thing; what, the words being changed, loses its salt, has all its charm in the words.

And so those most eloquent men have, as assistants in causes, men skilled in law, though they themselves are most unskilled—those who, as was said by you a little while ago, are called pragmatici; in which respect ours have done altogether much better, in that they wished the laws and the law to be protected by the authority of most distinguished men. But yet this would not have escaped the Greeks, if they had thought it so necessary, to instruct the orator himself in the civil law, and not to give him a pragmaticus as a helper.

Ambiguities are among the first acute and placed in the word, not in the thing; but they do not often move great laughter; rather they are praised as prettily, as learnedly said; as in the case of that Titius, who, since he played at ball studiously and was at the same time thought to break the sacred statues by night, and his comrades, when he had not come to the field, sought him, was excused by Vespa Terentius, who said he had broken his arm; as that of Africanus, which is in Lucilius: 'What of Decius? Do you wish to make a little nut (nuculam) or to be pierced (confixum)?' said he:

For as to your saying that old age is rescued from solitude by the knowledge of the civil law, perhaps also by greatness of money; but we are inquiring not what is useful to us, but what is necessary for the orator. Although—since we take many things for our likeness of the orator from one artist—that same Roscius is wont to say that, the more years are added to him, the slower will he make the measures of the flute-player and the more relaxed the songs. But if he, bound by a certain fixed regulation of numbers and feet, yet devises something for the rest of old age, how much more easily can we, not relax our measures, but change them wholly?

as your friend, Crassus, Granius, 'it is not worth a sixth-part.' And if you ask, he who is called railing will most excel in this kind; but other things move greater laughter. Ambiguity in itself is indeed approved, as I said before, even most of all; for it seems the mark of a man of talent to be able to lead the force of a word into another sense than the rest take it; but it moves admiration rather than laughter, except sometimes when it falls upon some other kind of the ridiculous too, which kinds I will myself run through.

For it does not escape you, Crassus, how many and how various are the kinds of speaking—a thing which I scarcely know whether you were not the first to show, who now for a long time speak much more remissly and gently than you used to; and yet this gentleness of your most weighty discourse is no less approved than that highest force and vehemence: and there have been many orators, as we hear of that Scipio and Laelius, who carried through everything in a discourse a little more intense, never, like Servius Galba, contending with lungs or clamour. But if you now cannot or will not do this, do you fear lest your house, that of such a man and citizen, if it be not courted by litigious men, should be deserted by the rest? For my part, I am so far from that opinion that I not only do not think the support of old age is to be placed in the multitude of those who come to consult, but I look forward to that solitude which you fear as to a kind of haven. For I think that leisure is the most beautiful support of old age.
